\begin{theorem}[Global quotient and topology obstructions]
\hypertarget{tag-0374}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-obstructions}
For the established sphere \(X\) and its native radial fibre metrics,
take the admissible radial parameters \(T\) with
\(0<r_T=e^{-2\pi T}<\epsilon\), equivalently
\(T>-\log\epsilon/(2\pi)\) within that native admissible range.
The following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let \(r\geq1\), and let \(N\subset\Lambda^{\oplus r}\) be a primitive
kernel defining a connected fibrewise torus quotient over the full regular
base \(B^\circ\), or over a connected finite cover of \(B^\circ\).
Give the quotient the norm induced by the unrescaled Euclidean metric
on the original marked fibres.  Divergence of its quotient systole on
the radial cusp implies
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq r.
 \hypertarget{tag-037H}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-rank-bound}
\end{equation}
For two copies this excludes a full-base four-torus quotient with
diverging systole.  The \(S^{12}\) construction of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-S12-route} uses the quotient on the cusp and collapses
the exterior to the outer suspension pole.

\item The subgroup \(K_\Lambda\) is not a sub-local system over any
connected finite cover of \(B^\circ\), including covers obtained by
branching over the original singular values.  For an integer \(M>1\), the local
change \(t=s^M\) in the degree-\(M^2\) fibre cover cannot extend as a
connected cover of \(B\cong\mathbb P^1\) branched only at \(p_0\).
For \(M=1\), that base change and the local fibre cover are identities.

\item No map from \(X^2\) or \(X\wedge X\) to a fixed \(T^4\) retains on
a regular fibre the four characters of \(Q_T^2\).  No map from \(X^4\)
or \(X^{\wedge4}\) to a fixed \(T^4\) retains the four characters of
the four-circle quotient.  In either route, no map to a fixed \(S^4\)
restricts to the degree-one collapse of the indicated four-torus,
even at one regular fibre.  On the conical targets the exact restriction
maps in degrees \(k=1,4\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 j_T^*:H^k(\mathcal A^{\wedge2};\mathbb Z)&\longrightarrow
             H^k(Q_T^2;\mathbb Z),\\
 (k_T^{\mathcal B})^*:H^k(\mathcal B^{\wedge4};\mathbb Z)&\longrightarrow
             H^k(C_T^4;\mathbb Z),\\
 (k_T^{\mathcal C})^*:H^k(\mathcal C^{\wedge4};\mathbb Z)&\longrightarrow
             H^k(C_T^4;\mathbb Z);
\end{aligned}
\qquad\text{all three maps are zero.}
\]
Thus the four primitive character classes and their orientation product
do not extend as global classes on these conical targets.

\item The Cartesian products satisfy
\begin{equation}
 X^2\cong S^6\times S^6\not\simeq S^{12},\qquad
 X^4\cong(S^6)^4\not\simeq S^{24}.
 \hypertarget{tag-0378}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-products-not-spheres}
\end{equation}
The two- and four-fold synchronized fibre products have real dimensions
\(10\) and \(18\) over the regular base.  Their completed cusp fibres
are singular, and their total completions contain the singular loci
described in the proof.  The join homeomorphisms are
\begin{equation}
 X*X\cong S^{13},\qquad X^{*4}\cong S^{27}.
 \hypertarget{tag-036T}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-join-dimensions}
\end{equation}

\item Every connected unbranched finite cover of \(X\), \(X^r\) for
\(r\geq1\), \(X\wedge X\cong S^{12}\), or \(X^{\wedge4}\cong S^{24}\)
has degree one.  For \(M>1\), the local degree-\(M^2\) fibre cover cannot
be the restriction of such a cover; for \(M=1\) the identity extends
as the global identity.  The finite flat normal covers in
\cref{maps:src:C.1.5} have the explicit regular-base factorization and
integral-closure completion given below.

\item No smooth manifold homeomorphic to \(S^{12}\) or \(S^{24}\),
with any differentiable structure, admits an almost-complex structure.
In particular these smash sources cannot carry a compact complex
structure.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the native marking
\[
 (g,u,w,\delta)
 =(\widehat\gamma,\widehat u,\widehat w,\widehat\delta),\qquad
 K_\Lambda=\mathbb Z\langle w,\delta\rangle,\qquad
 L_\Lambda=\mathbb Z\langle u,w,\delta\rangle.
\]
On the positive radial ray the physical period matrix is
\[
 P_T=\begin{pmatrix}
 6\alpha&\eta&1&0\\
 6m&L&0&0\\
 c&\alpha&0&1\\
 -q&m&0&0
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Y_T=\begin{pmatrix}6m&L\\-q&m\end{pmatrix},
 \quad D_T=Lq+6m^2>0,
\]
where \(L=T+H\), \(q=L-B\), and the remaining coefficients are bounded.
The marking is \(x_T([a])=[P_Ta]\).  In particular
\(P_Tw=(1,0,0,0)\) and \(P_T\delta=(0,0,1,0)\), both of norm one.

\emph{The global rank bound.}
For a rank-zero quotient the conclusion is immediate.  For a positive
rank quotient its systole is the shortest nonzero period length.
For the primitive kernel \(N\), the quotient real space is
\[
 V_T=(\mathbb R^4)^r/
            P_T^{\oplus r}(N\otimes\mathbb R),
\]
with the infimum norm, and its period lattice is the image of
\(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N\).  Primitivity gives
\((N\otimes\mathbb R)\cap\Lambda^{\oplus r}=N\).
The image of each \(w_i\) and \(\delta_i\), when nonzero as a period
vector, has quotient length at most one.  The divergent systole forces
\begin{equation}
 K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\subset N.
 \hypertarget{tag-036U}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-kernel-contained}
\end{equation}

The left-deck matrices give
\[
 U=A_2M_0A_2^{-1}
   =\begin{pmatrix}
      1&0&0&0\\-6&1&-1&0\\0&0&1&0\\5&0&1&1
     \end{pmatrix}=I+L_0,\qquad L_0^2=0.
\]
Consequently, for every integer \(h\),
\[
 U^h=I+hL_0,\qquad
 U^h w=w-hu+h\delta,\qquad U^h\delta=\delta.
\]
The opposite loop has the exact word and matrix
\[
 H_*=A_2A_1=U^{-1}=I-L_0,\qquad
 U=A_2(A_1A_2)^{-1}A_2^{-1}=A_1^{-1}A_2^{-1}.
\]
Thus \(N_*=H_*-I=-L_0\) satisfies \(N_*^2=0\), and
\begin{equation}
 H_*^n w=w+n(u-\delta)\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z).
 \hypertarget{tag-036Q}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-finite-index-orbit}
\end{equation}
The matrix convention is fixed by
\((x,1)\sim(A^{-1}x,0)\): forward interval transport is the inverse
of the corresponding left-deck operator.  Invariance under either
operator is equivalent to invariance under its inverse.

For a finite-index based covering subgroup \(\mathcal H\), two nonnegative
powers of the loop with matrix \(U\) have the same \(\mathcal H\)-coset.
Their difference is a positive power in \(\mathcal H\).  Thus \(N\) is invariant
under \(U^h\) for some \(h>0\), including for a nonnormal base cover.
Applying \(U^h\) to \(w_i\in N\) gives \(hu_i\in N\); primitivity
then gives \(u_i\in N\).  Hence
\[
 \bigl(\mathbb Z\langle u,w,\delta\rangle\bigr)^{\oplus r}
 \subset N,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq r.
\]
On the original base the same inclusion also follows directly from
\(A_1w=u-w\).
A cover branched over the original singular values restricts to a
connected finite cover of \(B^\circ\), so this argument also applies there.

The bound is attained by \(N^\sharp=L_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\).
The first rows of \(A_1,A_2\) are \((1,0,0,0)\), so this kernel
is invariant and its quotient has rank \(r\).  The dual character and
the native arclength map are
\[
 P_T^{-{\mathsf T}}e_\gamma
   =(0,m/D_T,0,-L/D_T)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 \chi_{\gamma,T}([P_Ta])=[a_g]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,
\]
\[
 \ell_T=\frac{D_T}{\sqrt{L^2+m^2}},\qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}=\vartheta_T\circ\chi_{\gamma,T},\qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}([P_Ta])=[\ell_Ta_g]\in C_T.
\]
The real covector \(\ell_TP_T^{-{\mathsf T}}e_\gamma\) has norm one
and kernel \(P_T(L_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)\) in each factor, proving the
quotient isometry.  Equivalently, for
\(b_{\min}=-am(6L-q)/(L^2+m^2)\),
\[
 \|Y_T(a,b)\|^2
 =\frac{a^2D_T^2}{L^2+m^2}+(L^2+m^2)(b-b_{\min})^2.
\]
Since \(Y_T=TB_0+E_T\), with
\(B_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\)
orthogonal and \(\|E_T\|\leq C\),
minimizing over the kernel gives systole at least \(T-C\).
This uses the original quotient norm throughout.

\emph{The local quotient and the base-cover obstruction.}
The cusp map is
\((t,\bar\pi_t):N_0\setminus W\to D_0^*\times\overline T^2\),
with \(\pi_T=\iota_T\bar\pi_T\).  Its map to the suspension is
\[
 c_{\mathcal A}(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 [|t|,t/|t|,\bar\pi_t(x)],&0<|t|<\epsilon,\\
 v_0,&x\in W,\\
 v_\epsilon,&x\notin\operatorname{int}N_0.
 \end{cases}
\]
The angular torus is compact, so every neighborhood of either collapsed
endpoint contains a uniform radial collar.  This proves continuity at
both ends; the middle formula is continuous by the cusp quotient.
With the source basepoint in \(W\), the exact restriction is
\[
 (c_{\mathcal A}\wedge c_{\mathcal A})|_{F_T^2}
      =j_T\circ(\pi_T\times\pi_T).
\]
Thus the \(S^{12}\) map uses the cusp quotient and the specified
exterior collapse.

For every \(h>0\), \(U^hw\notin K_\Lambda\).  The same finite-index
power argument proves that \(K_\Lambda\) never becomes a sub-local
system over a finite full-base cover.  Its planes
\(\operatorname{span}(\delta,w-hu)\) are pairwise distinct:
their projections to the \((u,w)\)-plane have coefficients \((-h,1)\).

For each positive integer \(M\), the finite-index cover lattice is
related to this kernel by the exact diagram
\[
\begin{array}{ccccccccc}
0&\longrightarrow&MK_\Lambda&\longrightarrow&
 \Lambda_M&\longrightarrow&\Lambda/K_\Lambda&\longrightarrow&0\\
&&\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow&&\big\Vert\\
0&\longrightarrow&K_\Lambda&\longrightarrow&
 \Lambda&\longrightarrow&\Lambda/K_\Lambda&\longrightarrow&0,
\end{array}
\quad
\Lambda_M=\mathbb Z\langle g,u,Mw,M\delta\rangle.
\]
The two downward maps are inclusions.  On tori they give the
degree-\(M^2\) map
\(\mathbb R^4/\Lambda_M\to\mathbb R^4/\Lambda\), with identity on
the long quotient.  In the basis \(S_M=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,M,M)\),
\[
 M_0^MS_M=S_MM_0,\qquad
 S_M^{-1}A_2S_Mu=(0,0,1/M,0)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
This proves the local changed-base compatibility and the failure on
the original full base for \(M>1\).  A congruence base subgroup does
preserve \(\Lambda_M\), since
\[
 S_M^{-1}(I+MB)S_M
 =\begin{pmatrix}I+MB_{11}&M^2B_{12}\\
                  B_{21}&I+MB_{22}\end{pmatrix},
\]
and the same formula applies to the inverse.  These explicit maps
retain the separate finite-index and kernel statements.

A connected compact base cover branched only at \(p_0\) restricts,
after removing the finite inverse image of \(p_0\), to a connected
unbranched cover of \(\mathbb P^1\setminus\{p_0\}\cong\mathbb C\).
That punctured source is connected, and the target is simply connected,
so its degree is one.  Thus the local change \(t=s^M\) has the stated
obstruction precisely for \(M>1\).  At \(M=1\), \(S_1=I\) and the
base-change isomorphism \(y\mapsto(y,f_0(y))\), inverse to projection,
identifies the local factors with identities.  The global identity
of \(\mathbb P^1\) extends the base map and has empty branch locus.

\emph{Character and orientation restrictions.}
The marked identifications are
\(\iota_T([a])=[Y_Ta]\) and
\(\vartheta_T([a])=[\ell_Ta]\), with inverses induced by \(Y_T^{-1}\)
and division by \(\ell_T\), respectively.
The fixed-fibre quotient maps and their sections are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \pi_T([P_Ta])&=[Y_T(a_g,a_u)],&
 \sigma_Q([Y_T(a,b)])&=[P_T(a,b,0,0)],\\
 \pi_{\gamma,T}([P_Ta])&=[\ell_Ta_g],&
 \sigma_C([\ell_Ta])&=[P_T(a,0,0,0)].
\end{aligned}
\]
They are well defined under integral representative changes and satisfy
\(\pi_T\sigma_Q=\operatorname{id}\) and
\(\pi_{\gamma,T}\sigma_C=\operatorname{id}\).
Under \(\iota_T^{-1}\) on each \(Q_T\) factor and \(\vartheta_T^{-1}\)
on each circle factor, the four primitive character pullbacks are
\[
 (g_1^*,u_1^*,g_2^*,u_2^*)\quad\text{and}\quad
 (g_1^*,g_2^*,g_3^*,g_4^*),
\]
respectively.  Their exterior products evaluate to one on
\(\sigma_Q^2\) and \(\sigma_C^4\), so they are nonzero.
In particular, let \(\omega_T=(\iota_T^{-1})^*(x_1\smile x_2)\),
where \(x_1,x_2\) are the ordered primitive characters of \(T^2\).
This is the positive integral orientation class of \(Q_T\), and
\begin{equation}
 (\pi_T\times\pi_T)^*(\omega_T\times\omega_T)
 =g_1^*\smile u_1^*\smile g_2^*\smile u_2^*
 \ne0\quad\text{in }H^4(F_T^2;\mathbb Z).
 \hypertarget{tag-036P}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-fibre-H4-nonzero}
\end{equation}

For each listed product or smash source \(Z\),
\[
 H^1(Z;\mathbb Z)=H^4(Z;\mathbb Z)=0.
\]
Write \(i_T:F_T\to X\) for the fibre inclusion and
\(q_{X,r}:X^r\to X^{\wedge r}\) for the source smash quotient.
The two-torus route uses \(i_T^2\) and \(q_{X,2}\circ i_T^2\);
the four-circle route uses \(i_T^4\) and \(q_{X,4}\circ i_T^4\).
Composing these maps with \(\sigma_Q^2\) or \(\sigma_C^4\) gives
the corresponding section-torus restrictions.
Hence the pullbacks of the four characters
of any fixed \(T^4\) map restrict to zero.  A degree-one collapse of the
target four-torus pulls the orientation generator of \(S^4\) back to
the exterior product just computed, with the chosen positive
orientations.  Its pullback to the section torus has evaluation one.
Reversing the sphere orientation multiplies this class and its
evaluation by \(-1\), so both choices are nonzero, whereas restriction
of any global degree-four class from \(Z\) is zero.
This proves both nonextension assertions,
also when the restriction is taken directly along the section torus.

For the three conical targets, replace every \(r_T\) in \(j_T\),
\(k_T^{\mathcal B}\), or \(k_T^{\mathcal C}\) by \((1-s)r_T\),
\(0\leq s\leq1\), leaving all angular coordinates fixed.
These are continuous homotopies in the literal radial quotient
presentations.  At \(s=1\) each factor is its radial-zero basepoint,
so each smash map is constant.  Their positive-degree cohomology
restrictions factor through the zero groups of a point.  This proves
the displayed zero maps in degrees one and four.

\emph{Products, synchronized products and joins.}
Choose a based homeomorphism \(X\to S^6\).  Factor inclusions and
projections give \(H_6((S^6)^r;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^r\);
the integral K\"unneth formula has Poincar\'e polynomial \((1+t^6)^r\).
For four factors the groups in degrees \(6,12,18\) therefore have
ranks \(4,6,4\).  For two factors the degree-six rank is two.
The corresponding sphere groups vanish, so an induced homology
isomorphism from either product to its named sphere is impossible.
The source smash homeomorphism is obtained by identifying each based
\(S^6\) with \(\mathbb R^6\cup\{\infty\}\): retain the ordered Euclidean
tuple off the fat wedge and send its collapsed class to infinity.
Its inverse retains finite tuples and sends infinity to the fat wedge.
Continuity at infinity follows because a neighborhood there has compact
complement in the ordered Euclidean product.  The resulting continuous
bijection is a homeomorphism between compact Hausdorff spaces, giving
\(X^{\wedge r}\cong S^{6r}\).

Over the regular base, the synchronized product has coordinates
\((t,z_{11},z_{12},\ldots,z_{r1},z_{r2})\), hence real dimension \(4r+2\).
At two cusp double points the local equation is
\[
 x_1y_1=x_2y_2,
\]
with two further complex coordinates free.  Its complex dimension is
five and its tangent dimension at the crossing is six.  With two
additional smooth factors the equations are
\[
 x_1y_1=x_2y_2,\qquad t_3=x_1y_1,\qquad t_4=x_1y_1.
\]
Eliminating \(t_3,t_4\) gives the same quadric node times six free
complex coordinates, with dimension nine and tangent dimension ten.
These are actual singular loci of the two completed products.
The cusp fibres \(W^r\) themselves contain products of \(xy=0\)
and are singular, while the regular-base products are smooth.

The join map is
\[
 [x,y,t]\longmapsto
       \bigl(\sqrt{1-t}\,x,\sqrt t\,y\bigr)\in S^{13}.
\]
Its inverse uses \(t=\|v_2\|^2\) and the normalized nonzero blocks;
the endpoint relation discards the undefined zero block.  For four
factors the map uses simplex weights and has formula
\[
 [(\lambda_i,x_i)_{i=1}^4]\longmapsto
             (\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,x_i)_{i=1}^4\in S^{27}.
\]
The inverse has \(\lambda_i=\|v_i\|^2\) and
\(x_i=v_i/\|v_i\|\) on nonzero blocks.  At zero weights the join
relation removes that coordinate.  These continuous bijections are
homeomorphisms by compactness and Hausdorffness.

\emph{The global covers and their finite normal counterparts.}
The products and smash sources above are simply connected.  For a
connected unbranched cover, choose one point over a basepoint and lift
paths from it.  Simple connectivity makes the endpoint independent of
the path.  Covering charts make this assignment continuous, and
connectedness makes it the two-sided inverse of the cover.  Thus its
degree is one, including every finite cover in the statement.

For the construction of \cref{maps:src:C.1.5}, let its integer cover
parameter be \(N\geq1\), and write
\[
 \Gamma=\Lambda\rtimes F(\rho_1,\rho_2),\quad
 G_N=\langle(A_1\bmod N,-1\bmod N),(A_2\bmod N,0)\rangle,
\]
and let \(b_N:F\to G_N\) be the displayed base homomorphism.
The subgroup defining its regular cover has normal form
\(K_N=\Lambda_N\rtimes\ker b_N\).
Indeed its finite quotient requires trivial \(G_N\) coordinate and
a translation in the long two-generator submodule modulo \(N\).
Let \(\widetilde B^\circ\to B^\circ\) be the universal base cover.
In the common vector cover \(\widetilde B^\circ\times\mathbb C^2\)
the exact factorization is
\[
 \frac{\widetilde B^\circ\times\mathbb C^2}{\Lambda_N\rtimes\ker b_N}
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{\widetilde B^\circ\times\mathbb C^2}{\Lambda\rtimes\ker b_N}
       =X^\circ\times_{B^\circ}B_N^\circ
 \longrightarrow X^\circ.
\]
Both maps are induced by the identity on the vector cover; their
degrees are \(N^2\) and \(|G_N|\).
For a local component subgroup \(S\leq\mathbb Z^k\), choose
\(m\mathbb Z^k\subset S\).  The completion uses \(x_i=z_i^m\)
and quotient by \(S/m\mathbb Z^k\).  Its invariant algebra is the
integral closure in the given cover's meromorphic-function sheaf.
The unique local closures glue to the finite flat normal map \(Y\to X\).
On its selected cusp component the map is
\((s_v,\zeta_v)\mapsto(Ns_v,N\zeta_v)\), with
\(NZ_N(s_v)=Z(Ns_v)\), image lattice \(\Lambda_N\), and base
generator \(\rho_0^N\).
At \(N=1\) these maps and the integral closure are identities.
For \(N>1\) the connected completed map has degree
\(N^2|G_N|>1\); the preceding path-lifting inverse excludes its being
globally unbranched.  Its failure occurs over the deleted divisor,
since its restriction over \(X^\circ\) is a covering.

\emph{Almost-complex structures.}
The Borel--Serre proposition and its following remark exclude an
almost-complex structure for every differentiable structure on
\(S^{2n}\) when \(n\geq4\)
\cite[\S15, Proposition~15.1 and the following remark,
p.~434]{BorelSerre1953}.
To apply this precise scope, let \(h:M\to S^{2n}\) be a homeomorphism
from a smooth manifold \(M\).  Transport its smooth charts
\((V,\phi)\) to \((h(V),\phi\circ h^{-1})\).  In this transported
smooth structure \(h\) is a diffeomorphism, and an almost-complex
endomorphism \(J\) on \(TM\) transports to
\(dh\circ J\circ dh^{-1}\) on the sphere.
For \(2n=12,24\), the resulting \(n=6,12\) are both in the cited
range, which excludes \(J\).
Finally, multiplication by \(i\) on each holomorphic coordinate
tangent space is preserved by holomorphic transition derivatives;
it gives a global endomorphism with square \(-I\).
Every compact complex structure claimed here would therefore give
the excluded almost-complex structure.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimality within the native connected torus-quotient class]
\hypertarget{tag-0375}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-optimal-exponents}
\StatementRecord{wb:cusp-cone-optimal-exponents}{proved}{0375}{the definitions and constructions stated in the proof}

Consider only native connected fibrewise torus quotients of copies of the
original marked fibres, and equip every such quotient with the induced,
unscaled Euclidean quotient metric.

\begin{enumerate}
\item For a native connected torus quotient of \(r\) copies over the
punctured cusp, if the quotient systole tends to infinity on the positive
radial ray, then its lattice rank is at most \(2r\).  A rank-four quotient
therefore requires \(r\geq2\).  Equality is attained for \(r=2\) by
\[
 (\Lambda/K_\Lambda)^{\oplus2},
 \qquad K_\Lambda=
 \mathbb Z\langle\widehat w,\widehat\delta\rangle,
\]
whose physical period lattice is
\[
 L_T^{(12)}=\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T)\mathbb Z^4.
\]
The corresponding smash source is
\(X^{\wedge2}\cong S^{12}\).

\item For a native connected torus quotient of \(r\) copies over the full
regular base, or over a finite cover of that base, radial divergence of the
quotient systole forces its lattice rank to be at most \(r\).  A rank-four
quotient therefore requires \(r\geq4\).  Equality is attained by the four
copies of the full-monodromy-invariant character \(\chi_\gamma\); on the
radial fibre its period lattice is
\[
 L_T^{(24)}=\ell_T\mathbb Z^4,
 \qquad
 \ell_T=T+H-B+O(T^{-1}),
\]
and the corresponding smash source is
\(X^{\wedge4}\cong S^{24}\).
\end{enumerate}

Thus, among precisely these native connected torus quotients with their
induced unscaled marked Euclidean metrics, \(S^{12}\) is the smallest smash
sphere produced by the cusp-local rank-two quotient, and \(S^{24}\) is the
smallest smash sphere produced by a quotient which survives the full
regular-base monodromy.  No optimality is asserted here among arbitrary
continuous quotient maps or after a \(T\)-dependent rescaling of the metric.
\end{theorem}



\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item For \(r\) copies, every element of
\[
 K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}
 =\mathbb Z\langle\widehat w,\widehat\delta\rangle^{\oplus r}
\]
has uniformly bounded physical length on the radial cusp.  Let
\(N\subset\Lambda^{\oplus r}\) be a primitive sublattice defining a
connected torus quotient.  If some \(v\in K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\) had
nonzero class in \(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N\), that nonzero quotient period
would have quotient norm at most the original norm of \(v\), uniformly in
\(T\).  The quotient systole could not diverge.  Hence
\[
 K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\subset N,
\]
and
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)
 \leq 4r-2r=2r.
\]
For \(r=2\), the primitive kernel \(K_\Lambda^{\oplus2}\) attains this
bound.  The cusp monodromy is the identity modulo \(K_\Lambda\), so the
quotient descends over the punctured cusp.  Its radial lattice is exactly
\(\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T)\mathbb Z^4\), and
\[
 \operatorname{sys}(L_T^{(12)})
 =\operatorname{sys}(Y_T\mathbb Z^2)\geq T-C\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

\item For a quotient over the full regular base, monodromy invariance gives a
stronger bound.  Since \(\widehat w\in N\) and
\[
 A_1\widehat w=\widehat u-\widehat w,
\]
one has \(\widehat u\in N\).  Together with
\(\widehat w,\widehat\delta\in N\), this places the rank-three lattice
\[
 \mathbb Z\langle\widehat u,\widehat w,
 \widehat\delta\rangle^{\oplus r}
\]
inside \(N\), and hence
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq r.
\]
The same conclusion holds after a finite base cover.  Indeed, if
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{mon}}\) is the corresponding finite-index monodromy
subgroup and \(G_*=A_2A_1=I+N_*\), then \(N_*^2=0\), and
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{mon}}\) contains \(G_*^m\) for
some \(m>0\).  The exact orbit formula
\[
 G_*^m\widehat w
 =\widehat w+m(\widehat u-\widehat\delta)
\]
implies \(m\widehat u\in N\); primitivity of \(N\) implies
\(\widehat u\in N\).

\item The invariant character \(\chi_\gamma\) has precisely the complementary
rank-one quotient in each copy.  The full-base construction, including the
two finite Seifert fillings and the cone at the unipotent cusp, proves that
four copies attain rank four.  Finally, after choosing the based
diffeomorphism \(X\cong_{\mathrm{diff}}S^6\) already reconstructed in this
workbench,
\(X^{\wedge r}\cong(S^6)^{\wedge r}\cong S^{6r}\), which gives the two
claimed sphere dimensions.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimality within the native connected torus-quotient class]
\hypertarget{tag-0375}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-optimal-exponents}
Let \(r\geq1\) be an integer.  Consider connected fibrewise torus quotients
of \(r\) copies of the original marked fibres.  Their kernels are primitive
integral sub-local systems \(N\subset\Lambda^{\oplus r}\), constant in the
marking along a lifted radial ray.  Give every quotient the metric induced
by the original, unscaled Euclidean product metric.  Use the native
admissible parameters \(T\) with
\[
 0<r_T=e^{-2\pi T}<\epsilon,
 \qquad T>-\frac{\log\epsilon}{2\pi},
\]
and take the limit \(T\to+\infty\) within that range.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Over the punctured cusp, divergence of the quotient systole forces
\(\operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq2r\).
A rank-four quotient therefore requires \(r\geq2\).  The least value
\(r=2\) is attained by the primitive kernel
\[
 K_\Lambda^{\oplus2},\qquad
 K_\Lambda=\mathbb Z\langle\widehat w,\widehat\delta\rangle,
\]
whose physical quotient period lattice is
\[
 L_T^{(12)}=\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T)\mathbb Z^4.
\]
Its systole equals \(\operatorname{sys}(Y_T\mathbb Z^2)\) and tends
to infinity.  The associated compact sphere source is
\(X^{\wedge2}\cong S^{12}\).

\item Over the full regular base \(B^\circ\), or over any connected finite
cover of \(B^\circ\) of positive degree, divergence of the quotient
systole forces
\(\operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq r\).
A rank-four quotient therefore requires \(r\geq4\).  The least value
\(r=4\) is attained already over \(B^\circ\) by four copies of the
full-monodromy-invariant character \(\chi_\gamma\), and hence also after
pullback to each such cover.  On the radial fibre the metric quotient is
given by \(\vartheta_T\circ\chi_{\gamma,T}\), where
\[
 \vartheta_T:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\longrightarrow
 C_T=\mathbb R/\ell_T\mathbb Z,\qquad [a]\longmapsto[\ell_Ta].
\]
Its physical product period lattice and systole are
\[
 L_T^{(24)}=\ell_T\mathbb Z^4,\qquad
 \operatorname{sys}(L_T^{(24)})=\ell_T
 =T+H-B+O(T^{-1}).
\]
The associated compact source of the original sphere construction is
\(X^{\wedge4}\cong S^{24}\).
\end{enumerate}
Thus the least sphere dimensions obtained from these original
\(r\)-fold smash sources and rank-four quotients are \(12\) in the cusp
class and \(24\) in the full-base class, with the stated metrics.
These minima concern precisely the specified native quotients; no
optimality assertion is made for arbitrary continuous quotient maps
or for metrics rescaled by a \(T\)-dependent factor.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write
\[
 (g,u,w,\delta)
 =(\widehat\gamma,\widehat u,\widehat w,\widehat\delta),\qquad
 L_\Lambda=\mathbb Z\langle u,w,\delta\rangle.
\]
In physical coordinate order
\((\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_1,
  \operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_2)\), the native marking is
\[
 x_T([a])=[P_Ta],\qquad
 P_T=\begin{pmatrix}
 6\alpha&\eta&1&0\\
 6m&L&0&0\\
 c&\alpha&0&1\\
 -q&m&0&0
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Y_T=\begin{pmatrix}6m&L\\-q&m\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(L=T+H\), \(q=L-B\),
\(D_T=\det Y_T=Lq+6m^2>0\), and the residual coefficients are bounded
on a sufficiently small radial tail.

\emph{The quotient and its character lattice.}
For a primitive kernel \(N\), put \(N_{\mathbb R}=N\otimes\mathbb R\).
The physical quotient real space and its period lattice are
\[
 V_{N,T}=(\mathbb R^4)^r/P_T^{\oplus r}N_{\mathbb R},
 \qquad
 \bigl\{[P_T^{\oplus r}a]:a\in\Lambda^{\oplus r}\bigr\}.
\]
The map
\[
 (\Lambda^{\oplus r}\otimes\mathbb R)/N_{\mathbb R}
 \longrightarrow V_{N,T},\qquad
 [a]\longmapsto[P_T^{\oplus r}a]
\]
has inverse induced by \((P_T^{\oplus r})^{-1}\).
Primitivity gives
\(N_{\mathbb R}\cap\Lambda^{\oplus r}=N\), so the displayed period
lattice is exactly \(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N\).  The torus quotient map
is induced by this real quotient; its connected kernel is
\((P_T^{\oplus r}N_{\mathbb R})/(P_T^{\oplus r}N)\).
Its metric is the infimum of the original product norm over each
real coset.

Pullback along the lattice quotient identifies its character lattice
with the integral annihilator
\[
 N^\perp=\{a\in(\Lambda^{\oplus r})^*:a(N)=0\}.
\]
In physical coordinates the character is
\([y]\mapsto a((P_T^{\oplus r})^{-1}y)\pmod{\mathbb Z}\).
A basis of \(N\) extends to an integral basis of
\(\Lambda^{\oplus r}\): lift a basis of the free quotient and use it
together with a basis of \(N\).  The corresponding dual basis proves
\[
 \operatorname{rank}N^\perp
 =\operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N),
 \qquad \operatorname{Ann}(N^\perp)=N
\]
over \(\mathbb Z\).
Rank zero satisfies both asserted upper bounds immediately.  For
positive rank, the systole is the least length of a nonzero quotient
period.

\emph{The cusp bound and its attainment.}
The vectors \(P_Tw=(1,0,0,0)\) and
\(P_T\delta=(0,0,1,0)\) have length one.  A nonzero quotient image of
any \(w_i\) or \(\delta_i\) therefore has length at most one.
Every fixed integral combination of these vectors is uniformly
bounded by the sum of the absolute values of its coefficients.
Divergent systole forces
\[
 K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\subset N,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq2r.
\]
This argument includes kernels that mix the factors.

Projection to the two imaginary coordinates has kernel
\(P_T(K_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)=
\mathbb R\langle(1,0,0,0),(0,0,1,0)\rangle\).
It is the orthogonal quotient projection and gives the exact
isometry
\[
 F_T/K_T\longrightarrow Q_T=\mathbb R^2/Y_T\mathbb Z^2,\qquad
 [P_Ta]\longmapsto[Y_T(a_g,a_u)],
 \quad
 K_T=P_T(K_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)/P_TK_\Lambda.
\]
The marked identification
\(\iota_T:(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2\to Q_T\) is
\([a]\mapsto[Y_Ta]\), with inverse induced by \(Y_T^{-1}\).
The fixed-fibre section
\([Y_T(a,b)]\mapsto[P_T(a,b,0,0)]\) is well defined and is a right
inverse to the quotient.

The cusp monodromy sends \(g\) to \(g-\delta\), \(u\) to \(u+w\),
and fixes \(w,\delta\); its specified affine drift is zero.
It therefore induces the identity on \(\Lambda/K_\Lambda\), so this
quotient descends over the entire punctured cusp.
Write
\[
 Y_T=T\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
       +E_T,\qquad
 E_T=\begin{pmatrix}6m&H\\B-H&m\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first matrix is orthogonal and \(\|E_T\|\leq C_E\) on a radial
tail.  Hence
\(\|Y_Tv\|\geq(T-C_E)\|v\|\) for every real \(v\) and \(T>C_E\).
For \(r=2\), the product metric gives
\[
 \operatorname{sys}\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T)\mathbb Z^4\bigr)
 =\operatorname{sys}(Y_T\mathbb Z^2)\geq T-C_E.
\]
Indeed a nonzero product vector has a nonzero component of at least
the single-factor systole, and a shortest single-factor vector placed
in one component attains that length.
This proves the first bound and its sharpness in the unscaled metric.

\emph{The full-base bound, including finite covers.}
For the original base, the exact identity
\(A_1w=u-w\), together with invariance of \(N\) and
\(w_i,\delta_i\in N\), gives \(u_i\in N\) for each factor.
For a finite cover use the left-deck word
\[
 G_*=A_2A_1=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&0\\
 6&1&1&0\\
 0&0&1&0\\
 -5&0&-1&1
 \end{pmatrix}
 =I+N_*,\qquad N_*^2=0.
\]
Let \(\Gamma'\) be the subgroup of \(\pi_1(B^\circ)\) defining the
connected cover, of index \(d_{\mathrm{base}}\geq1\).
Among the \(d_{\mathrm{base}}+1\) right cosets represented by the
first \(d_{\mathrm{base}}+1\) nonnegative powers of a loop with this
matrix, two coincide.  Their exponent difference gives an integer
\(1\leq h\leq d_{\mathrm{base}}\) whose loop power belongs to \(\Gamma'\).
No normality assumption is used.  Write \(\rho\) for the monodromy
representation.  The image of \(\Gamma'\) in the
monodromy image has finite index as well: the map of right-coset
sets \(\Gamma'\backslash\pi_1(B^\circ)\to
\rho(\Gamma')\backslash\rho(\pi_1(B^\circ))\) induced by \(\rho\) is onto.

The power formula gives
\[
 G_*^h=I+hN_*,
 \qquad G_*^hw=w+h(u-\delta).
\]
In each factor this puts \(hu_i\) in \(N\).  Since
\(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N\) is torsion free, it follows that \(u_i\in N\).
Consequently
\[
 L_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\subset N,
 \qquad \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq r.
\]
Equivalently, a covector already annihilating \(K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\)
has rows \((a_i,b_i,0,0)\), and the exact dual action is
\[
 (a_i,b_i,0,0)G_*^h=(a_i+6hb_i,b_i,hb_i,0).
\]
Invariance of \(N^\perp\) forces \(hb_i=0\), hence \(b_i=0\);
the integral double-annihilator identity gives the same inclusion.
For the clutch convention \((x,1)\sim(A^{-1}x,0)\), forward transport
uses the inverse matrix.  The equality \(AN=N\) is equivalent to
\(A^{-1}N=N\), and the covering subgroup contains inverse loops,
so the calculation applies with that convention as well.
A compact base cover branched over the original singular values
restricts to such a connected cover on the regular locus.
The radial metric there is the pullback of the original metric with
\(T=-\log|t|/(2\pi)\).

\emph{The attaining circle quotient and its metric.}
The primitive row \(\gamma=(1,0,0,0)\) satisfies
\(\gamma A_1=\gamma A_2=\gamma\).  Its kernel in \(\Lambda\) is
\(L_\Lambda\), and the quotient isomorphism
\(\Lambda/L_\Lambda\to\mathbb Z\) is induced by \(\gamma\), with
inverse \(n\mapsto[ng]\).
For an affine transition \(a\mapsto Aa+b\), its circle coordinate
changes by
\(\gamma(Aa+b)=\gamma(a)+\gamma(b)\).
These are the actual transition maps of the full-base circle
quotient bundle, and they pull back to every finite cover.

On a radial fibre,
\[
 d_T=P_T^{-T}\gamma^T
   =\left(0,\frac{m}{D_T},0,-\frac{L}{D_T}\right)^T,
 \qquad
 \ell_T=\frac{1}{\|d_T\|}
        =\frac{D_T}{\sqrt{L^2+m^2}}>0.
\]
Thus
\[
 \chi_{\gamma,T}([y])=[\langle d_T,y\rangle]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}:=\vartheta_T\circ\chi_{\gamma,T},
 \qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}([P_Ta])=[\ell_Ta_g].
\]
The inverse of \(\vartheta_T\) is \([s]\mapsto[s/\ell_T]\).
The covector \(\ell_Td_T\) has norm one and kernel
\(P_T(L_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)\).  Its scalar projection identifies
the quotient line isometrically with \(\mathbb R\), and sends its
period lattice to \(\ell_T\mathbb Z\).  The least-norm lift of a
scalar \(s\) is \(s\ell_Td_T\), of norm \(|s|\).
Equivalently, eliminating the \(u\)-coordinate from
\(G=Y_T^TY_T\) gives
\[
 G_{11}-\frac{G_{12}^2}{G_{22}}
 =\frac{(\det Y_T)^2}{L^2+m^2}=\ell_T^2.
\]
The four unit covectors in the four factors have disjoint supports.
Their product quotient therefore has exactly the lattice
\(\ell_T\mathbb Z^4\) and systole \(\ell_T\).

Put \(R_T=\sqrt{L^2+m^2}\).  On the tail where \(L>0\),
rationalization gives the exact identity
\[
 \ell_T-(L-B)=
 \frac{m^2}{R_T}
 \left(6-\frac{L-B}{R_T+L}\right).
\]
Boundedness of \(m,H,B\), and \(L=T+H\), make its right side
\(O(T^{-1})\).  This estimate needs no limit for those bounded
coefficients.  For \(m=0\) the identity is exactly
\(\ell_T=L-B\) on that tail.  It follows that
\(\ell_T=T+H-B+O(T^{-1})\to\infty\).

\emph{Attained minima and compact sphere maps.}
The inequalities for rank four give \(r\geq2\) and \(r\geq4\),
and the constructed quotients attain the two endpoints.
For \(r>2\) in the cusp class one may retain the first two
quotients using
\(K_\Lambda^{\oplus2}\oplus\Lambda^{\oplus(r-2)}\).
For \(r>4\) in the full-base class use
\(L_\Lambda^{\oplus4}\oplus\Lambda^{\oplus(r-4)}\).
At the minimal values the kernels are forced: \(N/K_\Lambda^{\oplus2}\),
respectively \(N/L_\Lambda^{\oplus4}\), is a rank-zero subgroup of
the corresponding free quotient, and is therefore zero.

We give the compactification maps, retaining the full-base fillings.
Use the based carriers
\[
 \mathcal A=
 \frac{[0,\epsilon]\times S^1\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2}
 {\text{each endpoint torus collapsed separately}},\qquad
 \mathcal B=
 \frac{[0,\epsilon]\times S^1\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)}
 {\text{each endpoint torus collapsed separately}},
\]
with radial-zero poles \(v_0,b_0\) and outer poles
\(v_\epsilon,b_\epsilon\).
The cusp quotient has marked coordinate \(\overline\pi_t\) with
\(\pi_T=\iota_T\overline\pi_T\).
Define \(c_{\mathcal A}:X\to\mathcal A\) by
\[
 x\longmapsto[|t|,t/|t|,\overline\pi_t(x)]
       \quad(0<|t|<\epsilon),\qquad
 W\longmapsto v_0,\qquad
 X\setminus\operatorname{int}N_0\longmapsto v_\epsilon.
\]
The two boundary rules agree with the endpoint identifications.
Compactness of the angular torus gives a uniform radial collar
inside every neighbourhood of either pole.  This proves continuity
at both endpoints; on the interior it follows from the quotient
formula.  Fibrewise surjectivity proves that \(c_{\mathcal A}\) is a
based surjection.
The product formula
\[
 \kappa:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad
 [s,z,(a_g,a_u)]\longmapsto[s,z,a_g]
\]
respects both collapsed endpoints and is continuous by the quotient
property.  Put \(c_{\mathcal B}=\kappa c_{\mathcal A}\).

For the full-base construction let
\[
 \mathcal C=\mathcal M\cup_{T_0}\operatorname{Cone}_\epsilon(T_0),
 \qquad T_0=\partial D_0\times S^1,
\]
and let \(c_{\mathcal C}=q_1:X\to\mathcal C\) be the based quotient
of Theorem~\ref{wb:cusp-cone-S24-route}.
It includes the core \(P\times S^1\), both finite Seifert fillings
\(C_1,C_2\), and the cusp cone.  Its defining finite overlap identity
\(\chi_\gamma h_j=h_j^{S^1}\overline\chi_j\) gives the actual gluing
to \(\mathcal M\); on the cusp it is
\[
 x\longmapsto[|t|,(\epsilon\,t/|t|,\chi_\gamma(x))],
 \qquad W\longmapsto c_0.
\]
There is an explicit based quotient
\[
 p_{\mathcal C\mathcal B}:\mathcal C\to\mathcal B,\qquad
 \mathcal M\longmapsto b_\epsilon,\qquad
 [s,(\epsilon z,\theta)]\longmapsto[s,z,\theta].
\]
At \(s=\epsilon\) the cone formula is the same constant as the core
formula, and at \(s=0\) it maps the cone vertex to \(b_0\).
The pushout property therefore proves continuity.
On \(0<s<\epsilon\) its inverse coordinates are
\([s,z,\theta]\mapsto[s,(\epsilon z,\theta)]\);
the two poles correspond to \(c_0\) and the collapsed \(\mathcal M\).
These formulas induce a continuous bijection
\(\mathcal C/\mathcal M\to\mathcal B\), hence a homeomorphism
by compactness and the Hausdorff property.
The definitions on the cusp, on \(W\), and on the exterior give the
equality of global based maps
\[
 p_{\mathcal C\mathcal B}c_{\mathcal C}=c_{\mathcal B}.
\]
In particular the two finite fillings are retained in
\(c_{\mathcal C}\) and are sent to the outer pole by
\(p_{\mathcal C\mathcal B}\).

For a radial slice put
\[
 \alpha_T(y)=[r_T,1,\iota_T^{-1}(y)]\in\mathcal A,\qquad
 \beta_T(z)=[r_T,1,\vartheta_T^{-1}(z)]\in\mathcal B,\qquad
 \zeta_T(z)=[r_T,(\epsilon,\vartheta_T^{-1}(z))]\in\mathcal C.
\]
Then \(p_{\mathcal C\mathcal B}\zeta_T=\beta_T\), and, writing
\(i_T:F_T\to X\) for the fibre inclusion,
\[
 c_{\mathcal A}i_T=\alpha_T\pi_T,\qquad
 c_{\mathcal B}i_T=\beta_T\pi_{\gamma,T},\qquad
 c_{\mathcal C}i_T=\zeta_T\pi_{\gamma,T}.
\]
With the product-to-smash quotients \(q_{X,r}:X^r\to X^{\wedge r}\)
and the interior carrier embeddings of
Definition~\ref{wb:cusp-cone-target-slice-embeddings}, these identities give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 c_{\mathcal A}^{\wedge2}q_{X,2}i_T^{\times2}
   &=j_T(\pi_T\times\pi_T),\\
 c_{\mathcal B}^{\wedge4}q_{X,4}i_T^{\times4}
   &=k_T^{\mathcal B}\pi_{\gamma,T}^{\times4},\\
 c_{\mathcal C}^{\wedge4}q_{X,4}i_T^{\times4}
   &=k_T^{\mathcal C}\pi_{\gamma,T}^{\times4},\qquad
 p_{\mathcal C\mathcal B}^{\wedge4}k_T^{\mathcal C}=k_T^{\mathcal B}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The based maps descend to smash powers because their product maps
send the source fat wedge to the target fat wedge.

Choose the established based diffeomorphism \(h:X\to S^6\) used in
\eqref{wb:cusp-cone-S24-source}, with the basepoint represented by
infinity in \((\mathbb R^6)^+\).
On the complement of the fat wedge, the map \(h_r\) sends an ordered
tuple to the concatenated \(r\) Euclidean coordinate blocks of its
\(h\)-images; the fat wedge maps to infinity.
Its inverse splits a finite vector into those \(r\) blocks and applies
\(h^{-1}\) to each, and sends infinity to the smash basepoint.
Compact complements prove continuity at infinity, giving
\[
 h_r:X^{\wedge r}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }S^{6r}.
\]
The actual compact source maps are
\[
 c_{\mathcal A}^{\wedge2}h_2^{-1}:S^{12}\to\mathcal A^{\wedge2},
 \qquad
 c_{\mathcal C}^{\wedge4}h_4^{-1}:S^{24}\to\mathcal C^{\wedge4},
\]
and the latter composed with \(p_{\mathcal C\mathcal B}^{\wedge4}\)
is \(c_{\mathcal B}^{\wedge4}h_4^{-1}\).
Their radial restrictions are precisely the two attaining rank-four
quotients above.  Thus the least factor numbers give the claimed
dimensions \(12\) and \(24\).  Different values of \(6r\) have distinct
top reduced integral homology degrees, so these dimension comparisons
also respect the stated sphere identifications.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact sphere-to-sphere carriers with moving four-spheres]
\hypertarget{tag-036J}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}
\StatementRecord{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}{proved}{036J}{the definitions and constructions stated in the proof}

There are continuous surjective based quotient maps
\[
 \widehat q_3:(X,x_0)\longrightarrow(S^3,*),
 \qquad
 \widehat q_\gamma:(X,x_0)\longrightarrow(S^2,*),
\]
whose smash powers are continuous surjective quotient maps
\begin{equation}
 \widehat q_3^{\wedge2}:S^{12}\twoheadrightarrow S^6,
 \qquad
 \widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge4}:S^{24}\twoheadrightarrow S^8.
 \hypertarget{tag-037L}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-sphere-to-sphere-maps}
\end{equation}
Use the marked presentation \(\overline T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\) and
put
\[
 K^{(1)}
 =((\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times\{0\})
  \cup(\{0\}\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)),
 \qquad
 c:\overline T^2\longrightarrow\overline T^2/K^{(1)}\cong S^2.
\]
Here \(c\) is the quotient collapsing the coordinate one-skeleton.  For
every sufficiently large \(T\), put
\begin{align*}
 r_T&=e^{-2\pi T},\\
 K_T^{(1)}&:=\iota_T(K^{(1)})\subset Q_T,\\
 S_T^2&:=\overline T^2/K^{(1)}\cong Q_T/K_T^{(1)},\\
 c_T&:=c\circ\iota_T^{-1}:Q_T\longrightarrow S_T^2,
\end{align*}
where the identification of the two displayed quotients is induced by
\(\iota_T\).  Within this theorem and its proof, \(c_T\) denotes the
displayed collapse map; the earlier scalar \(c_T=\xi_T-\eta_T\) does not
enter.
At reduced-suspension cross-section height \(r_T\), the first target contains
a based topologically embedded four-sphere, equipped with its intrinsic
quotient length metric,
\[
 \mathbb S_{12,T}^4=S_T^2\wedge S_T^2\hookrightarrow S^6,
\]
and the second target contains, at the same cross-section height, a based
topologically embedded four-sphere, equipped with its intrinsic quotient
length metric,
\[
 \mathbb S_{24,T}^4=C_T^{\wedge4}\hookrightarrow S^8.
\]
On synchronized radial fibres, the exact restrictions factor as
\begin{align}
 F_T^2&\xrightarrow{\ \pi_T\times\pi_T\ }
 Q_T^2\xrightarrow{\ c_T\times c_T\ }(S_T^2)^2
 \xrightarrow{\ \rho_{12,T}\ }S_T^2\wedge S_T^2
 =\mathbb S_{12,T}^4,
 \hypertarget{tag-035R}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S12-S4-radial-map}\\
 F_T^4&\xrightarrow{\ \chi_{\gamma,T}^{\times4}\ }
 C_T^4\xrightarrow{\ \rho_{24,T}\ }C_T^{\wedge4}
 =\mathbb S_{24,T}^4,
 \hypertarget{tag-0361}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-S4-radial-map}
\end{align}
Here \(c_T\) collapses \(K_T^{(1)}\), and \(\rho_{12,T}\) and
\(\rho_{24,T}\) are the smash quotient maps.  Thus the
full collapsed locus in \(Q_T^2\) is exactly
\begin{equation}
 W_{12,T}
 =\bigl(K_T^{(1)}\times Q_T\bigr)
  \cup\bigl(Q_T\times K_T^{(1)}\bigr),
 \hypertarget{tag-035T}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S12-exact-collapsed-locus}
\end{equation}
and the full collapsed locus in \(C_T^4\) is exactly
\begin{equation}
 W_{24,T}
 =\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in C_T^4:
       x_j=0\pmod{\ell_T}\ \text{for some }j\}.
 \hypertarget{tag-0362}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-exact-collapsed-locus}
\end{equation}
The maps
\(\rho_{12,T}\circ(c_T\times c_T):Q_T^2\to
S_T^2\wedge S_T^2\) and
\(\rho_{24,T}:C_T^4\to C_T^{\wedge4}\) send exactly \(W_{12,T}\) and
\(W_{24,T}\), respectively, to the smash basepoint and are injective on

\begin{corollary}[Repeated smashes of the circle-quotient carrier]
\hypertarget{tag-036E}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-sphere-map-null}
Let \(f=\widehat q_\gamma:S^6\to S^2\) be the based quotient map of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}, using its chosen
based identification \((X,x_0)\cong(S^6,*)\), where \(x_0\in W\).
For every integer \(r\geq2\),
\begin{equation}
 \bigl[f^{\wedge r}\bigr]=0
 \quad\text{in}\quad
 \pi_{6r}(S^{2r}).
 \hypertarget{tag-0367}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-null-maps}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \bigl[\widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge2}\bigr]
 =0\in\pi_{12}(S^4),
 \qquad
 \bigl[\widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge4}\bigr]
 =0\in\pi_{24}(S^8).
 \hypertarget{tag-0368}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-null-special-cases}
\end{equation}
The specified map
\(\widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge4}:S^{24}\twoheadrightarrow S^8\)
is a continuous surjective quotient map and admits a global based
null-homotopy whose initial map is this representative.
For every native radial parameter with
\(0<r_T=e^{-2\pi T}<\epsilon\), its radial restriction is
\[
 F_T^4\xrightarrow{\ \pi_{\gamma,T}^{\times4}\ }C_T^4
 \xrightarrow{\ \rho_{24,T}\ }\mathbb S_{24,T}^4
 \xrightarrow{\ i_T\ }S^8,
 \qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}=\vartheta_T\circ\chi_{\gamma,T},
 \quad \vartheta_T[\theta]=[\ell_T\theta].
\]
Here \(C_T=\mathbb R/\ell_T\mathbb Z\), with \(\ell_T>0\), and
\(i_T\) is the fourth smash of the height section
\([u]\mapsto[r_T,[u/\ell_T]]\), using the chosen target sphere coordinates.
Give \(\mathbb S_{24,T}^4=C_T^{\wedge4}\) the quotient length metric
from the Euclidean product metric on \(C_T^4\), and put
\[
 \zeta_{24,T}=[\ell_T/2,\ell_T/2,\ell_T/2,\ell_T/2].
\]
For each \(R>0\), the parameters on the native tail with \(\ell_T>4R\)
give an isometry from the entire Euclidean radius-\(R\) ball onto the
entire intrinsic radius-\(R\) ball about \(\zeta_{24,T}\).
Consequently these based radial four-spheres have the pointed
local-isometric and pointed Gromov--Hausdorff limit \((\mathbb R^4,0)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the based cube model \(C_n=[0,1]^n/\partial[0,1]^n\) for \(S^n\).
The coordinate map
\(a_j\mapsto\tan(\pi(a_j-\tfrac12))\) on the open cube, with inverse
\(u_j\mapsto\tfrac12+\pi^{-1}\arctan u_j\), extends to the
one-point compactification by sending the boundary class to infinity.
Concatenation of cube coordinates induces a based homeomorphism
\[
 \beta_{p,q}:S^p\wedge S^q\longrightarrow S^{p+q}.
\]
Its inverse splits an interior tuple after its \(p\)-th coordinate
and sends the boundary class to the smash basepoint.  The quotient
identifications make these continuous inverse maps.
Repeated concatenation gives
\(\mu_{n,r}:(S^n)^{\wedge r}\to S^{nr}\);
all its parenthesizations have the same values on representatives.
Use these maps and their inverses in the sphere identifications below.

Writing the chosen source and target homeomorphisms as \(h_6\) and \(h_2\),
the actual single-factor map is
\[
 f=h_2\circ\widehat p_1\circ q_{1,\mathrm{cusp}}\circ h_6^{-1},
 \qquad \widehat p_1[r,z,\theta]=[r,\theta].
\]
The two end vertices of \(\mathcal B\) map to the basepoint of the
reduced suspension, so this formula is defined on the stated quotient.
It is the based surjective map in the cited construction.

The smash square has the exact factorization
\begin{equation}
 \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 S^6\wedge S^6
 \arrow[r,"f\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^6}"]&
 S^2\wedge S^6
 \arrow[r,"\operatorname{id}_{S^2}\wedge f"]&
 S^2\wedge S^2 .
 \end{tikzcd}
 \hypertarget{tag-036C}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-smash-square-factorization}
\end{equation}
For clarity, let
\(\tau_{p,q}:S^p\wedge S^q\to S^q\wedge S^p\) send
\([x,y]\) to \([y,x]\).  Its inverse is \(\tau_{q,p}\).
The precise comparison with left suspension is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 f\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^6}
   &=\tau_{6,2}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{S^6}\wedge f)
                         \circ\tau_{6,6},\\
 \beta_{6,2}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{S^6}\wedge f)
                         \circ\beta_{6,6}^{-1}
   &=\Sigma^6f:S^{12}\longrightarrow S^8.
 \end{aligned}
 \hypertarget{tag-036B}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-sixfold-suspension}
\end{equation}
The first equality sends \([x,y]\) through
\([y,x]\), \([y,f(x)]\), and \([f(x),y]\).
It also holds on the collapsed fat wedge because all maps are based.
Both orders of applying \(f\) to the two factors consequently give
\(f\wedge f\).

The suspension map is an isomorphism in degree \(i<2n-1\)
for \(S^n\), by \cite[Corollary~4.24, p.~360]{Hatcher2002}.
For \(i=12,n=8\), the inequality is \(12\leq14\), and it
remains strict in the form \(12+j<2(8+j)-1\) for every \(j\geq0\).
The canonical iterated-suspension map therefore gives
\phantomsection\hypertarget{tag-033R}{}\label{qa:III:layout:11}
\begin{equation}
 \pi_{12}(S^8)\cong\pi_4^{\mathrm S}=0.
 \hypertarget{tag-036R}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-fourth-stable-stem}
\end{equation}
The zero stable stem is the \(k=4\) row of
\cite[Corollary~1.3, p.~112, and Table~1, p.~113]{IsaksenWangXu2023};
the three homotopy summands in that row are all trivial.

For every integer \(s\geq1\), define the sphere-coordinate smash map
\[
 F_s=\mu_{2,s}\circ f^{\wedge s}\circ\mu_{6,s}^{-1},
 \qquad \mu_{n,1}=\operatorname{id}_{S^n}.
\]
Thus \(F_1=f\).  Take an integer \(r\geq2\) and put \(m=6(r-1)\).
There is a factorization \(F_r=B_rA_r\), where
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A_r&=\beta_{m,2}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{S^m}\wedge f)
                       \circ\beta_{m,6}^{-1}:
                 S^{6r}\longrightarrow S^{6r-4},\\
 B_r&=\beta_{2(r-1),2}\circ(F_{r-1}\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^2})
                       \circ\beta_{m,2}^{-1}:
                 S^{6r-4}\longrightarrow S^{2r}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first map applies \(f\) to the last factor, and the second applies
it to the preceding factors.  Thus their composite equals \(F_r\)
on every product representative, including those for which a
nonbasepoint coordinate has \(f\)-image \(*\).
The map \(A_r\) is \(\Sigma^{6(r-1)}f\).  Its group is
\(\pi_{n+4}(S^n)\), where \(n=6r-4\); the stable-range margin is
\[
 n-(4+1)=6(r-2)+3>0.
\]
The same iterated-suspension map identifies this group with
\(\pi_4^{\mathrm S}=0\).  Choose a based null-homotopy \(N_r\)
of \(A_r\), with \(N_r(-,0)=A_r\), \(N_r(-,1)=*\), and
\(N_r(*,s)=*\).  Then
\[
 H_r(x,s)=B_r(N_r(x,s))
\]
is a continuous global based homotopy from \(F_r\) to the constant map.
This proves both displayed nullity assertions.

For any nonbasepoint target tuple, choose a preimage under \(f\)
in each coordinate.  None of these preimages is the source basepoint.
This proves surjectivity of every \(F_r\); continuity and compactness
of the source with Hausdorff target make each \(F_r\) a quotient map.
In particular \(H_4(-,0)\) is exactly the specified surjective quotient.

For the radial assertion put
\[
 j_T[u]=h_2[r_T,[u/\ell_T]],\qquad
 i_T=\mu_{2,4}\circ j_T^{\wedge4}.
\]
For \(0<r_T<\epsilon\), the first map is injective:
away from the basepoint the height and circle coordinate are unchanged,
and its basepoint preimage is exactly \(0\in C_T\).
The same representative argument proves that \(i_T\) is an embedding.
The homeomorphism \(C_T^{\wedge4}\to[0,1]^4/\partial[0,1]^4\)
sends an uncollapsed tuple to its representatives \(u_j/\ell_T\in(0,1)\);
its inverse sends \(a\) to \([\ell_Ta_1,\ldots,\ell_Ta_4]\).
If \(\kappa_T:F_T^4\to S^{24}\) is induced by the native inclusions
and \(h_6\) in each source factor, the defining radial map gives
\[
 H_4(\kappa_T(x),0)
 =i_T\!\left(\rho_{24,T}
       (\pi_{\gamma,T}(x_1),\ldots,\pi_{\gamma,T}(x_4))\right).
\]
Here \(\vartheta_T^{-1}[u]=[u/\ell_T]\); thus every circle in this
identity has its stated angle or arclength coordinate.

Finally let \(E=C_T^4\), let \(W_T\) be its fat wedge, and put
\(b=(\ell_T/2,\ldots,\ell_T/2)\).  For a point \(x\) with lift \(u\),
\[
 a(x):=d_E(x,W_T)=\min_j\operatorname{dist}(u_j,\ell_T\mathbb Z).
\]
The quotient length metric is
\[
 d_{E/W_T}([x],[y])
   =\min\{d_E(x,y),a(x)+a(y)\}.
\]
A path chain without a jump through \(W_T\) costs at least the
first term; one with such a jump costs at least the second term.
Projected paths in \(E\), including paths from both endpoints to
\(W_T\), give the reverse inequalities.
For \(u,v\in\overline B_R(0)\) and \(\ell_T>4R\), every nonzero
period vector \(\lambda\) satisfies
\[
 \|u-v+\lambda\|\geq\ell_T-2R>2R\geq\|u-v\|,
\]
and
\[
 a([b+u])+a([b+v])\geq\ell_T-2R>2R.
\]
Thus \(v\mapsto\rho_{24,T}[b+v]\) preserves every distance on the
Euclidean radius-\(R\) ball.
For a quotient point within distance \(R\) of \(\rho_{24,T}(b)\),
the second branch of the quotient-distance formula exceeds \(R\),
because \(a(b)=\ell_T/2>R\).  Its uncollapsed representative therefore
has product-torus distance at most \(R\) from \(b\), and has a unique
lift \(b+v\) with \(\|v\|\leq R\).  This gives the inverse and proves
surjectivity onto the entire intrinsic ball.
These maps agree on nested balls.  Since \(\ell_T\to\infty\) on the
native tail, they prove the stated exact pointed limit for the radial
restrictions of the same initial representative \(H_4(-,0)\).
\end{proof}

\]

\[

\]

suspension. Contract $I$ to that pole and extend this contraction
to $H_t:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$, starting at the identity,
by the homotopy extension property. The map $H_1$ descends to

orientation. List the seven subsets by cardinality and then
lexicographically. Pinch the suspension coordinate into seven
equal subintervals and apply $\Sigma p_S$ to the corresponding
summand. This defines a based map
\[
 F:\Sigma T^3\longrightarrow
 W_A=\bigvee^3S^2\vee\bigvee^3S^3\vee S^4.

in degrees two, three and four. Indeed the oriented quotient

indexed by a different subset of the same size has a constant
circle coordinate and degree zero. Both spaces are simply

\cite[Corollary~4.33, pp.~367--368]{Hatcher2002} makes $F$ a based

\]

and every one of these images is open.  A closed equivalence relation with
an open quotient map has Hausdorff quotient: two inequivalent points admit
a product neighborhood disjoint from the relation, and the saturations of
the two factor neighborhoods are disjoint open sets.  Since the source is
second countable and the quotient map is open, images of a countable base
form a countable base of the quotient.

\item Fix \(x_0\in\mathbb R^4\).  Choose \(a>0\) and \(s_1>0\) such that
\(\operatorname{sys}(L_s)>2a\) for \(0<s<s_1\).  The quotient projection
is one-to-one on
\([0,s_1)\times B_a^\circ(x_0)\), where
\(B_a^\circ(x_0)=\{x:\|x-x_0\|<a\}\), and its restriction is an open continuous
bijection onto an open subset of \(\mathfrak E_\nu\); it is therefore a
homeomorphism.  These are half-space charts at \(s=0\).  The usual evenly
covered small balls give product charts for \(s>0\), and the same argument
at \(s=s_0\) gives the second boundary component.  This proves the
manifold assertion and the fibre identifications.

\item For the metric assertion, choose \(s_R\) so that
\(\operatorname{sys}(L_s)>4R\) for \(s<s_R\).  If
\(x,y\in B_R(0)\) and \(0\ne\lambda\in L_s\), then
\[
 \|x-y+\lambda\|
 \geq\|\lambda\|-\|x-y\|
 >4R-2R\geq\|x-y\|.
\]
Thus no translated representative shortens the Euclidean distance on that
ball, so \(q_{\nu,s}\) is an exact isometric embedding there.  It is also
onto the full quotient ball.  Indeed, if \(\xi=[s,x]\) satisfies
\(d([s,0],\xi)\leq R\), discreteness of \(L_s\) makes the infimum in
\[
 d([s,0],[s,x])=\min_{\lambda\in L_s}\|x+\lambda\|
\]
attained.  For a minimizing \(\lambda_0\), the representative
\(x+\lambda_0\) lies in \(B_R^{\mathbb R^4}(0)\) and maps to \(\xi\).  At
\(s=0\), \(q_{\nu,0}\) is the identity.  This proves the asserted onto
isometry, and since it holds for every fixed \(R\), it proves all three
pointed convergences.

\item It remains to define these comparison maps, which set-theoretically collapse
the zero fibres.  For \(s>0\), put
\(T=1/s\) and \(r=e^{-2\pi T}\).  In the \(S^{12}\) case, write
\(x=(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb R^2\) and set
\[
 \beta_{12}([s,x])
 =\bigl[r,
 \iota_T^{-1}([x_1]_{Y_T\mathbb Z^2}),
 \iota_T^{-1}([x_2]_{Y_T\mathbb Z^2})\bigr].
\]
In the \(S^{24}\) case, write
\(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_4)\) and set
\[
 \beta_{24}([s,x])
 =\bigl[r,
 [x_1/\ell_T],\ldots,[x_4/\ell_T]\bigr].
\]
These formulae are well defined on the positive fibres and are continuous
there.  Define \(\beta_\nu([0,x])=d_\nu\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^4\).
Every neighborhood of \(d_\nu\) in the cone contains all cross-sections
with sufficiently small \(r\).  Since \(e^{-2\pi/s}\to0\) as
\(s\downarrow0\), continuity at the zero fibre is uniform in \(x\).
Surjectivity follows because each positive fibre maps onto its complete
cross-section and the zero fibre maps onto the vertex.  The restriction away
from \(p_\nu^{-1}(0)\) is a homeomorphism because
\(s\mapsto e^{-2\pi/s}\) is a homeomorphism from \((0,s_0]\) to
\((0,r_0]\), and the displayed marked-torus identifications are fibrewise
homeomorphisms varying continuously with \(s\).  The vertex fibre is exactly
\(p_\nu^{-1}(0)\), so \(\beta_\nu\) is not proper.

\item It is also not a quotient map.  Choose
\(a\in\mathbb R^4\setminus\mathbb Z^4\), for example
\(a=(1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2)\), choose \(s_j\downarrow0\), and put
\[
 z_j=[s_j,A_{1/s_j}^{(\nu)}a]\in\mathfrak E_\nu.
\]
For \(\nu=12\),
\[
 \inf_{n\in\mathbb Z^4}
 \|A_{1/s_j}^{(12)}(a+n)\|
 \geq(1/s_j-C)\operatorname{dist}(a,\mathbb Z^4)
 \longrightarrow\infty,
\]
and for \(\nu=24\) the same infimum equals
\[
 \ell_{1/s_j}\operatorname{dist}(a,\mathbb Z^4)
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
More explicitly, for every fixed \(x_0\in\mathbb R^4\),
\[
 \inf_{n\in\mathbb Z^4}
 \|A_{1/s_j}^{(\nu)}(a+n)-x_0\|
 \geq
 \inf_{n\in\mathbb Z^4}\|A_{1/s_j}^{(\nu)}(a+n)\|-\|x_0\|
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Hence \(\{z_j:j\geq1\}\) is closed in \(\mathfrak E_\nu\): it has no
accumulation in a positive fibre and the last estimate shows that it
eventually misses every half-space chart about every point of the zero
fibre.  But
\[
 \beta_\nu(z_j)=[e^{-2\pi/s_j},a]\longrightarrow d_\nu,
\]
so \(\{\beta_\nu(z_j):j\geq1\}\) is not closed in \(\mathcal D_\nu\).
Since \(\beta_\nu\) is injective off the zero fibre and the latter maps to
\(d_\nu\), the inverse image of this nonclosed set is the closed set
\(\{z_j:j\geq1\}\).  Thus \(\beta_\nu\) is not a quotient map.  This proves
the two diagrams and their exact topological scope.  Since \(\beta_\nu\) is
constant exactly on \(p_\nu^{-1}(0)\) and otherwise injective, it induces the
continuous bijection \(\overline\beta_\nu\) displayed in the theorem.  Were
that bijection a homeomorphism, \(\beta_\nu\) would be the composite of the
quotient projection with a homeomorphism and hence a quotient map, contrary
to the counterexample.  Therefore \(\overline\beta_\nu\) is not a
homeomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact decompactification spaces with boundary
\(\mathbb R^4\)]
\hypertarget{tag-036N}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-exact-decompactification-space}
Fix $T_0>0$ so that the radial periods are defined and $D_T>0$
for all $T\geq T_0$, with $r_0=e^{-2\pi T_0}<\epsilon$,
and put $s_0=T_0^{-1}$.
For $\nu\in\{12,24\}$ set
\[
 A_T^{(12)}=\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T),\qquad
 A_T^{(24)}=\ell_T I_4.
\]
On $[0,s_0]\times\mathbb R^4$ define the fibrewise equivalence
relation
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (0,x)\sim_\nu(0,y)&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=y,\\
 (s,x)\sim_\nu(s,y)&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       x-y\in A_{1/s}^{(\nu)}\mathbb Z^4\qquad(0<s\leq s_0).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Let
\[
 \mathfrak E_\nu=([0,s_0]\times\mathbb R^4)/\!\sim_\nu,
 \qquad q_\nu(s,x)=[s,x],\qquad p_\nu([s,x])=s.
\]
Then $\mathfrak E_\nu$ is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological
five-manifold with boundary, with fibres
\begin{align}
 p_{12}^{-1}(s)&\cong Q_{1/s}^2 &(s>0),&&
 p_{12}^{-1}(0)\cong\mathbb R^4,
 \hypertarget{tag-035K}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-E12-fibres}\\
 p_{24}^{-1}(s)&\cong C_{1/s}^4 &(s>0),&&
 p_{24}^{-1}(0)\cong\mathbb R^4.
 \hypertarget{tag-035L}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-E24-fibres}
\end{align}
Its boundary has precisely two components: this zero fibre and
the compact four-torus over $s=s_0$.

Give each positive fibre its Euclidean quotient metric and the zero
fibre its Euclidean metric.  For every $R>0$ there is $s_R>0$ such
that, for $0\leq s<s_R$, the map $q_{\nu,s}(x)=[s,x]$ restricts to
an exact isometry
\[
 q_{\nu,s}:B_R^{\mathbb R^4}(0)
   \xrightarrow{\ \cong_{\mathrm{isom}}\ }
   B_R^{p_\nu^{-1}(s)}([s,0])
\]
onto the entire quotient ball.  The positive fibres converge to the
zero fibre in pointed local-isometric, pointed smooth and pointed
Gromov--Hausdorff topology.

There are continuous surjective comparison maps in the diagrams
\[
 \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 \mathbb R^4=p_{12}^{-1}(0)
 \arrow[r,hook,"q_{12,0}"]&
 \mathfrak E_{12}\arrow[r,"\beta_{12}"]&
 \mathcal D_{12}\arrow[r,hook,"\delta_{12}"]&
 \mathcal A^{\wedge2},
 \end{tikzcd}
\]
and
\[
 \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 \mathbb R^4=p_{24}^{-1}(0)
 \arrow[r,hook,"q_{24,0}"]&
 \mathfrak E_{24}\arrow[r,"\beta_{24}"]&
 \mathcal D_{24}\arrow[r,hook,"\delta_{24}"]&
 \mathcal C^{\wedge4}.
 \end{tikzcd}
\]
At positive $s$, $\beta_\nu$ is the marked homeomorphism from the
fibre to the full torus slice at radius $r=e^{-2\pi/s}$.
Its positive-stratum restriction is a homeomorphism
\[
 \beta_\nu:\mathfrak E_\nu\setminus p_\nu^{-1}(0)
       \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\mathcal D_\nu\setminus\{d_\nu\},
\]
and
\[
 \beta_\nu^{-1}(d_\nu)=p_\nu^{-1}(0)\cong\mathbb R^4.
\]
Neither comparison map is proper or a quotient map.
The induced continuous bijection
\[
 \overline\beta_\nu:
 \mathfrak E_\nu/p_\nu^{-1}(0)\longrightarrow\mathcal D_\nu
\]
is not a homeomorphism: the cone topology is strictly coarser than
the quotient topology induced by $\beta_\nu$.
Thus the limiting $\mathbb R^4$ is an actual boundary fibre of
$\mathfrak E_\nu$, and the displayed comparison sends that whole
fibre to the cone vertex.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The exact radial formulas give continuous invertible matrices
$Y_T$ and positive continuous $\ell_T$ on $T\geq T_0$.
Write
\[
 Y_T=TJ+E_T,\qquad
 J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 E_T=\begin{pmatrix}6m_T&H_T\\B_T-H_T&m_T\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The holomorphic residual functions are bounded on the radial ray,
so the finite constant
\[
 C=\sup_{T\geq T_0}
       \sqrt{37m_T^2+H_T^2+(B_T-H_T)^2}
\]
bounds $\lVert E_T\rVert$.  Orthogonality of $J$ gives
$\lVert Y_Tv\rVert\geq(T-C)\lVert v\rVert$.
The same constant also bounds the circle period below.
With the subscripts $T$ suppressed, direct completion of the square gives
\[
 \left\lVert Y\binom{1}{z}\right\rVert^2
 =(L^2+m^2)\left(z+\frac{m(6L-q)}{L^2+m^2}\right)^2
       +\frac{D^2}{L^2+m^2}.
\]
By \eqref{wb:cusp-spec-global-circle-circumference},
$\ell_T=D_T/\sqrt{L_T^2+m_T^2}$; since $D>0$, the last minimum
is $\ell_T^2$.
For $T>C$ this implies $\ell_T\geq T-C$ by the norm bound and
$\lVert(1,z)\rVert\geq1$; for $T\leq C$ the inequality follows
from positivity of $\ell_T$.
Consequently the shortest nonzero period $\lambda_\nu(T)$ of either
$A_T^{(\nu)}\mathbb Z^4$ satisfies
\[
 \lambda_\nu(T)\geq T-C\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

Put $M=[0,s_0]\times\mathbb R^4$, $M_+=(0,s_0]\times\mathbb R^4$,
and abbreviate $A(s)=A_{1/s}^{(\nu)}$ for $s>0$.
The saturation of an open subset $U\subset M$ is
\[
 U\ \cup\!\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z^4}
   \{(s,x+A(s)n):(s,x)\in U\cap M_+\}.
\]
Every positive-stratum translation is a homeomorphism with inverse
translation by $-A(s)n$, and $M_+$ is open in $M$.
Thus the saturation is open and $q_\nu$ is an open quotient map.

The equivalence relation is closed.  Indeed, in a convergent sequence
of related pairs whose parameters tend to $s>0$, the integer vectors
$A(s_j)^{-1}(x_j-y_j)$ converge and hence are eventually constant.
The limiting pair is therefore related.  When $s_j\to0$, the
differences $x_j-y_j$ are bounded, whereas every nonzero period has
length at least $\lambda_\nu(1/s_j)\to\infty$ at positive indices.
The differences are eventually zero, including the zero-level
indices by definition, so $x=y$.  This proves closedness because
$M\times M$ is metrizable.
For unrelated representatives, choose a product neighbourhood disjoint
from the relation.  The images of its two factors under the open
map $q_\nu$ are disjoint open neighbourhoods.  Hence the quotient
is Hausdorff.  Images of a countable base of $M$ under $q_\nu$ form
a countable base, proving second countability.

The projection $p_\nu$ is continuous by the quotient property.
For an open $V\subset\mathbb R^4$ and a relative open interval
$I\subset[0,s_0]$ containing $s$,
\[
 q_{\nu,s}(V)=p_\nu^{-1}(s)\cap q_\nu(I\times V).
\]
Thus $q_{\nu,s}$ is open onto its fibre.
At zero it is bijective, giving the stated homeomorphism with
$\mathbb R^4$.  At positive $s$ it induces a homeomorphism from
$\mathbb R^4/A(s)\mathbb Z^4$ onto the fibre.  Splitting the four
coordinates into two pairs for $\nu=12$, or taking their individual
residues modulo $\ell_{1/s}$ for $\nu=24$, gives
\eqref{wb:cusp-cone-E12-fibres} and \eqref{wb:cusp-cone-E24-fibres}.

For a zero-fibre point represented by $x_0$, choose $a>0$ and
$0<\eta<\min\{s_0,(2a+C+1)^{-1}\}$.
The map $q_\nu$ is injective on $[0,\eta)\times B_a^\circ(x_0)$,
because a difference of two vectors in that ball has length less
than $2a$, while every nonzero period has greater length.
Its restriction is an open continuous bijection, giving a half-space
chart of dimension five.  Near any $s_*>0$, continuity of $A(s)^{-1}$
gives a uniform positive lower bound on $\lVert A(s)v\rVert/\lVert v\rVert$.
An interval around $s_*$ times a sufficiently small ball therefore
gives the same injective open quotient chart.  For $0<s_*<s_0$
this is an interior chart; at $s_*=s_0$ the coordinate $s_0-s$
gives a half-space chart.  These charts cover the entire space.
Their local homology identifies the boundary precisely as the two
end fibres.  Both end fibres are connected and are separated inside
the boundary by their $p_\nu$ values, proving the boundary assertion.

For the metric conclusion take
$s_R=\min\{s_0,(4R+C+1)^{-1}\}$.
For $0<s<s_R$ and $x,y\in B_R(0)$, every nonzero period $\lambda$
satisfies
\[
 \lVert x-y+\lambda\rVert
 \geq\lVert\lambda\rVert-2R
 \geq1/s-C-2R>2R\geq\lVert x-y\rVert.
\]
The quotient therefore preserves all distances on this ball.
Every lattice coset has a closest representative, since the full
rank lattice has finitely many points in bounded sets and its
vectors tend to infinity with their integer coefficients.
A point in the quotient radius-$R$ ball consequently has a
representative of norm at most $R$, proving surjectivity onto the
whole ball.  The same argument applies to open balls with strict
inequalities.  At $s=0$ the given Euclidean identification is the
identity.  On open balls the quotient maps are smooth local
isometries and pull the metric tensor back exactly to the Euclidean
tensor.  For every fixed radius these identifications give the
local-isometric and smooth limits; exact isometry of the closed
balls also gives the pointed Gromov--Hausdorff limit.

Let $c_{12}:(\overline T^2)^2\to\mathbb R^4/\mathbb Z^4$ concatenate
the two coordinate pairs, and let $c_{24}$ take the four individual
circle coordinates, as in Proposition~\ref{wb:cusp-cone-explicit-carriers}.
The comparison formulas are
\[
 \beta_\nu([s,x])=
 \begin{cases}
 [e^{-2\pi/s},c_\nu^{-1}([A(s)^{-1}x])],&s>0,\\
 d_\nu,&s=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
Adding $A(s)n$ to $x$ adds $n$ to the marked coordinate, so the
formula is well defined.  Its positive-stratum cylinder map is
continuous.  Every vertex neighbourhood in the cone contains a
full collar of sufficiently small radius by compactness of its
link.  The limit $e^{-2\pi/s}\to0$ therefore proves continuity
at the zero fibre, uniformly in $x$, and the formula descends
continuously through $q_\nu$.

The map $[s,x]\mapsto(s,[A(s)^{-1}x])$ identifies the positive
stratum with $(0,s_0]\times(\mathbb R^4/\mathbb Z^4)$.
Its inverse is $(s,[a])\mapsto[s,A(s)a]$; both maps descend from
continuous cylinder maps through the open torus quotient.
The radius map $s\mapsto e^{-2\pi/s}$ has inverse
$r\mapsto-2\pi/\log r$ on $(0,r_0]$, where $r_0<1$.
Together with $c_\nu^{-1}$ these formulas give the full continuous
inverse of $\beta_\nu$ on the positive stratum.
In the first family they apply $\iota_T^{-1}$ to each of the two
$Q_T$ factors; in the second they apply $\vartheta_T^{-1}[b]
=[b/\ell_T]$ to each $C_T$ factor.  Thus these are precisely the
marked slice maps of that proposition, and composition with the
displayed $\delta_\nu$ gives the full diagrams.
The zero embedding is $q_{\nu,0}$; it is closed because it is the
fibre of the continuous $p_\nu$ over zero.  The positive-stratum
homeomorphism proves surjectivity and shows that the vertex inverse
image is exactly that zero fibre.  Its homeomorphism with the
noncompact $\mathbb R^4$ makes the inverse image of the compact
singleton $\{d_\nu\}$ noncompact, proving that $\beta_\nu$ is not proper.

For any $a\in\mathbb R^4\setminus\mathbb Z^4$, the attained distance
$d=\operatorname{dist}(a,\mathbb Z^4)$ is positive.  Applying the
$Y_T$ bound to both blocks gives
\[
 \inf_{k\in\mathbb Z^4}\|A_T^{(12)}(a+k)\|\geq(T-C)d,
 \qquad
 \inf_{k\in\mathbb Z^4}\|A_T^{(24)}(a+k)\|=\ell_Td.
\]
For $T\leq C$ the first inequality follows from nonnegativity.
Both bounds tend to infinity, and subtracting any fixed $x_0$
decreases them by at most $\|x_0\|$.  Thus every such nonintegral
marked coset escapes all bounded zero-fibre charts as $s=1/T\to0$.

For a concrete quotient-topology witness, take $v=\tfrac12 e_1$ and,
for integers $n\geq1$, put
\[
 T_n=T_0+n,\qquad s_n=T_n^{-1},\qquad
 z_n=q_\nu(s_n,A_{T_n}^{(\nu)}v),\qquad
 S_\nu=\{z_n:n\geq1\}.
\]
Every representative of $z_n$ is $A_{T_n}^{(\nu)}(v+k)$ for
$k\in\mathbb Z^4$.  Twice this vector is
$A_{T_n}^{(\nu)}(e_1+2k)$, a nonzero period because its first
integer coefficient is odd.  Thus every representative has norm
at least $(T_n-C)/2\to\infty$.
The full inverse image $q_\nu^{-1}(S_\nu)$ is closed: at a positive
base level a sufficiently small interval meets only finitely many
of these closed lattice cosets; at zero every bounded spatial
neighbourhood misses the tail, and a smaller base interval excludes
the remaining finitely many levels.  The quotient definition then
makes $S_\nu$ closed in $\mathfrak E_\nu$.

Its image is
\[
 B_\nu=\{[e^{-2\pi T_n},c_\nu^{-1}([v])]:n\geq1\}.
\]
This fixed-link sequence converges to $d_\nu$, which it omits.
Consequently $U_\nu=\mathcal D_\nu\setminus B_\nu$ contains the
vertex but is not open.  On the other hand,
$\beta_\nu^{-1}(U_\nu)=\mathfrak E_\nu\setminus S_\nu$ is open,
by the exact positive-stratum bijection and the vertex fibre.
This proves that $\beta_\nu$ is not a quotient map.

Finally let $c:\mathfrak E_\nu\to
\mathfrak E_\nu/p_\nu^{-1}(0)$ be the collapse quotient.
The quotient universal property gives the continuous
$\overline\beta_\nu$ with $\overline\beta_\nu c=\beta_\nu$;
the computed fibres make it bijective.
The set $\overline\beta_\nu^{-1}(U_\nu)$ is open because its
inverse image under $c$ is the open set
$\mathfrak E_\nu\setminus S_\nu$, while its image $U_\nu$ is not
open.  Hence the inverse of this bijection is not continuous.
Continuity of $\overline\beta_\nu$ gives the inclusion of cone-open
sets among quotient-open sets, and this $U_\nu$ makes the inclusion
strict.  This proves the stated comparison of the two topologies.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp global meaning of the Euclidean limit]
\hypertarget{tag-037J}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-sharp-global-R4-scope}
\StatementRecord{wb:cusp-cone-sharp-global-R4-scope}{proved}{037J}{\SeriesRef{wb:cusp-cone-literal-R4-open-cells}, \SeriesRef{wb:cusp-cone-explicit-carriers}, \SeriesRef{wb:cusp-cone-exact-decompactification-space}, \SeriesRef{wb:cusp-cone-carrier-local-homology}, \SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}}

The native routes constructed above exhibit the underlying space
\(\mathbb R^4\) in the following three precise senses:
\begin{enumerate}
\item as each of the nonclosed topologically embedded open cells
\(U_{12,T}\subset S^6\) and \(U_{24,T}\subset S^8\);
\item as the pointed intrinsic Euclidean limit of the four-torus slices in the
global quotient carriers of \(S^{12}\) and \(S^{24}\); and
\item as the Euclidean decompactification boundary fibre of
\(\mathfrak E_{12}\) and \(\mathfrak E_{24}\).
\end{enumerate}
It does not produce \(\mathbb R^4\) as the whole compact sphere, as the
whole compact conical target, or as a continuous quotient target of either
compact space.  Nor does the unrescaled restriction of any fixed compatible
ambient target metric have \(\mathbb R^4\) as its slice limit, and the open
cells in item \(1\) are not globally Euclidean-isometric in such a metric.
\end{corollary}



\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item The three positive assertions are
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-literal-R4-open-cells} and \cref{wb:cusp-cone-explicit-carriers} and \cref{wb:cusp-cone-exact-decompactification-space}.
For the negative assertions, a continuous image of a compact sphere or
compact conical target is compact, so it cannot be all of \(\mathbb R^4\).
The local homology calculation
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-carrier-local-homology} shows that the carrier vertex is not
an integral homology-manifold point, and hence not a manifold point, of any
dimension, with or without boundary.  Finally, in every fixed compatible
metric on a compact cone target, all sufficiently deep radial slices lie
uniformly in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of the vertex, so their ambient
diameters tend to zero.  Their intrinsic diameters tend to infinity because
their intrinsic systoles do.  Hence without a \(T\)-dependent rescaling no
fixed ambient metric realizes the intrinsic Euclidean limit on those slices.
The fixed cusp-adapted blow-ups are treated separately in
\cref{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}.  The comparison diagrams record the
unrescaled distinction exactly: they collapse the new \(\mathbb R^4\)
boundary rather than identify it with the compact target.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Three Euclidean realizations and their exact scope]
\hypertarget{tag-037J}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-sharp-global-R4-scope}
The two native routes realize $\mathbb R^4$ in the following ways:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for each admissible $T$, as the nonclosed topologically
embedded open cells $U_{12,T}\subset S^6$ and $U_{24,T}\subset S^8$;
\item as the pointed intrinsic Euclidean limit of the four-torus
slices in the global quotient carriers of $S^{12}$ and $S^{24}$;
\item as the Euclidean boundary fibre at $s=0$ of
$\mathfrak E_{12}$ and $\mathfrak E_{24}$.
\end{enumerate}
The cells in the first item are open in their moving four-spheres.
No whole compact sphere or whole compact conical target in these
routes is homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^4$, and no continuous map from
any of those compact spaces to $\mathbb R^4$ is surjective.
In particular $\mathbb R^4$ is not a continuous quotient target
of any of them.  For every fixed compatible ambient target metric,
the unrescaled restricted compact slices converge to a singleton.
Their slice limit is therefore not Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$.
At each fixed $T$, the restricted open-cell metrics admit no
distance-preserving map of all Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ into the cell.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
We use the exact maps of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-literal-R4-open-cells,wb:cusp-cone-explicit-carriers,
wb:cusp-cone-exact-decompactification-space,wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}.
First, the quotient restrictions
\[
 h_{12,T}=\rho_{12,T}(c_T\times c_T):
 (Q_T\setminus K_T^{(1)})^2\longrightarrow U_{12,T},
 \qquad
 h_{24,T}=\rho_{24,T}:(C_T\setminus\{0\})^4\longrightarrow U_{24,T}
\]
are homeomorphisms.  Off the closed collapsed sets each equivalence
class is a singleton, and every open subset of the complement is
an open saturated set, proving continuity of the inverse quotient
restrictions.  Let
\[
 u_T(a)=[Y_Ta],\quad a\in(0,1)^2,
 \qquad v_T(a)=[\ell_Ta],\quad a\in(0,1),
 \qquad
 \eta(t)=\frac12\left(1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}\right).
\]
The inverse of $u_T$ takes the representatives of $Y_T^{-1}y$ in
$(0,1)^2$, and the inverse of $v_T$ takes the representative in
$(0,\ell_T)$ and divides by $\ell_T$.  Also
\[
 \eta^{-1}(a)=\frac{2a-1}{2\sqrt{a(1-a)}}.
\]
The positive derivative of $\eta$, its limits $0,1$, and
$4\eta(t)(1-\eta(t))=(1+t^2)^{-1}$ prove both inverse identities.
Thus the two homeomorphisms from $\mathbb R^4$ are explicitly
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 t&\longmapsto h_{12,T}
   \bigl(u_T(\eta(t_1),\eta(t_2)),u_T(\eta(t_3),\eta(t_4))\bigr),\\
 t&\longmapsto h_{24,T}
   \bigl(v_T(\eta(t_1)),\ldots,v_T(\eta(t_4))\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Their inverses take the unique uncollapsed representatives, then
the indicated marked inverse coordinates, then $\eta^{-1}$.
In the ambient cube spheres the images have coordinates
\[
 (r_T/\epsilon,a_1,a_2,r_T/\epsilon,a_3,a_4),\qquad
 (r_T/\epsilon,a_1,r_T/\epsilon,a_2,
                  r_T/\epsilon,a_3,r_T/\epsilon,a_4),
 \quad a_j\in(0,1).
\]
Projection to the $a_j$ is the inverse on each image.  The compact
height-section embeddings therefore restrict to the claimed
embeddings.  Taking $a_1=1/n$, $n\geq2$, and the other three
coordinates equal to $1/2$ gives points tending to the omitted
basepoint.  The cells are consequently nonclosed, and their
ambient closures are their compact moving four-spheres.  Varying
the first radial coordinate alone also gives ambient points outside
each moving sphere arbitrarily near each cell point; these cells
are not ambient open subsets.

\[
 A_T^{(12)}=\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T),\qquad
 A_T^{(24)}=\ell_T I_4,\qquad

\[
 d_T([x],[y])=\min_{n\in\mathbb Z^4}|x-y+A_T^{(\nu)}n|.
\]
Let $c_{12}:(\overline T^2)^2\to\mathbb R^4/\mathbb Z^4$ concatenate
the coordinate pairs and $c_{24}$ concatenate the four circle
coordinates; their inverses split those coordinates.  The exact
slice maps are
\[
 k_{\nu,T}([x])=[r_T,c_\nu^{-1}([ (A_T^{(\nu)})^{-1}x])],
 \qquad j_{\nu,T}=\delta_\nu k_{\nu,T}.
\]
At positive height their inverses choose a lift $b$ of the marked
angular coordinate and take $[A_T^{(\nu)}b]$.  Changing that lift
by an integer changes this representative by a period.  The maps
therefore identify the whole flat quotient tori with the complete
height-$r_T$ target slices.  These are the actual sphere-carrier
restrictions, since
\[
 q_2^{\wedge2}i_{12,T}
   =j_{12,T}(\pi_T\times\pi_T),\qquad

   =j_{24,T}(\vartheta_T\chi_{\gamma,T})^{\times4}.

The right factor maps are surjective.

translated difference between two such vectors has norm at least

shortest representative of norm at most $R$, and two such

\cref{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization} is also exact.  If
$d_T^{\mathrm{slice}}$ is the intrinsic path metric of its induced

\[
 j_{12,T}^*d_T^{\mathrm{slice}}=(r_T/T)d_T,
 \qquad

homeomorphic to the noncompact $\mathbb R^4$, so $\mathfrak E_\nu$

through their defining quotient maps: the cube-sphere maps, the

the finite products and their smash quotients, and

omits $(M+1,0,0,0)$, so $F$ cannot be surjective.  This excludes

direction of any proposed homeomorphism with it.

connecting map is therefore an isomorphism to $H_{k-1}(T^4)$ for
$k\geq2$.  In degrees $0,1$ the relative groups vanish because
the $H_0$ inclusion is the identity.  The product circle cells have
zero boundary and give ranks $4,6,4,1$ in degrees $1,2,3,4$.
Orienting a coned cell by its positive outer boundary makes the
connecting map send its class to that torus cell.  Thus the local
groups are $\mathbb Z^4,\mathbb Z^6,\mathbb Z^4,\mathbb Z$ in
degrees $2,3,4,5$, and zero otherwise, as in
\eqref{wb:cusp-cone-carrier-local-homology}.  Excision makes these

\[

subsequence whose two components have the same limit; compatibility
then forces $D(x_n,y_n)\to0$.  Consequently
\[

 \operatorname{diam}_D\Sigma_T\leq2\omega_D(r_T)\longrightarrow0.

quotient metric $d_0([x],*)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial I^n)$:
