$r_T/\epsilon$.  The identity modulus for any fixed compatible
sphere metric thus bounds the entire moving four-sphere's diameter
by $2\omega_D(r_T/\epsilon)\to0$.

the vertex.  The correspondence sending every slice point to one
point has distortion equal to the slice diameter and respects any
chosen slice basepoint, so the unrescaled pointed restricted limit
is a singleton.  A Euclidean radius-two ball contains $0,e_1$ at
distance one; no correspondences of vanishing distortion from
spaces of vanishing diameter can approximate that pair.  Hence
this restricted limit cannot be $\mathbb R^4$.
For each fixed $T$, the open cell's restricted distance has the
finite diameter bound of its compact ambient sphere.  A
distance-preserving map from all $\mathbb R^4$ would send $0,ne_1$
to points at distance $n$, exceeding that bound for large $n$.
This proves the last assertion for every compatible ambient metric.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The full external smash pairing is zero]
\hypertarget{tag-038V}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-full-carrier-null}
\StatementRecord{wb:cusp-s12-full-carrier-null}{proved}{038V}{\SeriesRef{wb:cusp-s12-toda-smash-formula}; \cite[opening table, p.~339]{Hatcher2002}; \cite[Table~1, p.~113]{IsaksenWangXu2023}}

For every pair of based maps \(x,y:S^6\to S^3\),
\[
 [x\wedge y]=0\qquad\text{in}\qquad\pi_{12}(S^6).
\]
In particular,
\(\widehat q_3^{\wedge2}:S^{12}\twoheadrightarrow S^6\) is simultaneously
surjective as a point-set quotient and based null-homotopic.
\end{theorem}



\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item Write \(E\) for reduced suspension, using the ordered smash coordinates on
spheres.  The external smash product has the exact factorization
\begin{equation}
 x\wedge y
 =
 (x\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^3})
 \circ
 (\operatorname{id}_{S^6}\wedge y):
 S^6\wedge S^6\longrightarrow S^6\wedge S^3
 \longrightarrow S^3\wedge S^3.
 \hypertarget{tag-0390}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-smash-factorization}
\end{equation}
Under the displayed ordered sphere identifications, the two factors, in
order of application, represent \(E^6y\in\pi_{12}(S^9)\) and
\(E^3x\in\pi_9(S^6)\).  Equivalently, Toda's
Barratt--Hilton reduced-join formula gives, with
\(p=q=k=h=3\),
\begin{equation}
 [x\wedge y]=(E^3[x])\circ(E^6[y]).
 \hypertarget{tag-0392}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-toda-smash-formula}
\end{equation}
Here Toda's sign is \((-1)^{(p+k)h}=(-1)^{18}=+1\).  Reversing the
two displayed factors introduces the separate twist sign
\((-1)^{ph}=-1\); no such reversal is used here.

\item The three exact groups needed below are
\begin{equation}
 \pi_6(S^3)\cong\mathbb Z/12,
 \qquad
 \pi_{12}(S^9)\cong\mathbb Z/24,
 \qquad
 \pi_{12}(S^6)\cong\mathbb Z/2.
 \hypertarget{tag-0391}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-three-stem-groups}
\end{equation}
The first and third are the integral low unstable groups displayed in
Hatcher's table extracted from Toda; the middle group is in the stable
three-stem
\cite[opening table, p.~339]{Hatcher2002};
\cite[Table~1, p.~113]{IsaksenWangXu2023}.

\item Put \(\beta=E^6[y]\in\pi_{12}(S^9)\).  Since
\(12[y]=0\), functoriality of suspension gives \(12\beta=0\).  In the
cyclic group \(\mathbb Z/24\), the elements annihilated by \(12\) are
exactly the even elements.  Hence there is
\(\gamma\in\pi_{12}(S^9)\) such that \(\beta=2\gamma\).
Postcomposition with \(E^3[x]:S^9\to S^6\) induces a group homomorphism
\[
 (E^3[x])_*:\pi_{12}(S^9)\longrightarrow\pi_{12}(S^6).
\]
The target has exponent two, so \cref{wb:cusp-s12-toda-smash-formula} gives
\[
 [x\wedge y]
 =(E^3[x])_*(\beta)
 =2(E^3[x])_*(\gamma)
 =0.
\]
This proves the vanishing of the entire external smash pairing and hence
the theorem.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The full external smash pairing is zero]
\hypertarget{tag-038V}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-full-carrier-null}
For every pair of based maps $x,y:S^6\to S^3$,
\[
 [x\wedge y]=0\qquad\text{in }\pi_{12}(S^6).
\]
In particular, the continuous surjective quotient
$\widehat q_3^{\wedge2}:S^{12}\twoheadrightarrow S^6$ of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-sphere-to-sphere-maps} is based null-homotopic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the cube sphere identifications of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}, and write
$C_d=I^d/\partial I^d$.
The ordered based homeomorphism
\[
 \mu_{a,b}:C_a\wedge C_b\longrightarrow C_{a+b},
 \qquad [[u],[v]]\longmapsto[u,v]
\]
concatenates coordinates; its inverse splits an interior point into
the two blocks and sends the basepoint to the smash basepoint.
Let $p_d:C_d\to C_d\vee C_d$ pinch the first coordinate: on the two
halves it replaces $u_1$ by $2u_1$ and $2u_1-1$, respectively.
The middle face and the boundary go to the basepoint.
Thus $(f\vee g)p_d$ represents addition in $\pi_d$.

For $x,y:C_6\to C_3$ put
\[
 R(x)=\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_3})\mu_{6,3}^{-1}
       :C_9\longrightarrow C_6,
 \qquad
 L(y)=\mu_{6,3}(\mathrm{id}_{C_6}\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}
       :C_{12}\longrightarrow C_9.
\]
These are the right threefold and left sixfold suspensions in the
displayed block order.  The exact smash factorization is
\begin{equation}
 x\wedge y=(x\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_3})
              (\mathrm{id}_{C_6}\wedge y):
 C_6\wedge C_6\longrightarrow C_6\wedge C_3
                \longrightarrow C_3\wedge C_3.
 \hypertarget{tag-0390}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-smash-factorization}
\end{equation}
After the ordered identifications it gives
\[
 R(x)L(y)=\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}.
\]
To express this in one suspension convention, write
$E_R^r[f]=[\mu_{n,r}(f\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_r})\mu_{m,r}^{-1}]$
for $f:C_m\to C_n$.
The block twist $\tau_{a,b}:C_{a+b}\to C_{b+a}$,
$\tau_{a,b}[u,v]=[v,u]$, has inverse $\tau_{b,a}$ and degree
$(-1)^{ab}$, since its coordinate permutation has $ab$ inversions.
In particular,
\[
 L(y)=\tau_{3,6}\,
       \bigl(\mu_{3,6}(y\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_6})\mu_{6,6}^{-1}\bigr)
       \,\tau_{6,6}.
\]
Both twists here have degree one and hence are based homotopic to the
identity by \cite[Corollary~4.25]{Hatcher2002}.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 [\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}]
       =(E_R^3[x])\circ(E_R^6[y]).
 \hypertarget{tag-0392}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-toda-smash-formula}
\end{equation}
Pinching the first coordinate of the six-coordinate input block of
$x$ before concatenation gives
\[
 R((x\vee x')p_6)=(R(x)\vee R(x'))p_9.
\]
Hence $R_*:\pi_6(C_3)\to\pi_9(C_6)$, $[x]\mapsto[R(x)]$,
is a homomorphism.  Based homotopies descend through these smash
quotients because the fat wedge stays at the basepoint at every time;
the product of each compact quotient with the homotopy interval is
again a quotient map.

For fixed $y$, the map $L(y)$ leaves its first six coordinates
unchanged.  Consequently it satisfies the based-map identity
\[
 p_9L(y)=(L(y)\vee L(y))p_{12}.
\]
Indeed, both sides double the first coordinate in the first half and
replace it by $2u_1-1$ in the second half.  Both send the middle face,
the boundary, and every point whose $y$-coordinate is the basepoint
to the basepoint.  Thus
\[
 D_y:\pi_9(C_6)\longrightarrow\pi_{12}(C_6),
 \qquad [z]\longmapsto[zL(y)]
\]
is a homomorphism: applying the displayed pinch identity to
$(z\vee z')p_9$ proves additivity.

The integral computations in \cite[p.~339]{Hatcher2002} give the first,
second and fourth groups below:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 \pi_6(S^3)\cong\mathbb Z/12,\qquad
 \pi_9(S^6)\cong\mathbb Z/24,\\
 \pi_{12}(S^9)\cong\mathbb Z/24,\qquad
 \pi_{12}(S^6)\cong\mathbb Z/2.
 \end{gathered}
 \hypertarget{tag-0391}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-three-stem-groups}
\end{equation}
The remaining group is identified with $\pi_9(S^6)$ by the exact
suspension isomorphism
\[
 E_R^3:\pi_9(S^6)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_{12}(S^9).
\]
Indeed, the three Freudenthal inequalities are $9<11$, $10<13$ and
$11<15$ \cite[Corollary~4.24]{Hatcher2002}.
Choose a generator $\nu$ of $\pi_9(C_6)$, so that
$[k]_{24}\mapsto k\nu$ is its cyclic coordinate isomorphism.
Since $12[x]=0$ and $R_*$ is a homomorphism, writing
$R_*[x]=a\nu$ gives $24\mid12a$, hence $2\mid a$.
Equivalently, the kernel of multiplication by $12$ on $\mathbb Z/24$
is the image of the isomorphism
$[j]_{12}\mapsto[2j]_{24}$, whose inverse sends $[2j]_{24}$ to
$[j]_{12}$.  Therefore $R_*[x]=2\zeta$ for some
$\zeta\in\pi_9(C_6)$, and
\[
 [\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}]
   =D_y(R_*[x])=2D_y(\zeta)=0.
\]
All groups and homotopies here are based, so this is a homotopy to
the constant map that fixes the basepoint throughout.
Taking $x=y=\widehat q_3$ in the based sphere identifications proves
the asserted null-homotopy.  Its continuity, surjectivity and quotient
property follow from
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}.
\end{proof}

\hypertarget{tag-038S}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:thm}

ordered normal framing induced by \((r,c_1,c_2)\) is framed nullbordant
inside one original cusp chart times \([0,1]\), disjoint from
\(\{x_0\}\times[0,1]\).
\end{theorem}



\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item The proof constructs the complete inverse image, compares its actual
framing with an explicitly extendible framing, and gives the extension.

\item \textbf{1. The exact complete inverse image.}
Retain the lift
\[
 u^0=\begin{pmatrix}-1/4\\1/4\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \overline u^0=(3/4,1/4)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2},\qquad
 B_0u^0=\begin{pmatrix}1/4\\1/4\end{pmatrix}.
\]

interior of the original triangle \(\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2)\).
Use its original unimodular chart
\begin{equation}
 z_0=t/(x_1x_2),\qquad z_1=x_1,\qquad z_2=x_2,
 \qquad t=z_0z_1z_2.
 \hypertarget{tag-038H}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:chart}
\end{equation}

\[
 \ell=\log|t|<0,\qquad R(t)=-2\pi\operatorname{Im}C(t),\qquad
 A(t)=\ell B_0+R(t).
\]
For a representative \(\zeta=Z(s)u+k\), where \(u,k\in\mathbb R^2\),
\(\operatorname{Im}s=-\ell/(2\pi)\) gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}\log|x_1|\\\log|x_2|\end{pmatrix}
 =A(t)u.
 \hypertarget{tag-038L}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:moduli}
\end{equation}
The quotient value is \(u\bmod\mathbb Z^2\).

\begin{equation}

 \hypertarget{tag-038K}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:invertibility}
\end{equation}

sufficiently small punctured disc.

the appropriate original period, equivalently applying
\(\Psi_{-\lambda}\), gives a representative with the exact lift
\(u=u^0\). This representative is unique: another residual translate
has logarithmic moduli differing by \(A(t)\lambda\), which vanishes
only for \(\lambda=0\). Conversely every dense-torus point satisfying
\(\log|x|=A(t)u^0\) has this quotient value, since the remaining real
parts of \(\zeta\) are exactly the kernel coordinates \(k\).
For each fixed \(t\), varying \(k\bmod\mathbb Z^2\) gives all independent

\item The following change of coordinates uses the full original period units:
\begin{align}
 h_j^0(t)&=\exp\bigl(-2\pi i(C(t)u^0)_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,2,\\
 \mathcal F(z_0,z_1,z_2)

 \hypertarget{tag-038Q}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:straightening}
\end{align}
The functions \(h_j^0\) are nowhere-zero holomorphic units, including
at \(t=0\). The product \(w_0w_1w_2\) is exactly \(t\).
The inverse of \(\mathcal F\) is
\[
 (w_0,w_1,w_2)\longmapsto
 \left(w_0h_1^0(t)h_2^0(t),\,
 \frac{w_1}{h_1^0(t)},\,\frac{w_2}{h_2^0(t)}\right),
 \qquad t=w_0w_1w_2.
\]
Thus this is a biholomorphism of the original chart restricted to the
cusp disc, not a replacement of \(C(t)\).

\item For \(r_0\in(0,\epsilon)\), the entire inverse image of
\(y_0=[r_0,c(\overline u^0)]\) becomes exactly
\begin{equation}
 T_{r_0}=
 \{|w_0|=\rho_0,\ |w_1|=\rho_1,\ |w_2|=\rho_2\},\qquad
 (\rho_0,\rho_1,\rho_2)=
 (r_0^{1/2},r_0^{1/4},r_0^{1/4}).
 \hypertarget{tag-038R}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:torus}
\end{equation}
Indeed, \(\log|h^0(t)|=2\pi\operatorname{Im}C(t)u^0=-R(t)u^0\),
so \eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:moduli} gives \(\log|w_j|=\ell(B_0u^0)_j\) for
\(j=1,2\); the product identity gives the exponent \(1/2\) for
\(w_0\). Conversely these moduli recover \(u=u^0\) by invertibility
of \(A(t)\). The angular map is explicitly
\phantomsection\hypertarget{tag-033Q}{}\label{qa:III:layout:1}
\[
\begin{gathered}
 (\arg t,\arg w_1,\arg w_2)\longleftrightarrow
 (\arg w_0,\arg w_1,\arg w_2),\\
 \arg w_0=\arg t-\arg w_1-\arg w_2\pmod{2\pi},
\end{gathered}
\]
with inverse \(\arg t=\arg w_0+\arg w_1+\arg w_2\).
Its integral matrix has determinant one. This includes the complete
angular mapping torus and all kernel phases, with their original signs.

\item Let \(o\) be the origin of \eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:chart}. The original free properly
discontinuous action supplies a neighborhood \(V\) of \(o\) on which
the quotient projection is injective. To see the local injectivity
directly, first choose a relatively compact neighborhood; proper
discontinuity leaves only finitely many translates that can intersect it.
None of those nonidentity translates fixes \(o\). Shrinking finitely
many times separates the neighborhood from all of them. The quotient
map is a local biholomorphism, so its restriction to \(V\) is a chart
of the original source.
Choose a polydisc about \(0\) whose closure lies in \(\mathcal F(V)\).
For sufficiently small \(r_0\), both \(T_{r_0}\) and
\begin{equation}
 \{|w_0|\leq\rho_0,\ |w_1|=\rho_1,\ |w_2|=\rho_2\}
 \hypertarget{tag-038P}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:spatial-bound}
\end{equation}
lie in this polydisc. This proves that the whole inverse image embeds
in one chart and supplies space for the bounding manifold below.

\item \textbf{2. The actual normal framing, including its angle dependence.}
Put \(L_j=\log|w_j|\), and use the unique real lift of the quotient
coordinate near \(u^0\). From the exact change of coordinates,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}L_1\\L_2\end{pmatrix}
 =\ell B_0u^0+A(t)(u-u^0),\qquad
 L_0=\ell-L_1-L_2.
 \hypertarget{tag-038M}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:nearby-moduli}
\end{equation}
Differentiating on \(u=u^0\) annihilates the term
\((dA(t))(u-u^0)\). Hence no derivative of \(C(t)\) has been omitted:
the exact differential there is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}dL_0\\dL_1\\dL_2\end{pmatrix}
 =J(t)\begin{pmatrix}d\ell\\du_1\\du_2\end{pmatrix},\quad
 J(t)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1/2&-A_{11}-A_{21}&-A_{12}-A_{22}\\
 1/4&A_{11}&A_{12}\\
 1/4&A_{21}&A_{22}
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038B}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:J}
\end{equation}
Adding the second and third rows to the first gives \((1,0,0)\),
and expansion in that row proves \(\det J(t)=\det A(t)\).

\item Let \(D=Dc_{\overline u^0}\) be the actual two-by-two derivative in
the ordered open-cell target coordinates \((c_1,c_2)\). It is a fixed
invertible matrix; all its entries and signs are retained. Let
\[
 H=\begin{pmatrix}r_0&0&0\\0&D_{11}&D_{12}\\0&D_{21}&D_{22}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Let \(n_j\) be the real radial vector \(w_j\) in the \(j\)-th complex
coordinate, with other components zero. Then \(dL_i(n_j)=\delta_{ij}\).
Writing \(N=(n_0,n_1,n_2)\) as the matrix with these vector columns, the actual
\(dg\)-dual normal framing is, in the normal quotient bundle,
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak n(t)=N J(t)H^{-1}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038F}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:actual-frame}
\end{equation}
Indeed, \(dg(N)=HJ(t)^{-1}\), so multiplication by \(J(t)H^{-1}\)
gives the identity. In the Euclidean metric of this chart the radial
vectors are perpendicular to the product torus; a different source
metric changes their representatives by the canonical projection to its
normal bundle and preserves this normal-quotient framing.

\item Put \(\ell_0=\log r_0\). Decrease \(r_0\) further, if necessary, so
that \(|\ell_0|>2\sup_{|t|\leq r_0}\|R(t)\|\). For
\(0\leq\sigma\leq1\), define only a homotopy of frames by
\[
 A_\sigma(t)=\ell_0B_0+\sigma R(t),
\]
and let \(J_\sigma(t)\) be \eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:J} with \(A_\sigma\) in place
of \(A\). For every \(v\in\mathbb R^2\),
\[
 \|A_\sigma(t)v\|\geq
 (|\ell_0|-\|R(t)\|)\|v\|>0\quad(v\ne0).
\]
Thus all matrices are invertible. At \(\sigma=0\),
\begin{equation}
 J_0=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1/2&\ell_0&-\ell_0\\
 1/4&0&\ell_0\\
 1/4&-\ell_0&0
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \det J_0=\ell_0^2>0.
 \hypertarget{tag-038C}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:J0}
\end{equation}
Continuity also proves \(\det J_\sigma(t)>0\) for every \(\sigma,t\).
The homotopy \(N J_\sigma(t)H^{-1}\), run from \(\sigma=1\) to
\(\sigma=0\), compares the actual frame with the exact constant-matrix
frame \(N P\), where
\begin{equation}
 P=J_0H^{-1}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038D}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:P}
\end{equation}
The original embedded torus and original functions \(C(t)\) have not
changed. A framing homotopy is a framed cylinder: choose a smooth
parameter function constant near its endpoints and use the displayed
frames on \(T_{r_0}\times[0,1]\).

\item \textbf{3. A collared framed nullbordism with the exact constant matrix.}
Use a new time coordinate \(v\in[0,1]\). Define
\begin{equation}
 q(v)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&0\leq v\leq1/4,\\
 \rho_0^2\exp\bigl(4-1/(v-1/4)\bigr),&1/4<v\leq1.
 \end{cases}
 \hypertarget{tag-038O}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:q}
\end{equation}
This function is smooth: all right derivatives of
\(\exp(-1/(v-1/4))\) at \(1/4\) vanish. It is strictly increasing
for \(v>1/4\), satisfies \(q(1/2)=\rho_0^2\), and
\(q'(1/2)=16\rho_0^2>0\).
In the chart times \([0,1]\), put
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal W=
 \{|w_0|^2+q(v)=\rho_0^2,\quad
       |w_1|^2=\rho_1^2,\quad|w_2|^2=\rho_2^2\}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038G}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:bordism}
\end{equation}
No point has \(v>1/2\). The three defining differentials are independent:
the latter two have nonzero gradients in their separate complex factors;
the first has nonzero \(w_0\)-gradient whenever \(w_0\ne0\), and at
\(w_0=0\) it has the nonzero \(v\)-derivative \(q'(1/2)\).
Thus \(\mathcal W\) is a smooth compact four-manifold. Its only
boundary is \(T_{r_0}\times\{0\}\), and on \(0\leq v\leq1/4\)
it is the exact product collar \(T_{r_0}\times[0,1/4]\).
The north locus \(w_0=0,v=1/2\) is an interior cap: the implicit
function theorem expresses \(v\) smoothly in terms of
\((\operatorname{Re}w_0,\operatorname{Im}w_0)\) there. The first
factor is a disk obtained by rotating its radial profile with this smooth
cap and one boundary circle. Therefore
\(\mathcal W\cong D^2\times T^2\).
Its spatial coordinates lie in \eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:spatial-bound}, so the complete
manifold lies in the injective original chart.

\item In the Euclidean chart product metric define
\[
 V_0=(w_0,0,0,q'(v)/2),\qquad
 V_1=(0,w_1,0,0),\qquad V_2=(0,0,w_2,0).
\]
These are one half of the gradients of the three defining equations
in \eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:bordism}. They are mutually orthogonal and never zero.
For example, if \(F_0=|w_0|^2+q(v)-\rho_0^2\), then
\[
 dF_0(V_0)=2|w_0|^2+\frac12q'(v)^2>0
\]
at every point of \(\mathcal W\). On the entire collar \(q'=0\), so
\((V_0,V_1,V_2)=(N,0)\) exactly. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 (V_0,V_1,V_2)P
 \hypertarget{tag-038I}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:extended-frame}
\end{equation}
is a framing of the normal three-plane bundle of \(\mathcal W\),
and its restriction to the collar is exactly the framing \(NP\) from
\eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:P}, with every original target-coordinate sign retained.
Concatenate the framing cylinder of the preceding paragraph with this
nullbordism, rescaling the two interval lengths. Their framings agree
exactly on the common product collar, so the concatenation is a smooth
framed nullbordism of the actual inverse image.

\item \textbf{4. The based map represented by this framed inverse image.}
Choose the injective chart to exclude \(x_0\) if its center is not
\(x_0\). If its center is \(x_0\), the constructed nullbordism still
excludes \(x_0\), since \(|w_1|=\rho_1>0\) and
\(|w_2|=\rho_2>0\) everywhere on it. Compactness therefore gives
tubular neighborhoods for the framed cylinder and cap disjoint from
\(\{x_0\}\times[0,1]\).

\item The original continuous quotient map is smooth and a submersion near
its entire inverse image of \(y_0\). First make it constant in a
neighborhood of \(x_0\), by a based homotopy that changes nothing near
that inverse image. Explicitly, take a target chart
\(\kappa:O\to\mathbb R^3\) with \(\kappa(*)=0\), whose image is a ball,
and \(y_0\notin O\). By continuity choose a neighborhood \(U\) of
\(x_0\) with \(g(U)\subset O\), and a smooth bump function
\(\beta\) supported in \(U\) and equal to one near \(x_0\).
For \(x\in U\), replace \(g(x)\) during this homotopy by
\(\kappa^{-1}((1-a\beta(x))\kappa(g(x)))\), \(0\leq a\leq1\),
and leave \(g\) fixed off \(U\). Convexity of the target chart image
makes the formula well-defined, the vanishing of \(\beta\) near the
boundary of its support proves continuity of the pasted formula, and
\(\kappa(g(x_0))=0\) makes the homotopy based. It never introduces
an inverse image of \(y_0\). Its endpoint is smooth near \(x_0\) and
agrees with \(g\) near the entire old inverse image.

\item Denote the endpoint of the preceding homotopy by \(g_b\). Choose one
closed tubular neighborhood \(U_1\) of the inverse image, contained in
the smooth submersion region and with the entire inverse image contained
in \(\operatorname{int}U_1\). The compact set
\(X\setminus\operatorname{int}U_1\) has image under \(g_b\) missing
\(y_0\). In a fixed target metric put
\[
 d_0=\min_{x\in X\setminus\operatorname{int}U_1}
       d(g_b(x),y_0)>0.
\]
Relative smooth approximation, fixed on the whole closed set \(U_1\)
and on a neighborhood of \(x_0\), gives a smooth based representative
\(g_{\mathrm{sm}}\) whose error on
\(X\setminus\operatorname{int}U_1\) is less than \(d_0/2\).
One explicit relative approximation is obtained by embedding $S^3$ in $\mathbb R^4$, smoothing the coordinate functions by convolution in finitely many source charts and a partition of unity, and interpolating this approximation with $g_b$ using a smooth cutoff equal to one on the protected neighborhoods and supported where $g_b$ is smooth. Radial projection $v\mapsto v/\|v\|$ returns the result to $S^3$. A sufficiently small uniform error keeps $v$ nonzero, fixes the protected values exactly, and has the required target error; short target geodesics give the relative homotopy. It therefore has the same inverse image and differential on \(U_1\),
and \(d(g_{\mathrm{sm}}(x),y_0)>d_0/2\) on its complement. Thus there
is no uncontrolled intervening region and no additional inverse image.
Make the approximation also closer than a fixed target injectivity
radius; its short geodesics give the based homotopy.

\item The relative Pontryagin construction now applies to the explicit
framed nullbordism. It produces a based homotopy to a map missing
\(y_0\); stereographic contraction of \(S^3\setminus\{y_0\}\cong\mathbb R^3\)
to the image of \(*\) is based and contracts that last map.
For completeness, the dependence on the framed inverse image in this
argument is precisely the local product-neighborhood construction and
the interpolation lemma of \cite[\S7, Theorem B and Lemma 4,
pp.~43, 48--50]{CuspNullMilnor1965}. Their relative versions fix the source
basepoint because all tubular modifications are away from it and
stereographic interpolation between equal values keeps that value
fixed. A framed cylinder realizes a framing homotopy; the empty
Pontryagin manifold realizes a map missing the chosen regular value.
This proves the claimed based null-homotopy of the exact map \(g\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A framed nullbordism of the cusp fibre]
\hypertarget{tag-038S}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:thm}
The based map $g:(X,x_0)\to(S^3,*)$ of
\eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:g} is based null-homotopic.
There is an interior regular value whose inverse image, with the
ordered normal framing induced by $(r,c_1,c_2)$, is framed nullbordant
in one cusp coordinate chart times $[0,1]$, disjoint from
$\{x_0\}\times[0,1]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The based marking
\[
 \beta:[a\widehat\gamma+b\widehat u]\longmapsto[a,b],
 \qquad \beta^{-1}:[a,b]\longmapsto[a\widehat\gamma+b\widehat u]
\]
gives inverse torus maps carrying the two marked coordinate circles
onto the two coordinate circles. It induces inverse maps
$\bar\beta$ and $\bar\beta^{-1}$ on the skeleton collapses, and
inverse suspension maps $[r,z]\mapsto[r,\bar\beta(z)]$ and
$[r,z]\mapsto[r,\bar\beta^{-1}(z)]$.
Under the first suspension map the angle-forgetting map of
\cref{mapsIII:angle-forgotten-one-copy-null} is exactly $g$ on the
punctured cusp and at both collapsed radial ends.
Composing its based null-homotopy with this suspension homeomorphism
proves the first assertion.

For the framed inverse image, set
\[
 u^0=\binom{-1/4}{1/4},\qquad
 \overline u^0=(3/4,1/4),\qquad
 p^0=B_0u^0=\binom{1/4}{1/4}.
\]
Use the injective chart of \cref{wb:h24:ret:chart-lemma}, whose
toric coordinates are
\begin{equation}
 z_0=t/(x_1x_2),\qquad z_1=x_1,\qquad z_2=x_2,
 \qquad t=z_0z_1z_2.
 \hypertarget{tag-038H}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:chart}
\end{equation}
Write $\ell=\log|t|$, $R(t)=-2\pi\operatorname{Im}C(t)$ and
$A(t)=\ell B_0+R(t)$. The marking $\zeta=Z(s)u+k$, with
$u,k\in\mathbb R^2$ and $\operatorname{Im}s=-\ell/(2\pi)$, gives
\begin{equation}
 \binom{\log|x_1|}{\log|x_2|}=A(t)u.
 \hypertarget{tag-038L}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:moduli}
\end{equation}
Since $B_0^TB_0=I_2$, the reverse triangle inequality gives
\begin{equation}
 \|A(t)v\|\geq\bigl(|\ell|-\|R(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\bigr)\|v\|.
 \hypertarget{tag-038K}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:invertibility}
\end{equation}
The chart uses the full holomorphic units
\begin{align}
 h_j^0(t)&=\exp\bigl(-2\pi i(C(t)u^0)_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,2,\\
 \mathcal F(z_0,z_1,z_2)&=
 \left(\frac{z_0}{h_1^0(t)h_2^0(t)},
 h_1^0(t)z_1,h_2^0(t)z_2\right)=(w_0,w_1,w_2).
 \hypertarget{tag-038Q}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:straightening}
\end{align}
Its inverse is
\[
 (w_0,w_1,w_2)\longmapsto
 \left(w_0h_1^0(t)h_2^0(t),\frac{w_1}{h_1^0(t)},
 \frac{w_2}{h_2^0(t)}\right),\qquad t=w_0w_1w_2.
\]
Both formulas hold on the central coordinate planes as well.
The cited chart lemma gives inverse coordinate maps
$\phi:W_\delta\to U\subset X$ and $\phi^{-1}$, where
$W_\delta=\{|w_j|<\delta\}$, $0<\delta<1$; all nonidentity
period translates of $\mathcal F^{-1}(W_\delta)$ are disjoint.

On the closed period disc $|t|\leq a_0$ of that lemma, put
$M_R=\max\|R(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and choose
\[
 0<r_0<\min\{\delta^4,e^{-(2M_R+1)}\},\qquad
 \ell_0=\log r_0.
\]
The relation $\delta^3<a_0<\epsilon$ ensures that this choice is
inside the original cusp disc. We will also impose a basepoint
bound below. Set $y_0=[r_0,c(\overline u^0)]$.
Because $y_0$ is in the open target cell, its inverse image has
$|t|=r_0$ and $[u]=[u^0]$.
Applying the period translate $\Psi_{-\lambda}$ to a lift
$u=u^0+\lambda$ gives $u=u^0$. A residual translate changes
the logarithmic moduli by $A(t)\lambda$; invertibility from
\eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:invertibility} makes this lift unique.
The real kernel coordinates $k\bmod\mathbb Z^2$ supply all
independent phases of $x_1,x_2$.

Since $\log|h^0|=-R(t)u^0$, the complete inverse image is
\begin{equation}
 T_{r_0}=\{|w_0|=\rho_0,\ |w_1|=\rho_1,\ |w_2|=\rho_2\},
 \qquad (\rho_0,\rho_1,\rho_2)
 =(r_0^{1/2},r_0^{1/4},r_0^{1/4}).
 \hypertarget{tag-038R}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:torus}
\end{equation}
Conversely these moduli give $A(t)(u-u^0)=0$ and hence the same
quotient value. Its angular coordinates and their inverse are
\phantomsection\hypertarget{tag-033Q}{}\label{qa:III:layout:1}
\[
 (\varphi,a,b)\longmapsto(\varphi-a-b,a,b),\qquad
 (\theta_0,a,b)\longmapsto(\theta_0+a+b,a,b)
 \quad\pmod{2\pi}.
\]
Thus the full inverse image is the embedded three-torus
$(\rho_0e^{i(\varphi-a-b)},\rho_1e^{ia},\rho_2e^{ib})$.
Both it and the compact spatial set
\begin{equation}
 \{|w_0|\leq\rho_0,\ |w_1|=\rho_1,\ |w_2|=\rho_2\}
 \subset W_\delta
 \hypertarget{tag-038P}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:spatial-bound}
\end{equation}
lie in the injective chart: $\rho_1=\rho_2<\delta$ and
$\rho_0<\delta^2<\delta$.

Put $L_j=\log|w_j|$ and use the real lift $u$ near $u^0$.
The coordinate formulas give
\begin{equation}
 \binom{L_1}{L_2}=\ell B_0u^0+A(t)(u-u^0),\qquad
 L_0=\ell-L_1-L_2.
 \hypertarget{tag-038M}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:nearby-moduli}
\end{equation}
On the fibre $u=u^0$, the derivative term $(dA)(u-u^0)$ vanishes.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}dL_0\\dL_1\\dL_2\end{pmatrix}
 =J(t)\begin{pmatrix}d\ell\\du_1\\du_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 J(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
 1/2&-A_{11}-A_{21}&-A_{12}-A_{22}\\
 1/4&A_{11}&A_{12}\\
 1/4&A_{21}&A_{22}
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038B}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:J}
\end{equation}
Adding the last two rows to the first gives $(1,0,0)$, so
$\det J(t)=\det A(t)\ne0$.
Let $D=Dc_{\overline u^0}$ in the ordered open target cell,
and set $H=\operatorname{diag}(r_0,D)$.
For the open-cell coordinates $(u_1+1,u_2)$, $D=I_2$; the matrix
$H$ records the derivative of $(\ell,u)$ to $(r,c_1,c_2)$.
Let $n_j$ be the radial vector $w_j$ in complex coordinate $j$,
and put $N=(n_0,n_1,n_2)$. Since $dL_i(n_j)=\delta_{ij}$,
$dg(N)=HJ(t)^{-1}$, and the induced ordered normal framing is
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak n(t)=NJ(t)H^{-1}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038F}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:actual-frame}
\end{equation}
These vectors are normal in the Euclidean chart metric. For another
metric, orthogonal projection identifies their quotient-normal classes
with the corresponding metric normal vectors; the inverse sends a
normal vector to its class modulo the tangent bundle.

For $0\leq\sigma\leq1$, let
$A_\sigma(t)=\ell_0B_0+\sigma R(t)$ on $|t|=r_0$ and form
$J_\sigma$ from the same matrix formula.
For $v\ne0$, the bound
$\|A_\sigma v\|\geq(|\ell_0|-M_R)\|v\|>0$
makes every $J_\sigma$ invertible. At $\sigma=0$,
\begin{equation}
 J_0=\begin{pmatrix}
 1/2&\ell_0&-\ell_0\\
 1/4&0&\ell_0\\
 1/4&-\ell_0&0
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \det J_0=\ell_0^2>0.
 \hypertarget{tag-038C}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:J0}
\end{equation}
Run $NJ_\sigma H^{-1}$ from $\sigma=1$ to $\sigma=0$, using
a smooth time parameter constant near its endpoints.
This gives a framed product cylinder from $\mathfrak n$ to
$NP$, where
\begin{equation}
 P=J_0H^{-1}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038D}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:P}
\end{equation}

For the cap use a new time coordinate $v\in[0,1]$ and define
\begin{equation}
 q(v)=\begin{cases}
 0,&0\leq v\leq1/4,\\
 \rho_0^2\exp\bigl(4-1/(v-1/4)\bigr),&1/4<v\leq1.
 \end{cases}
 \hypertarget{tag-038O}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:q}
\end{equation}
All right derivatives at $1/4$ vanish. The function increases for
$v>1/4$, with $q(1/2)=\rho_0^2$ and
$q'(1/2)=16\rho_0^2$.
In $W_\delta\times[0,1]$, set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal W=\{|w_0|^2+q(v)=\rho_0^2,
 |w_1|^2=\rho_1^2,
 |w_2|^2=\rho_2^2\}.
 \hypertarget{tag-038G}{}\label{wb:cusp-null:eq:bordism}
\end{equation}
The three defining differentials are independent. The first has a
nonzero $w_0$ derivative off $w_0=0$, and at $w_0=0$ its time
derivative is $q'(1/2)>0$; the last two have nonzero derivatives in
their separate complex factors. This is a compact smooth
four-manifold with only boundary $T_{r_0}\times\{0\}$ and exact
collar $T_{r_0}\times[0,1/4]$; there are no points with $v>1/2$.
For an explicit parametrization of its disk factor, take
$z\in\overline{\mathbb D}$ and put
\[
 v=\frac{1-|z|^2}{2},\qquad w_0=f(|z|^2)z,
 \qquad
 f(s)=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_0^2-q((1-s)/2)}{s}},\quad
 f(0)=\sqrt{q'(1/2)/2}.
\]
The numerator has a simple zero with positive derivative at $s=0$,
so $f$ extends smoothly and positively. At $z=0$ the
$w_0$ derivative is $f(0)I_2$; elsewhere the radial time derivative
and angular $w_0$ derivative are nonzero.
Time recovers $|z|$ and the $w_0$ phase recovers its angle.
Thus this is an embedding onto the disk factor, giving
$\mathcal W\cong\overline{\mathbb D}\times T^2$.
Its spatial coordinates satisfy \eqref{wb:cusp-null:eq:spatial-bound}.

In the chart product metric, let
\[
 V_0=(w_0,0,0,q'(v)/2),\qquad
 V_1=(0,w_1,0,0),\qquad V_2=(0,0,w_2,0).
\]
They are half the three defining gradients, mutually orthogonal and
nonzero. In particular the first defining differential takes the

 \qquad \Theta_g([n])=n[g],
\]

$\chi:\pi_6(S^3)\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$,
$\chi\circ\Theta_g=0$.
The associated multiplicative character
$e^{2\pi i\chi}\circ\Theta_g$ is identically $1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $d:(S^6,*)\to(X,x_0)$ be the fixed based identification and
$H_g$ the based null-homotopy of \cref{wb:cusp-null:thm}.
The formula $H(u,s)=H_g(d(u),s)$ has initial map $g\circ d$,
constant terminal map and fixed basepoint, so $[g]=0$.
The right and left sixfold suspension homotopies have formulas
$([u,v],s)\mapsto[H(u,s),v]$ and

has value zero on every class.  Each additive character sends this
value to $0\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, whose exponential is $1$.

\begin{theorem}[One fixed cusp-adapted metric realizes the vertical
\(\mathbb R^4\) limits]
\hypertarget{tag-03D6}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}
\StatementRecord{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}{proved}{03D6}{\SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-normalized-Q-limit}}

There are fixed compatible length metrics
\[
 D_{12}\text{ on }Z_{12},\qquad
 D_{24}^{\mathcal B}\text{ on }Z_{24}^{\mathcal B},\qquad
 D_{24}^{\mathcal C}\text{ on }Z_{24}^{\mathcal C}
\]
with the following properties.

On the inner cone of \(\mathcal A\), the metric is induced by
\begin{equation}
 g_{\mathcal A}
 =dr^2+r^2du^2+\frac{r^2}{T(r)^2}h_{T(r)}.
 \hypertarget{tag-03CW}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-A-fixed-metric}
\end{equation}
On the cusp cone of either \(\mathcal B\) or \(\mathcal C\), it is induced
by
\begin{equation}
 g_{\mathcal D}=dr^2+r^2(du^2+d\theta^2),
 \qquad\mathcal D\in\{\mathcal B,\mathcal C\}.
 \hypertarget{tag-03CY}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-BC-fixed-metric}
\end{equation}
The metrics on the smash powers are the metric quotients of the product
length metrics after the closed fat wedge is collapsed.  Write
\(g_{Z_{12}}\) and \(g_{Z_{24}^{\mathcal D}}\) for the resulting smooth
Riemannian tensors on the open regular strata.

Let
\[
 p_T^{12}:=j_T(0,0),\qquad
 p_T^{24,\mathcal D}:=k_T^{\mathcal D}(0,0,0,0).
\]
Put
\[
 \Sigma_T^{12}:=j_T(Q_T^2),\qquad
 \Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D}:=k_T^{\mathcal D}(C_T^4).
\]
Let \(d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{slice}}\) and
\(d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{slice}}\) be the intrinsic Riemannian path
metrics of the first fundamental forms on these embedded slices.  These
must be distinguished from the restricted ambient distance functions
\[
 d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{amb}}
 :=D_{12}|_{\Sigma_T^{12}\times\Sigma_T^{12}},\qquad
 d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{amb}}
 :=D_{24}^{\mathcal D}|_{\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D}
                         \times\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D}}.
\]
In general the latter can be smaller, because an ambient path is allowed
to leave the slice.

Then the induced first fundamental forms on the target slices satisfy the
exact identities
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{T}{r_T}\right)^2
  j_T^*g_{Z_{12}}
 =g_{Q_T}\oplus g_{Q_T},
 \hypertarget{tag-03CX}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-A-slice-exact}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{\ell_T}{r_T}\right)^2
  (k_T^{\mathcal D})^*g_{Z_{24}^{\mathcal D}}
 =g_{C_T}^{\oplus4}.
 \hypertarget{tag-03CZ}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-BC-slice-exact}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \left(\Sigma_T^{12},\frac{T}{r_T}d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{slice}},
       p_T^{12}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^4,0),\\
 \left(\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D},
       \frac{\ell_T}{r_T}d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{slice}},
       p_T^{24,\mathcal D}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^4,0)
 \hypertarget{tag-03DE}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-slice-fixed-blowups}
\end{align}
in pointed local-isometric and pointed Gromov--Hausdorff topology, and
smoothly on the exhausting Euclidean slice balls.

The full ambient pointed blow-ups are instead
\begin{align}
 \left(Z_{12},\frac{T}{r_T}D_{12},p_T^{12}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^8,0),\\
 \left(Z_{24}^{\mathcal D},
       \frac{\ell_T}{r_T}D_{24}^{\mathcal D},
       p_T^{24,\mathcal D}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{12},0).
 \hypertarget{tag-03D3}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-ambient-fixed-blowups}
\end{align}
as pointed metric spaces in pointed Gromov--Hausdorff topology.  More
precisely, for every fixed radius the corresponding rescaled target ball is
eventually contained in an open regular-stratum coordinate neighborhood,
and the pulled-back Riemannian tensors converge there in every \(C^k\) norm.
Thus smooth convergence is asserted on an exhaustion by regular-stratum
neighborhoods, not globally on the singular compact targets.  Under these
limits, the slice \(\mathbb R^4\) is respectively the coordinate subspace
obtained by fixing the two radial and two base-angle coordinates, or by
fixing the four radial and four base-angle coordinates.
\end{theorem}



\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item Equation \eqref{wb:sphere-metric-normalized-Q-limit} shows that the metrics on
the compact cross-sections of \eqref{wb:sphere-metric-A-fixed-metric} remain
uniformly bounded and converge to a positive definite flat metric.
Therefore the cross-section diameter is \(O(r)\).  Moreover the radial
coordinate is \(1\)-Lipschitz and a radial segment from level \(r\) to the
vertex has length \(r\).  The length completion consequently adds exactly
one point at \(r=0\), and its topology is the prescribed cone topology.
The same assertions are immediate for
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-BC-fixed-metric}.  Interpolation on a closed annulus
away from the vertex extends these metrics to fixed compatible length
metrics on the compact spaces \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B,\mathcal C\).

\item If a compact metric space \((E,d)\) and a closed subset \(W\subset E\) are
given, the metric quotient which collapses \(W\) to one point is
\[
 d_{E/W}([x],[y])
 =\min\{d(x,y),d(x,W)+d(y,W)\}.
\]
Applying this to the fat wedges in the product length spaces gives the
claimed fixed compatible metrics on the smash targets.

\item On the \(r_T\)-slice of \(\mathcal A\), with \(u=0\), the first fundamental
form is
\[
 \frac{r_T^2}{T^2}h_T.
\]
The definition \(h_T=\iota_T^*g_{Q_T}\) proves
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-A-slice-exact}.  On the \(r_T\)-slice of
\(\mathcal B\) or \(\mathcal C\), with \(u=0\), the form is
\(r_T^2d\theta^2\).  Under
\(\vartheta_T:[\theta]\mapsto[\ell_T\theta]\), the native quotient-circle
metric is \(\ell_T^2d\theta^2\).  This proves
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-BC-slice-exact}.  The native systole estimates
\[
 \operatorname{sys}(Q_T^2)\geq T-C,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{sys}(C_T^4)=\ell_T
\]
then prove \eqref{wb:sphere-metric-slice-fixed-blowups}: every prescribed
radius ball is eventually exactly a Euclidean four-ball.

\item It remains to compute the ambient limits.  In one \(\mathcal A\)-factor,
put
\[
 \lambda_T=\frac{T}{r_T},\qquad
 s=\lambda_T(r-r_T),\qquad
 \eta=Tu,\qquad z=Y_Tx
\]
on the universal cover of the torus directions.  On every fixed bounded
set in \((s,\eta,z)\), one has
\[
 \frac r{r_T}=1+\frac sT,
 \qquad
 T(r)=T+O(T^{-1}),
 \qquad
 Y_{T(r)}Y_T^{-1}=I+O(T^{-2}),
\]
with the same estimates after any fixed number of derivatives.  Thus
\(\lambda_T^2g_{\mathcal A}\) converges in these coordinates to
\[
 ds^2+d\eta^2+dz_1^2+dz_2^2.
\]
The inward radial boundary is at distance \(T\), the \(u\)-period is \(T\),
and the \(z\)-period lattice is \(Y_T\mathbb Z^2\), whose systole is at
least \(T-C\).  The outward edge of the fixed cusp chart is also at scaled
distance
\[
 \frac{T}{r_T}(r_0-r_T)
 =T\left(\frac{r_0}{r_T}-1\right)\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus the inward vertex, all periods, and the outward edge recede to
infinity.  A single factor converges on exhausting regular-stratum
coordinate neighborhoods to \(\mathbb R^4\), and two factors converge to
\(\mathbb R^8\).

\item For one \(\mathcal B\)- or \(\mathcal C\)-factor, put
\[
 \lambda_T=\frac{\ell_T}{r_T},\qquad
 s=\lambda_T(r-r_T),\qquad
 \eta=\ell_Tu,\qquad \zeta=\ell_T\theta.
\]
Then
\[
 \lambda_T^2g_{\mathcal D}
 =ds^2+\left(\frac r{r_T}\right)^2
       (d\eta^2+d\zeta^2),
\]
which converges smoothly on bounded coordinate sets to the Euclidean metric
on \(\mathbb R^3\).  The two circle periods and the inward radial boundary
are all at scaled distance \(\ell_T\to\infty\), while the outward edge is
at scaled distance
\[
 \frac{\ell_T}{r_T}(r_0-r_T)
 =\ell_T\left(\frac{r_0}{r_T}-1\right)\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Four factors therefore converge on exhausting regular-stratum coordinate
neighborhoods to \(\mathbb R^{12}\).

\item Finally, a level-\(r_T\) factor point has distance exactly \(r_T\) from its
cone vertex.  Indeed, the radial segment has that length.  A competing
curve contained in the inner chart has length at least \(r_T\), while one
which leaves has inner-chart portions of total length at least
\((r_0-r_T)+r_0>r_T\).  The Riemannian-\(\ell^2\)-product distance from a
synchronized point to the fat wedge is the minimum of the factor
distances, and hence is also \(r_T\).

\item For the chosen scale put
\[
 b_T=\lambda_Tr_T,\qquad a_T=\lambda_T(r_0-r_T),
\]
and let \(\sigma_T\) be the least scaled period in a factor.  Thus
\(\sigma_T\geq T-C\) in the \(\mathcal A\) calculation and
\(\sigma_T=\ell_T\) in the \(\mathcal B,\mathcal C\) calculation.  The
preceding computations give
\[
 a_T\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 b_T\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 \sigma_T\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Fix \(R\).  A curve of rescaled length at most \(R\) from \(p_T\) meets
neither the fat wedge nor \(r=r_0\) for all large \(T\), so the
radius-\(R\) target ball lies in the open regular stratum.  If \(x,y\) lie
in that ball, a competitor through the fat wedge has length at least
\[
 (b_T-R)+(b_T-R)>2R,
\]
and a competitor which exits the inner chart and returns has length at
least
\[
 2(a_T-R)>2R.
\]
Every remaining competitor of length at most \(2R\) stays in
\(r/r_T=1+o_R(1)\).  After lifting it to the angular and torus covers, a
nonzero deck translation has length at least
\((1-o_R(1))(\sigma_T-2R)>2R\) for all large \(T\).  Since the path through
\(p_T\) has length at most \(2R\), none of these three kinds of global
shortcut computes the distance between \(x\) and \(y\).  Thus the metric
on every fixed target ball is computed entirely in one lifted
regular-stratum chart.  The \(C^\infty\) convergence of the pulled-back
tensors on these exhausting charts implies the pointed
Gromov--Hausdorff limits in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-ambient-fixed-blowups}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

in pointed local-isometric and pointed Gromov--Hausdorff topology, and
smoothly on the exhausting Euclidean slice balls.

The full ambient pointed blow-ups are
\begin{align}
 \left(Z_{12},\frac{T}{r_T}D_{12},p_T^{12}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^8,0),\\
 \left(Z_{24}^{\mathcal D},
       \frac{\ell_T}{r_T}D_{24}^{\mathcal D},
       p_T^{24,\mathcal D}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{12},0).
 \hypertarget{tag-03D3}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-ambient-fixed-blowups}
\end{align}
as pointed metric spaces in pointed Gromov--Hausdorff topology.  More
precisely, for every fixed radius the corresponding rescaled target ball is
eventually contained in an open regular-stratum coordinate neighborhood,
and the pulled-back Riemannian tensors converge there in every \(C^k\) norm.
The smooth convergence uses an exhaustion by these regular-stratum
neighborhoods.  Under these limits, the slice \(\mathbb R^4\) is
respectively the coordinate subspace
obtained by fixing the two radial and two base-angle coordinates, or by
fixing the four radial and four base-angle coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write the period matrix on the radial locus as
\[
 Y_T=TJ+E(r_T),\qquad
 J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 E(t)=\begin{pmatrix}6m(t)&H(t)\\B(t)-H(t)&m(t)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The entries of \(E\) are the imaginary parts on the real \(t\)-axis of
the holomorphic residual functions.  They and all their derivatives of
each fixed order are bounded on the closed cusp interval.  Put
\(C_E=\sup_{0\leq t\leq r_0}\|E(t)\|\).  Since \(J\) is orthogonal,
\[
 (T-C_E)|v|\leq |Y_Tv|\leq(T+C_E)|v|.
\]
In particular \(T^{-2}h_T\) has coefficient matrix
\((J+E(r_T)/T)^{\mathsf T}(J+E(r_T)/T)\), which tends to \(I\).
Invertibility on the remaining compact part of the parameter interval
gives constants \(0<c_-\leq1\leq c_+\) such that
\[
 c_-|v|\leq |M(r)v|\leq c_+|v|,
 \qquad M(r):=J+\frac{E(r)}{T(r)},\quad 0<r\leq r_0.
\]
The exact quotient-circle formula also gives
\[
 \ell_T=\min_{z\in\mathbb R}|Y_T(1,z)|\geq T-C_E.
\]
Thus the shortest nonzero periods of \(Q_T^2\) and \(C_T^4\) tend to
infinity.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The factor metrics and their global extensions.}
On \(\mathcal A\) use
\[
 dr^2+r^2du^2+r^2dx^{\mathsf T}M(r)^{\mathsf T}M(r)dx
\]
for \(r\leq r_0\).  Extend its positive angular coefficient matrix
smoothly over the remainder of the cylinder up to \(r=\epsilon\),
keeping the radial summand \(dr^2\).  For example, continue it over a
short interval beyond \(r_0\) and take a fixed smooth convex combination
with a constant positive angular matrix, using a cutoff equal to one
on a neighborhood of the prescribed inner interval.  The choices are
made once and are independent of the slice parameter.

Complete this cylinder at \(r=0\), retaining its outer boundary torus.
The bounds for \(M(r)\) show that a level torus has diameter \(O(r)\).
A radial segment has length \(r\), and \(r\) is a \(1\)-Lipschitz
function.  Hence all sequences whose radii tend to zero converge to
one new point, uniformly in their angular coordinates; points whose
radii stay bounded below cannot converge to it.  Away from that point
the smooth tensor gives the usual cylinder topology.  These statements
identify the completion with the compact cone with its outer torus
retained.  Radial paths to its apex and approximating cylinder paths
show directly that its completed distance is a length metric.  Collapse
the outer torus to the other suspension pole, using the metric quotient
described below.  This gives the prescribed topology of \(\mathcal A\)
and its fixed factor distance \(d_{\mathcal A}\).

For \(\mathcal B\) use
\(dr^2+r^2(du^2+d\theta^2)\) on the whole open cylinder, add the
inner apex by completion, and collapse the outer torus to its separate
pole.  For \(\mathcal C\), give its attached cone the same tensor.
The boundary-coordinate map to \(\partial M=\partial D_0\times S^1\) is
\[
 \rho_0(z,[\theta])=(\epsilon z,e^{2\pi i\theta}),\qquad
 \rho_0^{-1}(p,w)
 =\left(p/\epsilon,\arg(w)/(2\pi)\bmod\mathbb Z\right).
\]
On a collar of its compact smooth core \(M\), with coordinate
\(\tau\geq0\) directed into the core, prescribe
\[
 d\tau^2+(\epsilon+\tau)^2(du^2+d\theta^2).
\]
Under \(r=\epsilon+\tau\), this matches the cone tensor and every
derivative at the boundary.  A fixed cutoff and convex combination with
a smooth positive tensor on the rest of \(M\) extend it over the core.
Completing at the inner apex gives the compact cone-attachment topology,
by the same radial and diameter estimates.  The tensor is smooth across
the attaching torus.

The radial function descends to each suspension and remains
\(1\)-Lipschitz after the outer collapse: a route through that pole
has length at least
\((\epsilon-r(x))+(\epsilon-r(y))\geq|r(x)-r(y)|\).
For \(\mathcal C\), extend \(r\) by the constant \(\epsilon\) on
the core.  The extension is \(1\)-Lipschitz, as follows by integrating
its derivative along each piece of a path.  Consequently, for every
cone point of each factor \(X\),
\[
 d_X(x_0,[r,a])=r.
\]
The radial path proves the upper bound and the radial function proves
the lower bound.  This equality holds on the entire prescribed interval,
including \(r=r_0\).  The same function bounds the distance from an
inner point to the outer pole or to the core below by \(\epsilon-r\).

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The smash metrics.}
For a compact length space \((P,d)\) and a closed subset \(F\) that
is collapsed to a point, the quotient distance is
\[
 D([x],[y])=\min\{d(x,y),d(x,F)+d(y,F)\},\qquad
 D([x],*)=d(x,F).
\]
To verify the triangle inequality, concatenate paths giving either
candidate for each successive pair.  A path that visits the collapsed
set has length at least the sum of its endpoint distances to that set;
a path that avoids it has length at least the direct distance.  Visits
after the first can be deleted.  Approximating the displayed candidates
by paths proves that the quotient is a length metric.  It is positive
between distinct classes because \(F\) is closed.  The quotient map
is continuous and \(1\)-Lipschitz, so the continuous bijection from
the compact topological quotient to this Hausdorff metric space is a
homeomorphism.  This also justifies the outer collapses used above.

Give \(P=X^n\) the product distance
\[
 d_P(x,y)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n d_X(x_i,y_i)^2.
\]
It is the length metric of the product tensor on the regular stratum:
the lower bound follows by integrating the vector of component speeds,
and the upper bound follows by traversing constant-speed minimizing
factor paths simultaneously.  Such minimizing paths exist in these
compact length spaces, by taking a uniformly convergent subsequence of
constant-speed paths whose lengths decrease to the distance and using
lower semicontinuity of length.

For the fat wedge \(F=\bigcup_i\{x_i=x_0\}\), the product formula
gives
\[
 d_P(x,F)=\min_i d_X(x_i,x_0).
\]
Replacing only a minimizing factor by \(x_0\) gives the upper bound,
and every point of \(F\) gives the matching lower bound.  Applying
the quotient formula defines \(D_{12},D_{24}^{\mathcal B},
D_{24}^{\mathcal C}\) with their prescribed compact topologies.
If \(d_P(x,F)=\delta>0\), two points in a product ball of radius
\(\eta<\delta/2\) about \(x\) have direct distance at most
\(2\eta\), whereas a route through \(F\) costs at least
\(2(\delta-\eta)>2\eta\).  Thus the quotient is locally isometric
to the product off the fat wedge.  Restricting also away from the factor
singularities gives exactly the regular tensors in the statement.

At each synchronized basepoint, the distance to the fat wedge is
\(r_T\).  Put
\[
 K=T\quad\hbox{for }Z_{12},\qquad
 K=\ell_T\quad\hbox{for }Z_{24}^{\mathcal D},\qquad
 \lambda=K/r_T.
\]
For \(K>R\), the rescaled smash \(R\)-ball is the image of the
product \(R/\lambda\)-ball, since a route from the basepoint through
the fat wedge already costs \(K\).  Points of this product ball have
distance at least \(r_T-R/\lambda\) from the fat wedge.  A route
between two of them through it therefore has rescaled length at least
\(2(K-R)\), whereas their direct rescaled product distance is at most
\(2R\).  For \(K>2R\) the quotient is an isometry on this whole ball.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The slice forms.}
The maps of Definition~\ref{wb:cusp-cone-target-slice-embeddings} are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 j_T(y_1,y_2)
 &=\bigl[[r_T,1,[Y_T^{-1}y_1]],
          [r_T,1,[Y_T^{-1}y_2]]\bigr]_{\wedge},\\
 k_T^{\mathcal B}(c_1,\ldots,c_4)
 &=\bigwedge_{i=1}^4[r_T,1,[c_i/\ell_T]],\\
 k_T^{\mathcal C}(c_1,\ldots,c_4)
 &=\bigwedge_{i=1}^4[r_T,(1,[c_i/\ell_T])].
\end{aligned}
\]
Replacing a real representative \(y_i\) by \(y_i+Y_Tn\), or
\(c_i\) by \(c_i+\ell_Tm\), changes its displayed angular
representative by \(n\in\mathbb Z^2\) or \(m\in\mathbb Z\).
Thus these formulas have exactly the quotient domains stated above.
The inverse on each image first takes the unique nonbasepoint product
representative and then applies \(\iota_T\) or \(\vartheta_T\) to
the displayed angular class.  In particular these are smooth embeddings
in the regular stratum.  On \(j_T\), \(dr=du=0\) and
\(dx=Y_T^{-1}dy\).  Its single-factor first fundamental form is
\[
 \frac{r_T^2}{T^2}
 dy^{\mathsf T}(Y_T^{-1})^{\mathsf T}Y_T^{\mathsf T}Y_TY_T^{-1}dy
 =\frac{r_T^2}{T^2}\,dy^{\mathsf T}dy.
\]
On \(k_T^{\mathcal D}\), \(d\theta=dc/\ell_T\) and
\(dr=du=0\), so its single-factor form is
\(r_T^2dc^2/\ell_T^2\).  Summing factors proves
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-A-slice-exact} and
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-BC-slice-exact}, including the exact equalities
of intrinsic path metrics with those of \(Q_T^2\) and \(C_T^4\).

For a fixed \(R\), the period bounds eventually make every nonzero
period longer than \(4R\).  For points of a Euclidean \(R\)-ball,
a translated difference then has norm at least
\(\operatorname{sys}-2R>2R\), while the direct difference has norm
at most \(2R\).  Thus the Euclidean quotient map is an isometry on
that whole ball.  Every point in the quotient \(R\)-ball has a
shortest representative in the Euclidean ball, since a lattice is
discrete.  Composing these onto isometries with the slice embeddings
proves all the intrinsic limits in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-slice-fixed-blowups}.  Their pullback tensors
are exactly Euclidean on each such ball.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The ambient coordinate maps and their derivatives.}
In an \(\mathcal A\)-factor use
\[
 \Phi_{\mathcal A,T}(a,b,\xi)
 =\left[r_T(1+a/T),e^{2\pi ib/T},[Y_T^{-1}\xi]\right],
 \qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^2,
\]
on the open domain
\[
 |a|<T/2,\qquad |b|<T/4,\qquad
 Y_T^{-1}\xi\in(-1/4,1/4)^2.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(T\), the radial interval is contained
in \((0,r_0)\).  The inverse takes the unique angular lifts in these
windows and sends a representative to
\[
 a=T(r/r_T-1),\qquad b=Tu_{\rm lift},\qquad
 \xi=Y_Tx_{\rm lift}.
\]
Both compositions are the identity.  Take the two-factor product of
these maps and compose with the smash quotient.  Its image is an open
regular coordinate neighborhood, since the quotient has singleton
classes and is open off the fat wedge.  The domains contain every fixed
Euclidean ball eventually, by the lower singular-value bound for
\(Y_T\).

Put
\[
 \alpha=1+a/T,\qquad
 \tau_T(a)=T-\frac{\log(1+a/T)}{2\pi},\qquad
 F_T(a)=\frac{T}{\tau_T(a)},\qquad
 U_T(a)=F_T(a)Y_{\tau_T(a)}Y_T^{-1}.
\]
The exact rescaled single-factor pullback is
\[
 \left(\frac{T}{r_T}\right)^2\Phi_{\mathcal A,T}^*g_{\mathcal A}
 =da^2+\alpha^2db^2
   +\alpha^2d\xi^{\mathsf T}U_T(a)^{\mathsf T}U_T(a)d\xi.
\]
At \(a=0\), \(U_T(0)=I\).  To control all derivatives, for
\(j\geq1\) compute
\[
 \tau_T^{(j)}(a)
 =\frac{(-1)^j(j-1)!}{2\pi(T+a)^j},\qquad
 e^{-2\pi\tau_T(a)}=r_T(1+a/T),
\]
and
\[
 \frac{d^j}{da^j}E(r_T(1+a/T))
 =\left(\frac{r_T}{T}\right)^j E^{(j)}(r_T(1+a/T)).
\]
On each fixed interval \(|a|\leq L\),
\(\tau_T-T=O_L(T^{-1})\) and \(F_T-1=O_L(T^{-2})\).
Differentiating \(F_T\tau_T=T\) gives the recurrence
\[
 F_T^{(j)}
 =-\frac{1}{\tau_T}
   \sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\binom ji F_T^{(i)}\tau_T^{(j-i)},
\]
so induction yields \(F_T^{(j)}=O_{L,j}(T^{-j-1})\).  The matrix
identity
\[
 U_T(a)-I
 =\bigl[F_T(a)E(r_T(1+a/T))-E(r_T)\bigr]Y_T^{-1}
\]
and \(\|Y_T^{-1}\|\leq(T-C_E)^{-1}\) now show that
\(U_T\to I\) in every \(C^k\) norm on fixed intervals.  In fact,
for each fixed \(k\) the derivatives of order at most \(k\) of
\(U_T-I\) are \(O_{L,k}(T^{-3}+r_T/T^2)\).  This follows from
the residual chain rule, the bounded derivatives of \(E\), and the
recurrence just displayed.  It also gives
\(Y_{\tau_T(a)}Y_T^{-1}=I+O(T^{-2})\), with the same upper order
after every fixed number of derivatives.  Thus the two-factor rescaled
tensors converge in every \(C^k\) norm on bounded coordinate sets to
the Euclidean tensor of \(\mathbb R^8\).

For \(\mathcal D=\mathcal B,\mathcal C\) put \(K=\ell_T\) and use
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Phi_{\mathcal B,T}(a,b,\xi)
 &= [r_T(1+a/K),e^{2\pi ib/K},[\xi/K]],\\
 \Phi_{\mathcal C,T}(a,b,\xi)
 &= [r_T(1+a/K),(e^{2\pi ib/K},[\xi/K])]
\end{aligned}
\]
on \(|a|<K/2\), \(|b|<K/4\), \(|\xi|<K/4\).  The inverse reads
the unique lifts and sets \(a=K(r/r_T-1)\), \(b=Ku\),
\(\xi=K\theta\).  The boundary coordinate in the second line is
carried to \(\partial M\) by \(\rho_0\).  The exact pullback is
\[
 \left(\frac{\ell_T}{r_T}\right)^2
 \Phi_{\mathcal D,T}^*g_{\mathcal D}
 =da^2+(1+a/K)^2(db^2+d\xi^2).
\]
Its four-factor sum converges in every \(C^k\) norm on each bounded
coordinate set to the Euclidean tensor of \(\mathbb R^{12}\).
At \(a=b=0\), the coordinates \(\xi\) in all these charts are
exactly the physical flat coordinates of the slices.  Hence their
products identify the limiting slice with the stated coordinate
subspace in each ambient Euclidean space.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Whole ambient balls and their distances.}
In each factor consider the unscaled window
\[
 r_T/2<r<3r_T/2,\quad |u_{\rm lift}|<1/4,
\]
together with \(|x_{{\rm lift},j}|<1/4\) for \(\mathcal A\), or
\(|\theta_{\rm lift}|<1/4\) for \(\mathcal B,\mathcal C\).
A path from the center that leaves this window either reaches a
radial boundary, costing at least \(r_T/2\), or first reaches an
angular boundary while its radius is at least \(r_T/2\).  The latter
costs at least \(c_*r_T/8\), where \(c_*=\min(1,c_-)\), because
the variation of one lifted angle is at least \(1/4\).
Thus, with \(\rho=\min(1/2,c_*/8)>0\), every exit costs at least
\(\rho r_T\).  This estimate also applies to a path that subsequently
reaches a cone point, an outer pole or the core: it first leaves this
window.  Factor projections are \(1\)-Lipschitz for the product
distance, and the alternative quotient route through the fat wedge
costs \(r_T\).  Therefore the rescaled distance from \(p_T\) to
the complement of the product coordinate neighborhood is at least
\(\rho K\).

In particular every fixed rescaled \(R\)-ball is contained in the
open regular chart for all large \(T\).  The factor distances to
the inward vertex and the level \(r_0\) are respectively \(r_T\)
and \(r_0-r_T\), by the radial function and radial paths.  Their
rescaled values are
\[
 K\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 K\left(\frac{r_0}{r_T}-1\right)\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
The angular period lattices in the displayed coordinates are
\(T\mathbb Z\oplus Y_T\mathbb Z^2\) and
\(\ell_T\mathbb Z^2\); their least nonzero Euclidean lengths are
at least \(T-C_E\) and equal to \(\ell_T\), respectively.
The exit estimate above controls paths that vary their radii while
moving in these angular directions.

A minimizing path between two points of a rescaled \(R\)-ball has
length at most \(2R\), and all its points lie in the rescaled
\(3R\)-ball.  For \(\rho K>3R\) it stays in the regular chart.
On the large chart windows, \(1/2<\alpha<3/2\), and for the
\(\mathcal A\) tensor \(\tau_T=T+O(1)\).  For all large \(T\),
\[
 \sigma_{\min}(U_T)
 \geq\frac{T}{T+C_E}\left(1-\frac{C_E}{\tau_T}\right)
 \geq\frac14,\qquad
 \|U_T\|\leq\frac{T}{T-C_E}
                   \left(1+\frac{C_E}{\tau_T}\right)\leq3.
\]
The convenient common estimates for all three rescaled product tensors
are consequently
\[
 \frac18|v|\leq\sqrt{g_T(v,v)}\leq5|v|.
\]
Apply the lower bound to a minimizing origin path to a point of the
\(3R\)-ball.  Its coordinate length is at most \(24R\).
Thus the \(R\)-ball has coordinates in the Euclidean \(8R\)-ball,
and every minimizing path between its points stays in the Euclidean
\(24R\)-ball.

Choose \(0<\varepsilon_T<1/2\), tending to zero, so that the
rescaled norms on the fixed coordinate ball of radius \(24R+1\)
are between \((1-\varepsilon_T)|v|\) and
\((1+\varepsilon_T)|v|\).  A minimizing path gives the lower bound
below, and the
straight coordinate segment gives the upper bound:
\[
 (1-\varepsilon_T)|z-w|
 \leq\lambda D(\Phi_Tz,\Phi_Tw)
 \leq(1+\varepsilon_T)|z-w|
\]
for points in the target \(R\)-ball.  The origin comparison also gives
\[
 B_{R/(1+\varepsilon_T)}(0)
 \subset\Phi_T^{-1}(B_R(p_T;\lambda D))
 \subset B_{R/(1-\varepsilon_T)}(0).
\]
Radial projection of the middle set to the Euclidean \(R\)-ball
changes coordinates by \(O_R(\varepsilon_T)\), has distortion
\(O_R(\varepsilon_T)\), and has
\(O_R(\varepsilon_T)\)-dense image.  These maps prove the pointed
Gromov--Hausdorff limits of the whole target balls in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-ambient-fixed-blowups}.  The coordinate domains
exhaust their Euclidean spaces, their images contain every fixed
rescaled target ball eventually, and their pulled-back tensors converge
in all \(C^k\) norms.  This proves the stated smooth exhaustion.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Intrinsic and ambient paths on the slices.}
Inclusion of a slice preserves the length of every path it contains.
Taking infima over slice paths and over all ambient paths proves the
two distance inequalities in the statement.  Their strictness can be
seen directly.  In a \(\mathcal B\)- or \(\mathcal C\)-factor,
keep \(u=0\) and take character-angle endpoints \(0,\delta\), with
\(0<\delta<1/2\), at radius \(r_T\).  The map
\[
 (r,\theta)\longmapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)
\]
pulls the Euclidean tensor back to \(dr^2+r^2d\theta^2\) on this
sector.  The straight chord lifts to a cone path with radius between
\(r_T\cos(\delta/2)\) and \(r_T\), and has length
\[
 2r_T\sin(\delta/2)<r_T\delta.
\]
The right side is the intrinsic slice distance.  Holding the other
three factors fixed gives the strict inequality in each smash target.

For \(\mathcal A\) put \(G(r)=r^2M(r)^{\mathsf T}M(r)\).
Differentiation gives
\[
 rM'(r)=\frac{rE'(r)}{T(r)}+\frac{E(r)}{2\pi T(r)^2},\qquad
 r^{-1}G'(r)
 =2M^{\mathsf T}M+(rM')^{\mathsf T}M+M^{\mathsf T}(rM')
 \longrightarrow2I.
\]
Thus \(G'(r)\) is positive definite for every sufficiently small
positive \(r\).  Take such \(r_T\), with \(T-C_E>4\), and set
\(v=Y_T^{-1}(1,0)\).  The physical segment \(Y_Tsv=s(1,0)\)
is minimizing on the flat torus: every nonzero translated difference
has norm at least \(T-C_E-1>3\).  Choose a smooth nonnegative function
\(f\), supported in \((0,1)\) and positive somewhere.  The path
\[
 s\longmapsto[r_T-hf(s),1,[sv]],\qquad 0\leq s\leq1,
\]
stays in the cone for small \(h>0\) and has energy
\[
 \mathcal E(h)
 =\int_0^1\bigl(h^2f'(s)^2+v^{\mathsf T}G(r_T-hf(s))v\bigr)\,ds.
\]
Its derivative at zero is
\[
 \mathcal E'(0)
 =-\left(\int_0^1f(s)\,ds\right)v^{\mathsf T}G'(r_T)v<0.
\]
The unperturbed energy is the square of the intrinsic slice distance.
The perturbed path has length at most \(\sqrt{\mathcal E(h)}\),
which is strictly smaller for small \(h>0\).  Keeping the other
factor fixed proves strictness on \(\Sigma_T^{12}\).

On every bounded physical slice-coordinate set, the intrinsic rescaled
distance is eventually exactly Euclidean.  Restricting the ambient
distance estimates to \(a=b=0\) shows that its rescaled ambient
distance tends uniformly to the same Euclidean distance.  The whole
ambient-restricted slice \(R\)-ball lies in that coordinate subspace
by the chart-exit bound.  Intersecting the ball inclusions above with
the subspace proves its pointed Gromov--Hausdorff limit as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete intrinsic scalar-rescaling trichotomy]
\hypertarget{tag-03DC}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-scaling-trichotomy}
\StatementRecord{wb:sphere-metric-scaling-trichotomy}{proved}{03DC}{\SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}, \SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-outward-shortcut-exclusion}}

For the fixed metrics of
\cref{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}, let \(\lambda_T>0\) be arbitrary
and put
\[
 \beta_T:=\lambda_Tr_T.
\]
Choose one of the following triples, retaining the indicated ambient
metric:
\[
 \begin{split}
  (\Sigma_T,d_T^{\mathrm{slice}},d_T^{\mathrm{amb}},p_T;D)
  &=(\Sigma_T^{12},d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{slice}},
      d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{amb}},p_T^{12};D_{12}),\\
  (\Sigma_T,d_T^{\mathrm{slice}},d_T^{\mathrm{amb}},p_T;D)
  &=(\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D},
      d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{slice}},
      d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{amb}},
      p_T^{24,\mathcal D};D_{24}^{\mathcal D}),
      \qquad \mathcal D\in\{\mathcal B,\mathcal C\}.
 \end{split}
\]
After passing to a subsequence so that \(\beta_T\) has a limit in
\([0,\infty]\), the intrinsic pointed slice limit is
\begin{equation}
 (\Sigma_T,\lambda_Td_T^{\mathrm{slice}},p_T)
 \longrightarrow
 \begin{cases}
  \{\mathrm{pt}\},&\beta_T\longrightarrow0,\\
  ((\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^4,0),
      &\beta_T\longrightarrow L\in(0,\infty),\\
  (\mathbb R^4,0),&\beta_T\longrightarrow\infty.
 \end{cases}
 \hypertarget{tag-03DD}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-scaling-trichotomy-result}
\end{equation}
The convergence in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-scaling-trichotomy-result} is pointed
Gromov--Hausdorff in all three cases.  In the finite positive case the flat
metrics converge smoothly under the fixed marked-torus identifications; in
the unrolling case the convergence is pointed local-isometric and smooth on
the exhausting Euclidean balls.
In the middle line the lattice is orthogonally equivalent to the square
lattice \(L\mathbb Z^4\).  At the same time,
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_TD(p_T,*)=\beta_T
 \hypertarget{tag-03DI}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-vertex-distance}
\end{equation}
for every one of the displayed choices.

Only in the unrolling regime \(\beta_T\to\infty\) do we compare the
intrinsic metric with the restricted ambient distance.  In that regime, for
every \(R\in(0,\infty)\),
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{x,y\in

\begin{corollary}[Unit-volume normalization does not give
\(\mathbb R^4\)]
\hypertarget{tag-03DH}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-unit-volume}
Write $D_T=\det Y_T>0$ on the native admissible radial range.
The four-volume of $Q_T^2$ is $D_T^2\sim T^4$, and its
unit-volume length factor is $D_T^{-1/2}\sim T^{-1}$.
Under the marked torus identifications, these unit-volume metrics
converge smoothly and in Gromov--Hausdorff topology to the square
unit four-torus.  They have no pointed $\mathbb R^4$ limit.
The four-volume of $C_T^4$ is $\ell_T^4$.  For every admissible
$T$, its unit-volume metric is isometric to the square unit
four-torus by
\[
 ([y_1],\ldots,[y_4])\longmapsto
 ([y_1/\ell_T],\ldots,[y_4/\ell_T])\in\mathbb R^4/\mathbb Z^4.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The Euclidean fundamental parallelepiped of a period matrix $A$
has volume $|\det A|$.  Multiplication of a length metric by
$c>0$ multiplies four-volume by $c^4$.
For $A_T=\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T)$ this gives volume $D_T^2$
and the unique positive unit-volume scale $c_T=D_T^{-1/2}$.
Put $B_T=c_TA_T$.  The map
\[
 (Q_T^2,c_Td_{Q_T^2})\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4/B_T\mathbb Z^4,
 \qquad[y]\longmapsto[c_Ty]
\]
is an isometry with inverse $[z]\mapsto[c_T^{-1}z]$:
it carries every period $A_Tn$ to $B_Tn$, and multiplies every
term in the quotient-distance infimum by $c_T$.
The marked map $[a]\mapsto[B_Ta]$ from $\mathbb R^4/\mathbb Z^4$
has inverse $[z]\mapsto[B_T^{-1}z]$ and pulls back the metric to
\[
 G_T=D_T^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(Y_T^{\mathsf T}Y_T,
                                 Y_T^{\mathsf T}Y_T).
\]

Since $Y_T=TJ+E_T$ with bounded $E_T$ and
$J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
we have $D_T/T^2\to1$ and
$B_T\to R=\operatorname{diag}(J,J)$.
This proves both stated volume and scale asymptotics.
The matrix $R$ is orthogonal and $R\mathbb Z^4=\mathbb Z^4$;
the map $[z]\mapsto[R^{\mathsf T}z]$, inverse $[a]\mapsto[Ra]$,
identifies its quotient with the square unit four-torus.
Also $G_T\to I_4$ in every $C^k$ norm, because the tensors have
constant coefficients in the fixed marked coordinates.

For the metric convergence, set $\eta_T=\lVert B_T-R\rVert$.
The inequalities
\[
 (1-\eta_T)|v|\leq|B_Tv|\leq(1+\eta_T)|v|
\]
give the same bounds on quotient distances after taking infima
over $v=a-b+n$, $n\in\mathbb Z^4$.
The square unit four-torus has diameter one.  Hence the identity
of the marked torus has distance distortion at most $\eta_T\to0$,
and its graph gives the stated Gromov--Hausdorff convergence.

For $C_T^4$, the period matrix is $\ell_TI_4$, so its volume is
$\ell_T^4$ and the scale is $\ell_T^{-1}$.
The displayed division map carries its periods to $\mathbb Z^4$;
its inverse multiplies all four coordinates by $\ell_T$.
The quotient-distance formula proves exact isometry at every $T$.

Finally the first family has diameter at most $1+\eta_T<2$ for
large $T$, and the second has diameter one.  The Euclidean
points $0$ and $3e_1$ in the radius-four ball have distance three.
Every map of that ball into either family has distortion at
least three minus its diameter.  These lower bounds stay positive,
so the approximations required for a pointed $\mathbb R^4$ limit
cannot have errors tending to zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[What vertex tangents and compact asymptotic cones can
mean]
\hypertarget{tag-03DF}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-tangent-scope}
\StatementRecord{wb:sphere-metric-tangent-scope}{proved}{03DF}{\SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}, \SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-C-boundary-quotient-homeomorphism}, \SeriesRef{wb:cusp-cone-S24-route}, \SeriesRef{wb:sphere-metric-boundary-link-local-shift}}

The compact target topology alone determines no metric tangent cone.
For an exact conic length metric built from fixed piecewise-Riemannian
metrics on the links, however, the vertex links have topological and
Hausdorff dimensions \(7\) for \(Z_{12}\) and \(11\) for both
\(Z_{24}\) targets.  The resulting vertex cones have topological and
Hausdorff dimensions \(8\) and \(12\), and are not \(\mathbb R^4\).

More precisely, writing \(L_3=T^3\) and \(L_2=T^2\), one has the based
topological models
\[
 Z_{12}\cong\operatorname{Susp}(L_3*L_3),
 \qquad
 Z_{24}^{\mathcal B}
 \cong\operatorname{Susp}(L_2*L_2*L_2*L_2).
\]
At the suspension base point their conic links are respectively
\(L_3*L_3\) and \(L_2^{*4}\).  Also
\[
 (\mathcal C,c_0)
 \cong
 (\mathcal M/\partial\mathcal M,[\partial\mathcal M]),
 \qquad
 (Z_{24}^{\mathcal C},*)
 \cong
 (\mathcal M^4/\partial(\mathcal M^4),
  [\partial(\mathcal M^4)]),
\]
so an exact conic metric at the collapsed boundary has link
\(\partial(\mathcal M^4)\).  At the collapsed point of
\(Z_{24}^{\mathcal C}\), the complete integral local-homology calculation is
\begin{equation}
 H_i\bigl(Z_{24}^{\mathcal C},
          Z_{24}^{\mathcal C}\setminus\{*\};\mathbb Z\bigr)
 \cong
 \begin{cases}
  \mathbb Z^{\binom4{i-1}},&2\leq i\leq5,\\
  0,&i=6,7,\\
  \mathbb Z^{\binom4{i-8}},&8\leq i\leq12,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
 \hypertarget{tag-03D1}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-C-smash-local-homology}
\end{equation}
In particular, its local homology is not concentrated in top degree.  For
the first two targets the top local homology occurs in degree \(8\) and
\(12\), respectively; for the third target
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-C-smash-local-homology} includes a top
\(\mathbb Z\) in degree \(12\).  None has the local homology of
\(\mathbb R^4\).

Finally, the standard asymptotic cone obtained by blowing down any fixed
compact metric target is a point.  Indeed, if \(R_n\to\infty\), then
\[
 \operatorname{diam}(Z,R_n^{-1}D)
 =R_n^{-1}\operatorname{diam}(Z,D)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus the limits in \cref{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization} are
moving-base-point blow-ups, often called bubbles.  They are neither
vertex-based tangent cones nor asymptotic cones of the compact targets.
\end{proposition}



\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item For compact spaces \(V_i\) with closed subspaces \(A_i\), there is a
canonical homeomorphism
\[
 (V_1/A_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(V_m/A_m)
 \cong
 \frac{V_1\times\cdots\times V_m}
      {\bigcup_iV_1\times\cdots\times A_i\times\cdots\times V_m}.
\]
First reverse the suspension coordinate, $r\mapsto\epsilon-r$, so that the chosen inner basepoint is carried to the outer suspension vertex. Take $V_i=\operatorname{Cone}(L_i)$ and $A_i=L_i$, its outer boundary.
The actual map from the product cones to the cone on the iterated join uses radial coordinate $\rho=\max_i r_i$ and join weights $t_i=r_i/\sum_jr_j$ away from the common vertex. Its inverse is $r_i=\rho t_i/\max_jt_j$; zero weights discard exactly the irrelevant cone-link coordinates. These maps extend continuously at the vertex, and the union of outer faces goes to $\rho=1$.
Collapsing that link gives its suspension.  This proves the first two
models and the link dimensions
\[
 \dim(T^3*T^3)=3+3+1=7,
 \qquad
 \dim((T^2)^{*4})=4\cdot2+3=11.
\]

\item We next prove the based homeomorphism for \(\mathcal C\), rather than
identifying the two presentations without a map.  Put
\(L=\partial\mathcal M\), write the attached cone as
\[
 \operatorname{Cone}(L)
 =L\times[0,1]/(L\times\{0\}),
\]
with base \(L\times\{1\}\), and choose a collar
\(\kappa:L\times[0,1]\hookrightarrow\mathcal M\) satisfying
\(\kappa(x,0)=x\).  There is a homeomorphism
\[
 \Phi:\mathcal C\setminus\{c_0\}
       \longrightarrow\operatorname{int}\mathcal M
\]
given on the punctured cone, the inner collar, and the remaining core by
\[
 \Phi([x,t])=\kappa(x,t/e)\quad(0<t\leq1),\qquad
 \Phi(\kappa(x,s))=\kappa(x,e^{s-1})\quad(0\leq s\leq1),
\]
\[
 \Phi(q)=q
 \quad\text{for}\quad
 q\in\mathcal M\setminus\kappa(L\times[0,1)).
\]
The first two formulas agree at the glued points
\([x,1]=\kappa(x,0)\), and the second and third agree at
\(\kappa(x,1)\).  Their collar-coordinate images are respectively
\(L\times(0,e^{-1}]\) and \(L\times[e^{-1},1]\); hence the displayed
piecewise map and its piecewise inverse are continuous.

\item The compact Hausdorff spaces \(\mathcal C\) and
\(\mathcal M/L\) are both one-point compactifications of
\(\operatorname{int}\mathcal M\): for \(\mathcal C\) use \(\Phi\), and for
\(\mathcal M/L\) use the quotient map on
\(\mathcal M\setminus L=\operatorname{int}\mathcal M\).  Uniqueness of the
one-point compactification therefore extends \(\Phi\) to a based
homeomorphism
\begin{equation}
 (\mathcal C,c_0)
 \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }
 (\mathcal M/\partial\mathcal M,[\partial\mathcal M]).
 \hypertarget{tag-03D0}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-C-boundary-quotient-homeomorphism}
\end{equation}
Only after establishing
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-C-boundary-quotient-homeomorphism} do we apply the
quotient identity at the start of the proof.  It gives
\[
 \mathcal C^{\wedge4}
 \cong
 \frac{\mathcal M^4}
 {\displaystyle\bigcup_{a=1}^4
  \mathcal M^{a-1}\times\partial\mathcal M
  \times\mathcal M^{4-a}}
 =\mathcal M^4/\partial(\mathcal M^4),
\]
and carries the smash base point to the collapsed boundary.

\item Put \(N=\mathcal M^4\).  Rounding its product corners preserves the
homeomorphism type of the pair \((N,\partial N)\) and makes
\(\partial N\) an eleven-dimensional closed manifold.  A boundary collar
descends in \(N/\partial N\) to a cone neighborhood of the collapsed
point, so the local link is exactly \(\partial N\) and
\begin{equation}
 H_i(N/\partial N,(N/\partial N)\setminus\{*\};\mathbb Z)
 \cong\widetilde H_{i-1}(\partial N;\mathbb Z).
 \hypertarget{tag-03D5}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-boundary-link-local-shift}
\end{equation}

\item The integral homology calculation in the proof of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-S24-route} for the specific compact orientable
three-manifold \(\mathcal M\) gives
\[
 H_j(\mathcal M;\mathbb Z)\cong
 \begin{cases}
  \mathbb Z,&j=0,1,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
All groups are free, so the integral Kunneth theorem gives
\[
 H_j(N;\mathbb Z)\cong
 \begin{cases}
  \mathbb Z^{\binom4j},&0\leq j\leq4,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Poincare--Lefschetz duality, with the product orientation retained, gives
\[
 H_j(N,\partial N;\mathbb Z)
 \cong H^{12-j}(N;\mathbb Z)
 \cong
 \begin{cases}
  \mathbb Z^{\binom4{j-8}},&8\leq j\leq12,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The long exact sequence of \((N,\partial N)\) now has disjoint absolute
and relative degree ranges.  It gives
\[
 \widetilde H_j(\partial N;\mathbb Z)\cong
 \begin{cases}
  \mathbb Z^{\binom4j},&1\leq j\leq4,\\
  0,&j=5,6,\\
  \mathbb Z^{\binom4{j-7}},&7\leq j\leq11,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Substitution in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-boundary-link-local-shift} proves
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-C-smash-local-homology}.

\item To see explicitly why topology alone does not fix the tangent metric, compare the cone tensors $dr^2+r^2h$ and $dr^2+4r^2h$ on the same link of dimension $d$. The identity is a homeomorphism, while their unit-ball Hausdorff volumes differ by the factor $2^d$, so the marked metric cones are not isometric. An exact metric cone is invariant under every radial blow-up at its vertex,
and its Hausdorff dimension is one plus that of its fixed
piecewise-Riemannian link.  For the first target,
\[
 H_8\bigl(\operatorname{Cone}(T^3*T^3),T^3*T^3;\mathbb Z\bigr)
 \cong\mathbb Z;
\]
the analogous top local group for the \(\mathcal B\) target is
\(\mathbb Z\) in degree \(12\), while the full \(\mathcal C\) calculation
is \eqref{wb:sphere-metric-C-smash-local-homology}.  Euclidean
\(\mathbb R^4\) has local homology \(\mathbb Z\) only in degree \(4\), so
none of these conic vertex models is \(\mathbb R^4\).  The diameter
calculation proves the final assertion.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}
