\subsection{Recognition of a two-sphere and three-sphere wedge}

\begin{lemma}[The two-generator wedge]
\hypertarget{tag-02QC}{}\label{mapsIII:carrier-three-complex-wedge}
{\normalfont\scriptsize tag 02QC}\par
Let $C$ be a simply connected CW complex with
$\widetilde H_2(C;\mathbb Z)=\widetilde H_3(C;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$
and zero reduced integral homology in every other degree.
For any chosen generators $u\in H_2(C;\mathbb Z)$ and
$v\in H_3(C;\mathbb Z)$, there are based maps
$a:S^2\to C$ and $b:S^3\to C$ carrying the oriented sphere
classes to $u$ and $v$. The map $F=a\vee b:S^2\vee S^3\to C$
is a based homotopy equivalence.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The Hurewicz isomorphism $\pi_2(C)\to H_2(C;\mathbb Z)$
supplies a based cellular map $a$ representing $u$.
Naturality shows that $a$ induces an isomorphism on $\pi_2$
as well as on $H_2$. Form its mapping cylinder
\[
 M=(S^2\times[0,1])\amalg C/((z,1)\sim a(z)),
 \qquad A=S^2\times\{0\}.
\]
The retraction $r:M\to C$ has $r([z,t])=a(z)$ and is the
identity on $C$. Its deformation retraction sends
$[z,t]$ to $[z,(1-s)t+s]$ and fixes $C$. The basepoint path
$[z_0,t]$ identifies the bottom basepoint with $a(z_0)$;
all homotopy groups below use this path. If $i:A\to M$ is
the inclusion, then $ri=a$ and
$i_\#=r_\#^{-1}a_\#$, with inverse basepoint transport along
the reversed path. Both $A$ and $M$ are simply connected.
The pair exact sequence therefore gives
$\pi_1(M,A)=\pi_2(M,A)=0$.

Relative Hurewicz and the homology exact sequence give the
isomorphisms
\[
 h:\pi_3(M,A)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_3(M,A;\mathbb Z),
 \qquad q_H:H_3(M;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_3(M,A;\mathbb Z).
\]
Here $H_3(A)=0$ and $i_*:H_2(A)\to H_2(M)$ is an isomorphism,
which prove both sides of the second assertion. The next
homotopy boundary has image
$\ker(i_\#: \pi_2(A)\to\pi_2(M))=0$; thus
$q_\pi:\pi_3(M)\to\pi_3(M,A)$ is surjective. Choose
$[g]\in\pi_3(M)$ with
\[
 q_\pi[g]=h^{-1}q_H(r_*^{-1}v),\qquad b=rg.
\]
Give $S^3=D^3/\partial D^3$ its disk orientation.
Naturality gives
$q_H(g_*[S^3])=h(q_\pi[g])=q_H(r_*^{-1}v)$.
The injectivity of $q_H$ proves $b_*[S^3]=v$.
These are the canonical relative maps of
\cite[Theorem~4.37 and Lemma~4.38, pp.~370--372]{Hatcher2002}.

The wedge map $F=a\vee b$ induces the chosen generator maps
in degrees two and three, the identity on the connected
degree-zero groups, and the unique isomorphisms between zero
groups in every other degree. It is an integral homology
equivalence between simply connected CW complexes. To specify
its homotopy inverse, form its mapping cylinder $N$ with
bottom inclusion $j_W:W\to N$, $W=S^2\vee S^3$, top inclusion
$j_C:C\to N$ and retraction $p:N\to C$. The pair $(N,W)$
is acyclic. Relative Hurewicz, starting with its simply
connected pair and proceeding through every degree, gives
$\pi_n(N,W)=0$ for all $n\ge1$. The CW Whitehead theorem
\cite[Theorem~4.5 and Corollary~4.33, pp.~346--347 and~367--368]{Hatcher2002}
therefore gives a retraction $k:N\to W$ and a deformation
$T_s$ from $1_N$ to $j_Wk$, fixed on $W$. Set $G=kj_C$.
The cylinder paths $U_t(w)=[w,t]$ give
$kU_t:1_W\simeq GF$, and $pT_sj_C$ gives
$1_C\simeq FG$. In a reduced based mapping cylinder these
homotopies fix the basepoint. This constructs the inverse
for the actual chosen generator map, without imposing a bound
on the dimension or number of cells of $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The actual degree-three finite-band map]
\hypertarget{tag-02QE}{}\label{mapsaudit:finite-degree-three}
\StatementRecord{mapsaudit:finite-degree-three}{proved}{02QE}{the definitions and constructions stated in the proof}

Let $V=\mathbb Z\langle\gamma,u,w,\delta\rangle=H^1(F;\mathbb Z)$,
with $\operatorname{vol}=\gamma u w\delta$, and write
\[
 b=\gamma uw,\qquad
 c_1=uw\delta-4\gamma u\delta-2\gamma w\delta,\qquad
 c_2=uw\delta-3\gamma u\delta-3\gamma w\delta.
\]
For the degree-three and degree-four finite coverings $\pi_j:F\to S_j$,
\[
 \pi_1^*H^3(S_1;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Zb\oplus\mathbb Zc_1,
 \qquad
 \pi_2^*H^3(S_2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z(2b)\oplus\mathbb Zc_2.
\]
Choose the unique cohomology bases having those ordered pullbacks and the
Kronecker-dual bases of $H_3(S_j;\mathbb Z)$. Relative to the ordered
homology basis dual to $(\gamma uw,\gamma u\delta,\gamma w\delta,uw\delta)$,
the finite-band Mayer--Vietoris map is
\[
 \alpha_3=(\pi_{1*},-\pi_{2*})=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&0\\
 0&-4&-2&1\\
 -2&0&0&0\\
 0&3&3&-1
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its Smith form has nonzero entries $(1,1,1)$ and its kernel is generated
by $(0,1,1,6)^t$. The order-three pushforward on $H_3$ is surjective;
the order-four pushforward has index two. In particular neither is
identified with its degree-one pushforward by integral changes of bases.
\end{proposition}


\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label={$\langle1\rangle$\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item The integral fixed subgroups of $\bigwedge^3 V$ are
$\langle b,c_1\rangle$ and $\langle b,c_2\rangle$, respectively, by
solving the two integral invariance equations. The degree-one pullback
lattices are $\langle3\gamma,\eta_1\rangle$ and
$\langle4\gamma,\eta_2\rangle$, where
$\eta_1=2u+w+3\delta$ and $\eta_2=u+w+2\delta$.
The pairings of these bases with $(b,c_j)$ have matrices
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}0&3\\-3&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}0&4\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The downstairs $H^1$--$H^3$ pairing is unimodular, because the finite
surfaces have torsion-free integral cohomology and are oriented closed
four-manifolds. Pullback multiplies every pairing by the covering degree.
Thus its degree-three image has index one in the first invariant lattice
and index two in the second. If $rb+sc_2$ descends, pairing with the
descended class $\eta_2$ is divisible by four, so $-2r$ is divisible by
four. Hence its coefficient $r$ is even. This parity sublattice already
has index two, so it is the whole image. This proves the two displayed
pullback formulas, including sufficiency.

\item For $z\in H_3(F)$ and $a\in H^3(S_j)$, naturality of the actual
Kronecker pairing gives $\langle a,\pi_{j*}z\rangle
=\langle\pi_j^*a,z\rangle$. Evaluating the four listed classes therefore
gives the stated matrix, with the minus sign on the second summand.
Its $3\times3$ minors include $1$, and its rank is three. Solving its
kernel equations gives $z_1=0$, $z_3=z_2$, $z_4=6z_2$, proving the
remaining assertions. The first two rows have image all of $\mathbb Z^2$;
the last two have image $2\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z$. In degree one the
corresponding image indices are three and four. These indices are
unchanged by unimodular changes of basis and rule out the asserted
degree-one/degree-three identification in the working proof.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The full external smash pairing is zero]
\hypertarget{tag-038V}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-full-carrier-null}
For every pair of based maps $x,y:S^6\to S^3$,
\[
 [x\wedge y]=0\qquad\text{in }\pi_{12}(S^6).
\]
In particular, the continuous surjective quotient
$\widehat q_3^{\wedge2}:S^{12}\twoheadrightarrow S^6$ of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-sphere-to-sphere-maps} is based null-homotopic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the cube sphere identifications of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}, and write
$C_d=I^d/\partial I^d$.
The ordered based homeomorphism
\[
 \mu_{a,b}:C_a\wedge C_b\longrightarrow C_{a+b},
 \qquad [[u],[v]]\longmapsto[u,v]
\]
concatenates coordinates; its inverse splits an interior point into
the two blocks and sends the basepoint to the smash basepoint.
Let $p_d:C_d\to C_d\vee C_d$ pinch the first coordinate: on the two
halves it replaces $u_1$ by $2u_1$ and $2u_1-1$, respectively.
The middle face and the boundary go to the basepoint.
Thus $(f\vee g)p_d$ represents addition in $\pi_d$.

For $x,y:C_6\to C_3$ put
\[
 R(x)=\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_3})\mu_{6,3}^{-1}
       :C_9\longrightarrow C_6,
 \qquad
 L(y)=\mu_{6,3}(\mathrm{id}_{C_6}\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}
       :C_{12}\longrightarrow C_9.
\]
These are the right threefold and left sixfold suspensions in the
displayed block order.  The exact smash factorization is
\begin{equation}
 x\wedge y=(x\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_3})
              (\mathrm{id}_{C_6}\wedge y):
 C_6\wedge C_6\longrightarrow C_6\wedge C_3
                \longrightarrow C_3\wedge C_3.
 \hypertarget{tag-0390}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-smash-factorization}
\end{equation}
After the ordered identifications it gives
\[
 R(x)L(y)=\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}.
\]
To express this in one suspension convention, write
$E_R^r[f]=[\mu_{n,r}(f\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_r})\mu_{m,r}^{-1}]$
for $f:C_m\to C_n$.
The block twist $\tau_{a,b}:C_{a+b}\to C_{b+a}$,
$\tau_{a,b}[u,v]=[v,u]$, has inverse $\tau_{b,a}$ and degree
$(-1)^{ab}$, since its coordinate permutation has $ab$ inversions.
In particular,
\[
 L(y)=\tau_{3,6}\,
       \bigl(\mu_{3,6}(y\wedge\mathrm{id}_{C_6})\mu_{6,6}^{-1}\bigr)
       \,\tau_{6,6}.
\]
Both twists here have degree one and hence are based homotopic to the
identity by \cite[Corollary~4.25]{Hatcher2002}.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 [\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}]
       =(E_R^3[x])\circ(E_R^6[y]).
 \hypertarget{tag-0392}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-toda-smash-formula}
\end{equation}
Pinching the first coordinate of the six-coordinate input block of
$x$ before concatenation gives
\[
 R((x\vee x')p_6)=(R(x)\vee R(x'))p_9.
\]
Hence $R_*:\pi_6(C_3)\to\pi_9(C_6)$, $[x]\mapsto[R(x)]$,
is a homomorphism.  Based homotopies descend through these smash
quotients because the fat wedge stays at the basepoint at every time;
the product of each compact quotient with the homotopy interval is
again a quotient map.

For fixed $y$, the map $L(y)$ leaves its first six coordinates
unchanged.  Consequently it satisfies the based-map identity
\[
 p_9L(y)=(L(y)\vee L(y))p_{12}.
\]
Indeed, both sides double the first coordinate in the first half and
replace it by $2u_1-1$ in the second half.  Both send the middle face,
the boundary, and every point whose $y$-coordinate is the basepoint
to the basepoint.  Thus
\[
 D_y:\pi_9(C_6)\longrightarrow\pi_{12}(C_6),
 \qquad [z]\longmapsto[zL(y)]
\]
is a homomorphism: applying the displayed pinch identity to
$(z\vee z')p_9$ proves additivity.

The integral computations in \cite[p.~339]{Hatcher2002} give the first,
second and fourth groups below:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 \pi_6(S^3)\cong\mathbb Z/12,\qquad
 \pi_9(S^6)\cong\mathbb Z/24,\\
 \pi_{12}(S^9)\cong\mathbb Z/24,\qquad
 \pi_{12}(S^6)\cong\mathbb Z/2.
 \end{gathered}
 \hypertarget{tag-0391}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-three-stem-groups}
\end{equation}
The remaining group is identified with $\pi_9(S^6)$ by the exact
suspension isomorphism
\[
 E_R^3:\pi_9(S^6)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_{12}(S^9).
\]
Indeed, the three Freudenthal inequalities are $9<11$, $10<13$ and
$11<15$ \cite[Corollary~4.24]{Hatcher2002}.
Choose a generator $\nu$ of $\pi_9(C_6)$, so that
$[k]_{24}\mapsto k\nu$ is its cyclic coordinate isomorphism.
Since $12[x]=0$ and $R_*$ is a homomorphism, writing
$R_*[x]=a\nu$ gives $24\mid12a$, hence $2\mid a$.
Equivalently, the kernel of multiplication by $12$ on $\mathbb Z/24$
is the image of the isomorphism
$[j]_{12}\mapsto[2j]_{24}$, whose inverse sends $[2j]_{24}$ to
$[j]_{12}$.  Therefore $R_*[x]=2\zeta$ for some
$\zeta\in\pi_9(C_6)$, and
\[
 [\mu_{3,3}(x\wedge y)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}]
   =D_y(R_*[x])=2D_y(\zeta)=0.
\]
All groups and homotopies here are based, so this is a homotopy to
the constant map that fixes the basepoint throughout.
Taking $x=y=\widehat q_3$ in the based sphere identifications proves
the asserted null-homotopy.  Its continuity, surjectivity and quotient
property follow from
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Higher smash powers]
\hypertarget{tag-038T}{}\label{wb:cusp-s12-all-higher-smashes-null}
For every continuous based map $g:S^6\to S^3$ and every integer
$r\geq2$, the ordered external smash
\[
 g^{\wedge r}:S^{6r}\longrightarrow S^{3r}
\]
is based null-homotopic.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the cube models $C_d=[0,1]^d/\partial[0,1]^d$ and the ordered
concatenation homeomorphisms of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}.
Write $\mu_{d_1,\ldots,d_k}$ for concatenation of these blocks;
its inverse splits the nonboundary coordinates into the same blocks
and sends the quotient basepoint to the smash basepoint.
By \cref{wb:cusp-s12-full-carrier-null}, there is a based homotopy
$H_2:C_{12}\times I\to C_6$ with initial map
$\mu_{3,3}(g\wedge g)\mu_{6,6}^{-1}$ and constant terminal map.
This proves the case $r=2$.

For $r>2$, split the source by
$a_r=\mu_{12,6,\ldots,6}^{-1}$ and put
$b_r=\mu_{6,3,\ldots,3}$, with $r-2$ remaining blocks in each.
Define
\[
 H_r\bigl(a_r^{-1}[w,u_3,\ldots,u_r],s\bigr)
 =b_r[H_2(w,s),g(u_3),\ldots,g(u_r)].
\]
The fat wedge maps to the target basepoint at every time, so the
formula descends continuously to $C_{6r}\times I$.
Indeed, the product-to-smash quotient is a closed surjection between
compact Hausdorff spaces, and its product with $I$ is also a quotient.
Concatenating the first two blocks and then the remaining blocks is
the same map as concatenating all blocks at once. Thus
$H_r(-,0)=\mu_{3,\ldots,3}g^{\wedge r}\mu_{6,\ldots,6}^{-1}$.
At time one the first smash factor is the basepoint, so $H_r(-,1)=*$;
the source basepoint remains fixed for every time.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Three Euclidean realizations and their exact scope]
\hypertarget{tag-037J}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-sharp-global-R4-scope}
The two native routes realize $\mathbb R^4$ in the following ways:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for each admissible $T$, as the nonclosed topologically
embedded open cells $U_{12,T}\subset S^6$ and $U_{24,T}\subset S^8$;
\item as the pointed intrinsic Euclidean limit of the four-torus
slices in the global quotient carriers of $S^{12}$ and $S^{24}$;
\item as the Euclidean boundary fibre at $s=0$ of
$\mathfrak E_{12}$ and $\mathfrak E_{24}$.
\end{enumerate}
The cells in the first item are open in their moving four-spheres.
No whole compact sphere or whole compact conical target in these
routes is homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^4$, and no continuous map from
any of those compact spaces to $\mathbb R^4$ is surjective.
In particular $\mathbb R^4$ is not a continuous quotient target
of any of them.  For every fixed compatible ambient target metric,
the unrescaled restricted compact slices converge to a singleton.
Their slice limit is therefore not Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$.
At each fixed $T$, the restricted open-cell metrics admit no
distance-preserving map of all Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ into the cell.
\end{corollary}

We use the exact maps of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-literal-R4-open-cells,wb:cusp-cone-explicit-carriers,
wb:cusp-cone-exact-decompactification-space,wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}.
First, the quotient restrictions
\[
 h_{12,T}=\rho_{12,T}(c_T\times c_T):
 (Q_T\setminus K_T^{(1)})^2\longrightarrow U_{12,T},
 \qquad
 h_{24,T}=\rho_{24,T}:(C_T\setminus\{0\})^4\longrightarrow U_{24,T}
\]
are homeomorphisms.  Off the closed collapsed sets each equivalence
class is a singleton, and every open subset of the complement is
an open saturated set, proving continuity of the inverse quotient
restrictions.  Let
\[
 u_T(a)=[Y_Ta],\quad a\in(0,1)^2,
 \qquad v_T(a)=[\ell_Ta],\quad a\in(0,1),
 \qquad
 \eta(t)=\frac12\left(1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}\right).
\]
The inverse of $u_T$ takes the representatives of $Y_T^{-1}y$ in
$(0,1)^2$, and the inverse of $v_T$ takes the representative in
$(0,\ell_T)$ and divides by $\ell_T$.  Also
\[
 \eta^{-1}(a)=\frac{2a-1}{2\sqrt{a(1-a)}}.
\]
The positive derivative of $\eta$, its limits $0,1$, and
$4\eta(t)(1-\eta(t))=(1+t^2)^{-1}$ prove both inverse identities.
Thus the two homeomorphisms from $\mathbb R^4$ are explicitly
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 t&\longmapsto h_{12,T}
   \bigl(u_T(\eta(t_1),\eta(t_2)),u_T(\eta(t_3),\eta(t_4))\bigr),\\
 t&\longmapsto h_{24,T}
   \bigl(v_T(\eta(t_1)),\ldots,v_T(\eta(t_4))\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Their inverses take the unique uncollapsed representatives, then
the indicated marked inverse coordinates, then $\eta^{-1}$.
In the ambient cube spheres the images have coordinates
\[
 (r_T/\epsilon,a_1,a_2,r_T/\epsilon,a_3,a_4),\qquad
 (r_T/\epsilon,a_1,r_T/\epsilon,a_2,
                  r_T/\epsilon,a_3,r_T/\epsilon,a_4),
 \quad a_j\in(0,1).
\]
Projection to the $a_j$ is the inverse on each image.  The compact
height-section embeddings therefore restrict to the claimed
embeddings.  Taking $a_1=1/n$, $n\geq2$, and the other three
coordinates equal to $1/2$ gives points tending to the omitted
basepoint.  The cells are consequently nonclosed, and their
ambient closures are their compact moving four-spheres.  Varying
the first radial coordinate alone also gives ambient points outside
each moving sphere arbitrarily near each cell point; these cells
are not ambient open subsets.

For the intrinsic assertion, put
\[
 A_T^{(12)}=\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T),\qquad
 A_T^{(24)}=\ell_T I_4,\qquad
 P_{\nu,T}=\mathbb R^4/A_T^{(\nu)}\mathbb Z^4.
\]
Splitting the four coordinates into two pairs identifies $P_{12,T}$
isometrically with $Q_T^2$; taking the four separate residues
identifies $P_{24,T}$ with $C_T^4$.  Their common quotient formula is
\[
 d_T([x],[y])=\min_{n\in\mathbb Z^4}|x-y+A_T^{(\nu)}n|.
\]
Let $c_{12}:(\overline T^2)^2\to\mathbb R^4/\mathbb Z^4$ concatenate
the coordinate pairs and $c_{24}$ concatenate the four circle
coordinates; their inverses split those coordinates.  The exact
slice maps are
\[

 \qquad j_{\nu,T}=\delta_\nu k_{\nu,T}.
\]
At positive height their inverses choose a lift $b$ of the marked
angular coordinate and take $[A_T^{(\nu)}b]$.  Changing that lift
by an integer changes this representative by a period.  The maps
therefore identify the whole flat quotient tori with the complete
height-$r_T$ target slices.  These are the actual sphere-carrier
restrictions, since
\[
 q_2^{\wedge2}i_{12,T}
   =j_{12,T}(\pi_T\times\pi_T),\qquad
 q_1^{\wedge4}i_{24,T}
   =j_{24,T}(\vartheta_T\chi_{\gamma,T})^{\times4}.
\]
Here $i_{12,T}$ and $i_{24,T}$ are the specified embeddings of
$F_T^2$ and $F_T^4$ into the respective sphere-smash sources.
The right factor maps are surjective.

Transport $d_T$ to each slice by $j_{\nu,T}$.  The shortest nonzero
period $\lambda_\nu(T)$ satisfies $\lambda_\nu(T)\geq T-C\to\infty$.
For $\lambda_\nu(T)>4R$, the actual map
$x\mapsto j_{\nu,T}([x])$ is an onto isometry of the entire
Euclidean radius-$R$ ball onto the pointed slice ball.  A nonzero
translated difference between two such vectors has norm at least
$\lambda_\nu(T)-2R>2R$, while their direct difference has norm at
most $2R$.  Every quotient point of distance at most $R$ has a
shortest representative of norm at most $R$, and two such
representatives cannot differ by a nonzero period.  This gives
the inverse of the whole-ball map and proves the pointed intrinsic
Euclidean limit.  The open-ball charts pull back the quotient
tensors exactly to the Euclidean tensor.
These intrinsic diameters tend to infinity as well.  Choose a
shortest nonzero period vector $\lambda$, of length
$\lambda_\nu(T)$.  For every period $\mu$, the vector $\lambda+2\mu$
is nonzero, since otherwise $-\mu=\lambda/2$ would be a shorter
nonzero period.  Therefore $|\lambda/2+\mu|\geq\lambda_\nu(T)/2$,
with equality for $\mu=0$.  The quotient points $[0]$ and
$[\lambda/2]$ are thus at distance $\lambda_\nu(T)/2\to\infty$.

The relation to the fixed metric of
\cref{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization} is also exact.  If
$d_T^{\mathrm{slice}}$ is the intrinsic path metric of its induced
first fundamental form, then
\[
 j_{12,T}^*d_T^{\mathrm{slice}}=(r_T/T)d_T,
 \qquad
 j_{24,T}^*d_T^{\mathrm{slice}}=(r_T/\ell_T)d_T.
\]
Inclusion preserves lengths of slice paths, so the restricted
ambient distance is at most this intrinsic path distance.
The indicated rescalings recover exactly the physical flat metrics
used above.  The unrescaled path-metric diameters for this fixed
metric are at most $r_T(1+C_E/T)$ and $r_T$, respectively.

For the third assertion, the quotient defining $\mathfrak E_\nu$
identifies $(s,x)$ and $(s,y)$ at positive $s$ by the period lattice
$A_{1/s}^{(\nu)}\mathbb Z^4$, and identifies no distinct vectors at
$s=0$.  The map $e_\nu(x)=[0,x]$ and its unique-coordinate inverse
give a homeomorphism $\mathbb R^4\to p_\nu^{-1}(0)$.  The quotient
is open, so for every open $V\subset\mathbb R^4$ and base interval
$I$ containing $0$,
$e_\nu(V)=p_\nu^{-1}(0)\cap q_\nu(I\times V)$ is open in that fibre.
The half-space charts in
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-exact-decompactification-space} make it a boundary
component.  Its assigned metric is exactly Euclidean, and the
positive-fibre maps $x\mapsto[s,x]$ have the preceding entire-ball
isometries for $s<(4R+C+1)^{-1}$ within the parameter interval.
The comparison to the compact carrier is the actual map
\[
 \beta_\nu[s,x]=
 \begin{cases}
 [e^{-2\pi/s},c_\nu^{-1}([(A_{1/s}^{(\nu)})^{-1}x])],&s>0,\\
 d_\nu,&s=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
At positive height its inverse takes $s=-2\pi/\log r$, chooses a
lift $b$ of $c_\nu(a)$ and returns $[s,A_{1/s}^{(\nu)}b]$.
The two formulas are inverse and independent of representatives.
Compactness of the torus link gives continuity at the zero fibre,
since every cone-vertex neighbourhood contains a full small radial
collar.  Thus $\delta_\nu\beta_\nu e_\nu$ is the constant vertex
map, while the positive-fibre restrictions are exactly the torus
slices already identified.  The zero fibre is closed and
homeomorphic to the noncompact $\mathbb R^4$, so $\mathfrak E_\nu$
itself is noncompact.

The whole sphere and conical spaces in these routes are compact
through their defining quotient maps: the cube-sphere maps, the
two-end cylinder quotients defining $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, the
attachment of a compact cone to the compact core of $\mathcal C$,
the finite products and their smash quotients, and
$[0,r_0]\times T^4\to\mathcal D_\nu$ all have compact domains.
For any such space $K$ and continuous $F:K\to\mathbb R^4$, the
continuous function $|F|$ has a finite maximum $M$.  Its image
omits $(M+1,0,0,0)$, so $F$ cannot be surjective.  This excludes
both a quotient onto $\mathbb R^4$ and the continuous surjective
direction of any proposed homeomorphism with it.

The cone-vertex assertion has an independent local pair check.
The maps $[r,a]\mapsto[r/r_0,c_\nu(a)]$ and
$[s,b]\mapsto[r_0s,c_\nu^{-1}(b)]$ identify
$(\mathcal D_\nu,\mathcal D_\nu\setminus\{d_\nu\})$ with its
cone-on-$T^4$ pair.  The full cone contracts by
$[r,a]\mapsto[(1-t)r,a]$, while its punctured part retracts onto
the outer torus by $[r,a]\mapsto[(1-t)r+tr_0,a]$.  The pair
connecting map is therefore an isomorphism to $H_{k-1}(T^4)$ for
$k\geq2$.  In degrees $0,1$ the relative groups vanish because
the $H_0$ inclusion is the identity.  The product circle cells have
zero boundary and give ranks $4,6,4,1$ in degrees $1,2,3,4$.
Orienting a coned cell by its positive outer boundary makes the
connecting map send its class to that torus cell.  Thus the local
groups are $\mathbb Z^4,\mathbb Z^6,\mathbb Z^4,\mathbb Z$ in
degrees $2,3,4,5$, and zero otherwise, as in
\eqref{wb:cusp-cone-carrier-local-homology}.  Excision makes these
the groups on every small vertex neighbourhood.  A Euclidean
chart would induce pair-homology isomorphisms to a pair with one
$\mathbb Z$ in its dimension; radial retraction of punctured
Euclidean space proves that pattern.  A boundary half-space and
its punctured version are both contractible, the latter retracting
onto a contractible hemisphere, so their relative groups all
vanish.  In dimension zero the interior pair is a point relative
to the empty set.  The actual rank-four group in degree two
excludes every one of these chart-induced isomorphisms.
It also fails the interior and boundary local homology patterns
of an integral homology manifold in every dimension.

Finally let $D_0$ be the fixed compatible metric of
\cref{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization} on a conical smash target.
The synchronized torus slices satisfy $D_0(z,*)=r_T$ exactly:
the product distance to the fat wedge is the minimum of the
factor distances to their inward vertices, each of which is $r_T$.
For any fixed compatible metric $D$ on that same compact target,
the identity is a homeomorphism.  Define its modulus
\[
 \omega_D(t)=\sup\{D(x,y):D_0(x,y)\leq t\}.
\]
It is finite and tends to zero with $t$.  Indeed a contradicting
sequence of pairs with $D_0(x_n,y_n)\to0$ has a convergent
subsequence whose two components have the same limit; compatibility
then forces $D(x_n,y_n)\to0$.  Consequently
\[
 \sup_{z\in\Sigma_T}D(z,*)\leq\omega_D(r_T),\qquad
 \operatorname{diam}_D\Sigma_T\leq2\omega_D(r_T)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The corresponding sphere-target assertion follows from the cube
quotient metric $d_0([x],*)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial I^n)$:
the displayed synchronized coordinates give distance at most
$r_T/\epsilon$.  The identity modulus for any fixed compatible
sphere metric thus bounds the entire moving four-sphere's diameter
by $2\omega_D(r_T/\epsilon)\to0$.

These compact slices converge in ambient Hausdorff distance to
the vertex.  The correspondence sending every slice point to one
point has distortion equal to the slice diameter and respects any
chosen slice basepoint, so the unrescaled pointed restricted limit
is a singleton.  A Euclidean radius-two ball contains $0,e_1$ at
distance one; no correspondences of vanishing distortion from
spaces of vanishing diameter can approximate that pair.  Hence
this restricted limit cannot be $\mathbb R^4$.
For each fixed $T$, the open cell's restricted distance has the
finite diameter bound of its compact ambient sphere.  A
distance-preserving map from all $\mathbb R^4$ would send $0,ne_1$
to points at distance $n$, exceeding that bound for large $n$.
This proves the last assertion for every compatible ambient metric.
\end{proof}

slices already identified.  The zero fibre is closed and

through their defining quotient maps: the cube-sphere maps, the
two-end cylinder quotients defining $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, the
attachment of a compact cone to the compact core of $\mathcal C$,
the finite products and their smash quotients, and
$[0,r_0]\times T^4\to\mathcal D_\nu$ all have compact domains.

continuous function $|F|$ has a finite maximum $M$.  Its image
omits $(M+1,0,0,0)$, so $F$ cannot be surjective.  This excludes

direction of any proposed homeomorphism with it.

connecting map is therefore an isomorphism to $H_{k-1}(T^4)$ for

connecting map send its class to that torus cell.  Thus the local

degrees $2,3,4,5$, and zero otherwise, as in
\eqref{wb:cusp-cone-carrier-local-homology}.  Excision makes these

vanish.  In dimension zero the interior pair is a point relative

the product distance to the fat wedge is the minimum of the
factor distances to their inward vertices, each of which is $r_T$.

sequence of pairs with $D_0(x_n,y_n)\to0$ has a convergent

then forces $D(x_n,y_n)\to0$.  Consequently

 \operatorname{diam}_D\Sigma_T\leq2\omega_D(r_T)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The corresponding sphere-target assertion follows from the cube
quotient metric $d_0([x],*)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial I^n)$:
the displayed synchronized coordinates give distance at most
$r_T/\epsilon$.  The identity modulus for any fixed compatible
sphere metric thus bounds the entire moving four-sphere's diameter
by $2\omega_D(r_T/\epsilon)\to0$.

These compact slices converge in ambient Hausdorff distance to
the vertex.  The correspondence sending every slice point to one
point has distortion equal to the slice diameter and respects any
chosen slice basepoint, so the unrescaled pointed restricted limit
is a singleton.  A Euclidean radius-two ball contains $0,e_1$ at
distance one; no correspondences of vanishing distortion from
spaces of vanishing diameter can approximate that pair.  Hence
this restricted limit cannot be $\mathbb R^4$.
For each fixed $T$, the open cell's restricted distance has the
finite diameter bound of its compact ambient sphere.  A
distance-preserving map from all $\mathbb R^4$ would send $0,ne_1$
to points at distance $n$, exceeding that bound for large $n$.
This proves the last assertion for every compatible ambient metric.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Canonicity and exact scope.}
The lattice \(K_\Lambda=\ker(M_0-I)=\operatorname{im}(M_0-I)\) and the
punctured-cusp quotient are intrinsic to the marked cusp monodromy.
The compact map \(q_2\) additionally depends on the chosen cusp coordinate,
closed cusp disc, and the decision to collapse its outer boundary and the
exterior.  The identifications
\(X^{\wedge2}\cong S^{12}\) and \(X^{\wedge4}\cong S^{24}\) depend on a
based choice of \(X\cong S^6\).  None of these choices is claimed to be
holomorphic or canonical in the algebraic category.

The map \(q_2^{\wedge2}\) is the direct two-copy construction from the
native \(T^2\times\mathbb R^2\) cusp: it is globally defined on the smash
sphere, and its radial regular-fibre quotients are \(Q_T\times Q_T\), which
converge pointed local-isometrically, smoothly, and Gromov--Hausdorff to
\(\mathbb R^4\).  It is not a torus quotient over the full
regular base.  The map \(q_{1,\mathrm{cusp}}^{\wedge4}\) is the parallel
cusp-supported construction with target
\(\operatorname{Susp}(T^2)^{\wedge4}\).  The stronger map
\(q_1^{\wedge4}\) uses the quotient over every regular and finite-filled
fibre before the cusp cone is attached; four copies are minimal for that
full-base all-expanding group quotient.
Neither construction gives a compact complex \(S^{12}\) or \(S^{24}\), an
ambient Euclidean limit in a fixed compact metric target, or a claim about
the interacting Yang--Mills spectrum.

The argument does not rule out a separately constructed branched or
toroidal compactification of the auxiliary finite covers after additional
branching away from \(p_0\).  Such a construction would have to specify its
global base cover, normalize and resolve every pulled-back singular fibre,
track the lifted metric, and determine the topology of the resulting total
space.  No such smooth compact sphere construction follows from the present
data.


\subsubsection{Optimal sphere exponents and the exact Euclidean boundary}
\hypertarget{tag-0376}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-optimal-strengthening}

Within the class of native connected fibrewise torus quotients equipped with
the induced, unscaled quotient of the marked Euclidean metric, the two sphere
dimensions in the preceding constructions are forced by two different
integral quotient problems.  Cusp-locally, each copy has an expanding
quotient of rank two, so two copies are necessary and sufficient within that
class.  Over the full regular base, monodromy leaves at most one expanding
quotient direction per copy, so four copies are necessary and sufficient
within the same class.  We now prove this scoped optimality, identify the
compact conical carriers, and construct a noncompact comparison manifold in
which the limiting \(\mathbb R^4\) is an actual boundary fibre.  There is only
a continuous comparison map from this manifold to the compact conical
carrier: it set-theoretically collapses the new boundary, is a homeomorphism
away from that boundary, and is nonproper and nonquotient.

Throughout this subsubsection,
\[
 B_R^Z(z):=\{w\in Z:d_Z(z,w)\leq R\}
\]
denotes the closed radius-\(R\) ball; when the ambient space and center are
clear, superscripts and centers are suppressed.

\emph{The cusp bound and its attainment.}
The vectors \(P_Tw=(1,0,0,0)\) and
\(P_T\delta=(0,0,1,0)\) have length one.  A nonzero quotient image of
any \(w_i\) or \(\delta_i\) therefore has length at most one.
Every fixed integral combination of these vectors is uniformly
bounded by the sum of the absolute values of its coefficients.
Divergent systole forces
\[
 K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\subset N,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq2r.
\]
This argument includes kernels that mix the factors.

Projection to the two imaginary coordinates has kernel
\(P_T(K_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)=
\mathbb R\langle(1,0,0,0),(0,0,1,0)\rangle\).
It is the orthogonal quotient projection and gives the exact
isometry
\[
 F_T/K_T\longrightarrow Q_T=\mathbb R^2/Y_T\mathbb Z^2,\qquad
 [P_Ta]\longmapsto[Y_T(a_g,a_u)],
 \quad
 K_T=P_T(K_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)/P_TK_\Lambda.
\]
The marked identification
\(\iota_T:(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2\to Q_T\) is
\([a]\mapsto[Y_Ta]\), with inverse induced by \(Y_T^{-1}\).
The fixed-fibre section
\([Y_T(a,b)]\mapsto[P_T(a,b,0,0)]\) is well defined and is a right
inverse to the quotient.

The cusp monodromy sends \(g\) to \(g-\delta\), \(u\) to \(u+w\),
and fixes \(w,\delta\); its specified affine drift is zero.
It therefore induces the identity on \(\Lambda/K_\Lambda\), so this
quotient descends over the entire punctured cusp.
Write
\[
 Y_T=T\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
       +E_T,\qquad
 E_T=\begin{pmatrix}6m&H\\B-H&m\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first matrix is orthogonal and \(\|E_T\|\leq C_E\) on a radial
tail.  Hence
\(\|Y_Tv\|\geq(T-C_E)\|v\|\) for every real \(v\) and \(T>C_E\).
For \(r=2\), the product metric gives
\[
 \operatorname{sys}\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(Y_T,Y_T)\mathbb Z^4\bigr)
 =\operatorname{sys}(Y_T\mathbb Z^2)\geq T-C_E.
\]
Indeed a nonzero product vector has a nonzero component of at least
the single-factor systole, and a shortest single-factor vector placed
in one component attains that length.
This proves the first bound and its sharpness in the unscaled metric.

\emph{The full-base bound, including finite covers.}
For the original base, the exact identity
\(A_1w=u-w\), together with invariance of \(N\) and
\(w_i,\delta_i\in N\), gives \(u_i\in N\) for each factor.
For a finite cover use the left-deck word
\[
 G_*=A_2A_1=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&0\\
 6&1&1&0\\
 0&0&1&0\\
 -5&0&-1&1
 \end{pmatrix}
 =I+N_*,\qquad N_*^2=0.
\]
Let \(\Gamma'\) be the subgroup of \(\pi_1(B^\circ)\) defining the
connected cover, of index \(d_{\mathrm{base}}\geq1\).
Among the \(d_{\mathrm{base}}+1\) right cosets represented by the
first \(d_{\mathrm{base}}+1\) nonnegative powers of a loop with this
matrix, two coincide.  Their exponent difference gives an integer
\(1\leq h\leq d_{\mathrm{base}}\) whose loop power belongs to \(\Gamma'\).
No normality assumption is used.  Write \(\rho\) for the monodromy
representation.  The image of \(\Gamma'\) in the
monodromy image has finite index as well: the map of right-coset
sets \(\Gamma'\backslash\pi_1(B^\circ)\to
\rho(\Gamma')\backslash\rho(\pi_1(B^\circ))\) induced by \(\rho\) is onto.

The power formula gives
\[
 G_*^h=I+hN_*,
 \qquad G_*^hw=w+h(u-\delta).
\]
In each factor this puts \(hu_i\) in \(N\).  Since
\(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N\) is torsion free, it follows that \(u_i\in N\).
Consequently
\[
 L_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\subset N,
 \qquad \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda^{\oplus r}/N)\leq r.
\]
Equivalently, a covector already annihilating \(K_\Lambda^{\oplus r}\)
has rows \((a_i,b_i,0,0)\), and the exact dual action is
\[
 (a_i,b_i,0,0)G_*^h=(a_i+6hb_i,b_i,hb_i,0).
\]
Invariance of \(N^\perp\) forces \(hb_i=0\), hence \(b_i=0\);
the integral double-annihilator identity gives the same inclusion.
For the clutch convention \((x,1)\sim(A^{-1}x,0)\), forward transport
uses the inverse matrix.  The equality \(AN=N\) is equivalent to
\(A^{-1}N=N\), and the covering subgroup contains inverse loops,
so the calculation applies with that convention as well.
A compact base cover branched over the original singular values
restricts to such a connected cover on the regular locus.
The radial metric there is the pullback of the original metric with
\(T=-\log|t|/(2\pi)\).

\emph{The attaining circle quotient and its metric.}
The primitive row \(\gamma=(1,0,0,0)\) satisfies
\(\gamma A_1=\gamma A_2=\gamma\).  Its kernel in \(\Lambda\) is
\(L_\Lambda\), and the quotient isomorphism
\(\Lambda/L_\Lambda\to\mathbb Z\) is induced by \(\gamma\), with
inverse \(n\mapsto[ng]\).
For an affine transition \(a\mapsto Aa+b\), its circle coordinate
changes by
\(\gamma(Aa+b)=\gamma(a)+\gamma(b)\).
These are the actual transition maps of the full-base circle
quotient bundle, and they pull back to every finite cover.

On a radial fibre,
\[
 d_T=P_T^{-T}\gamma^T
   =\left(0,\frac{m}{D_T},0,-\frac{L}{D_T}\right)^T,
 \qquad
 \ell_T=\frac{1}{\|d_T\|}
        =\frac{D_T}{\sqrt{L^2+m^2}}>0.
\]
Thus
\[
 \chi_{\gamma,T}([y])=[\langle d_T,y\rangle]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}:=\vartheta_T\circ\chi_{\gamma,T},
 \qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}([P_Ta])=[\ell_Ta_g].
\]
The inverse of \(\vartheta_T\) is \([s]\mapsto[s/\ell_T]\).
The covector \(\ell_Td_T\) has norm one and kernel
\(P_T(L_\Lambda\otimes\mathbb R)\).  Its scalar projection identifies
the quotient line isometrically with \(\mathbb R\), and sends its
period lattice to \(\ell_T\mathbb Z\).  The least-norm lift of a
scalar \(s\) is \(s\ell_Td_T\), of norm \(|s|\).
Equivalently, eliminating the \(u\)-coordinate from
\(G=Y_T^TY_T\) gives
\[
 G_{11}-\frac{G_{12}^2}{G_{22}}
 =\frac{(\det Y_T)^2}{L^2+m^2}=\ell_T^2.
\]
The four unit covectors in the four factors have disjoint supports.
Their product quotient therefore has exactly the lattice
\(\ell_T\mathbb Z^4\) and systole \(\ell_T\).

Put \(R_T=\sqrt{L^2+m^2}\).  On the tail where \(L>0\),
rationalization gives the exact identity
\[
 \ell_T-(L-B)=
 \frac{m^2}{R_T}
 \left(6-\frac{L-B}{R_T+L}\right).
\]
Boundedness of \(m,H,B\), and \(L=T+H\), make its right side
\(O(T^{-1})\).  This estimate needs no limit for those bounded
coefficients.  For \(m=0\) the identity is exactly
\(\ell_T=L-B\) on that tail.  It follows that
\(\ell_T=T+H-B+O(T^{-1})\to\infty\).

 h&:\pi_{24}(S^8)\longrightarrow H_{24}(S^8;\mathbb Z)=0,
 \end{aligned}

\((G_{24})_*[S^{24}]=0\).

\(g_*[M]=\deg(g)[N]\) in \(H_n(N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[N]\).

\begin{corollary}[Repeated smashes of the circle-quotient carrier]
\hypertarget{tag-036E}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-sphere-map-null}
Let \(f=\widehat q_\gamma:S^6\to S^2\) be the based quotient map of
\cref{wb:cusp-cone-angle-forgotten-sphere-carriers}, using its chosen
based identification \((X,x_0)\cong(S^6,*)\), where \(x_0\in W\).
For every integer \(r\geq2\),
\begin{equation}
 \bigl[f^{\wedge r}\bigr]=0
 \quad\text{in}\quad
 \pi_{6r}(S^{2r}).
 \hypertarget{tag-0367}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-null-maps}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \bigl[\widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge2}\bigr]
 =0\in\pi_{12}(S^4),
 \qquad
 \bigl[\widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge4}\bigr]
 =0\in\pi_{24}(S^8).
 \hypertarget{tag-0368}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-null-special-cases}
\end{equation}
The specified map
\(\widehat q_\gamma^{\wedge4}:S^{24}\twoheadrightarrow S^8\)
is a continuous surjective quotient map and admits a global based
null-homotopy whose initial map is this representative.
For every native radial parameter with
\(0<r_T=e^{-2\pi T}<\epsilon\), its radial restriction is
\[
 F_T^4\xrightarrow{\ \pi_{\gamma,T}^{\times4}\ }C_T^4
 \xrightarrow{\ \rho_{24,T}\ }\mathbb S_{24,T}^4
 \xrightarrow{\ i_T\ }S^8,
 \qquad
 \pi_{\gamma,T}=\vartheta_T\circ\chi_{\gamma,T},
 \quad \vartheta_T[\theta]=[\ell_T\theta].
\]
Here \(C_T=\mathbb R/\ell_T\mathbb Z\), with \(\ell_T>0\), and
\(i_T\) is the fourth smash of the height section
\([u]\mapsto[r_T,[u/\ell_T]]\), using the chosen target sphere coordinates.
Give \(\mathbb S_{24,T}^4=C_T^{\wedge4}\) the quotient length metric
from the Euclidean product metric on \(C_T^4\), and put
\[
 \zeta_{24,T}=[\ell_T/2,\ell_T/2,\ell_T/2,\ell_T/2].
\]
For each \(R>0\), the parameters on the native tail with \(\ell_T>4R\)
give an isometry from the entire Euclidean radius-\(R\) ball onto the
entire intrinsic radius-\(R\) ball about \(\zeta_{24,T}\).
Consequently these based radial four-spheres have the pointed
local-isometric and pointed Gromov--Hausdorff limit \((\mathbb R^4,0)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the based cube model \(C_n=[0,1]^n/\partial[0,1]^n\) for \(S^n\).
The coordinate map
\(a_j\mapsto\tan(\pi(a_j-\tfrac12))\) on the open cube, with inverse
\(u_j\mapsto\tfrac12+\pi^{-1}\arctan u_j\), extends to the
one-point compactification by sending the boundary class to infinity.
Concatenation of cube coordinates induces a based homeomorphism
\[
 \beta_{p,q}:S^p\wedge S^q\longrightarrow S^{p+q}.
\]
Its inverse splits an interior tuple after its \(p\)-th coordinate
and sends the boundary class to the smash basepoint.  The quotient
identifications make these continuous inverse maps.
Repeated concatenation gives
\(\mu_{n,r}:(S^n)^{\wedge r}\to S^{nr}\);
all its parenthesizations have the same values on representatives.
Use these maps and their inverses in the sphere identifications below.

Writing the chosen source and target homeomorphisms as \(h_6\) and \(h_2\),
the actual single-factor map is
\[
 f=h_2\circ\widehat p_1\circ q_{1,\mathrm{cusp}}\circ h_6^{-1},
 \qquad \widehat p_1[r,z,\theta]=[r,\theta].
\]
The two end vertices of \(\mathcal B\) map to the basepoint of the
reduced suspension, so this formula is defined on the stated quotient.
It is the based surjective map in the cited construction.

The smash square has the exact factorization
\begin{equation}
 \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 S^6\wedge S^6
 \arrow[r,"f\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^6}"]&
 S^2\wedge S^6
 \arrow[r,"\operatorname{id}_{S^2}\wedge f"]&
 S^2\wedge S^2 .
 \end{tikzcd}
 \hypertarget{tag-036C}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-smash-square-factorization}
\end{equation}
For clarity, let
\(\tau_{p,q}:S^p\wedge S^q\to S^q\wedge S^p\) send
\([x,y]\) to \([y,x]\).  Its inverse is \(\tau_{q,p}\).
The precise comparison with left suspension is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 f\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^6}
   &=\tau_{6,2}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{S^6}\wedge f)
                         \circ\tau_{6,6},\\
 \beta_{6,2}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{S^6}\wedge f)
                         \circ\beta_{6,6}^{-1}
   &=\Sigma^6f:S^{12}\longrightarrow S^8.
 \end{aligned}
 \hypertarget{tag-036B}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-S24-sixfold-suspension}
\end{equation}
The first equality sends \([x,y]\) through
\([y,x]\), \([y,f(x)]\), and \([f(x),y]\).
It also holds on the collapsed fat wedge because all maps are based.
Both orders of applying \(f\) to the two factors consequently give
\(f\wedge f\).

The suspension map is an isomorphism in degree \(i<2n-1\)
for \(S^n\), by \cite[Corollary~4.24, p.~360]{Hatcher2002}.
For \(i=12,n=8\), the inequality is \(12\leq14\), and it
remains strict in the form \(12+j<2(8+j)-1\) for every \(j\geq0\).
The canonical iterated-suspension map therefore gives
\phantomsection\hypertarget{tag-033R}{}\label{qa:III:layout:11}
\begin{equation}
 \pi_{12}(S^8)\cong\pi_4^{\mathrm S}=0.
 \hypertarget{tag-036R}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-fourth-stable-stem}
\end{equation}
The zero stable stem is the \(k=4\) row of
\cite[Corollary~1.3, p.~112, and Table~1, p.~113]{IsaksenWangXu2023};
the three homotopy summands in that row are all trivial.

For every integer \(s\geq1\), define the sphere-coordinate smash map
\[
 F_s=\mu_{2,s}\circ f^{\wedge s}\circ\mu_{6,s}^{-1},
 \qquad \mu_{n,1}=\operatorname{id}_{S^n}.
\]
Thus \(F_1=f\).  Take an integer \(r\geq2\) and put \(m=6(r-1)\).
There is a factorization \(F_r=B_rA_r\), where
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 A_r&=\beta_{m,2}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{S^m}\wedge f)
                       \circ\beta_{m,6}^{-1}:
                 S^{6r}\longrightarrow S^{6r-4},\\
 B_r&=\beta_{2(r-1),2}\circ(F_{r-1}\wedge\operatorname{id}_{S^2})
                       \circ\beta_{m,2}^{-1}:
                 S^{6r-4}\longrightarrow S^{2r}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first map applies \(f\) to the last factor, and the second applies
it to the preceding factors.  Thus their composite equals \(F_r\)
on every product representative, including those for which a
nonbasepoint coordinate has \(f\)-image \(*\).
The map \(A_r\) is \(\Sigma^{6(r-1)}f\).  Its group is
\(\pi_{n+4}(S^n)\), where \(n=6r-4\); the stable-range margin is
\[
 n-(4+1)=6(r-2)+3>0.
\]
The same iterated-suspension map identifies this group with
\(\pi_4^{\mathrm S}=0\).  Choose a based null-homotopy \(N_r\)
of \(A_r\), with \(N_r(-,0)=A_r\), \(N_r(-,1)=*\), and
\(N_r(*,s)=*\).  Then
\[
 H_r(x,s)=B_r(N_r(x,s))
\]
is a continuous global based homotopy from \(F_r\) to the constant map.
This proves both displayed nullity assertions.

For any nonbasepoint target tuple, choose a preimage under \(f\)
in each coordinate.  None of these preimages is the source basepoint.
This proves surjectivity of every \(F_r\); continuity and compactness
of the source with Hausdorff target make each \(F_r\) a quotient map.
In particular \(H_4(-,0)\) is exactly the specified surjective quotient.

For the radial assertion put
\[
 j_T[u]=h_2[r_T,[u/\ell_T]],\qquad
 i_T=\mu_{2,4}\circ j_T^{\wedge4}.
\]
For \(0<r_T<\epsilon\), the first map is injective:
away from the basepoint the height and circle coordinate are unchanged,
and its basepoint preimage is exactly \(0\in C_T\).
The same representative argument proves that \(i_T\) is an embedding.
The homeomorphism \(C_T^{\wedge4}\to[0,1]^4/\partial[0,1]^4\)
sends an uncollapsed tuple to its representatives \(u_j/\ell_T\in(0,1)\);
its inverse sends \(a\) to \([\ell_Ta_1,\ldots,\ell_Ta_4]\).
If \(\kappa_T:F_T^4\to S^{24}\) is induced by the native inclusions
and \(h_6\) in each source factor, the defining radial map gives
\[
 H_4(\kappa_T(x),0)
 =i_T\!\left(\rho_{24,T}
       (\pi_{\gamma,T}(x_1),\ldots,\pi_{\gamma,T}(x_4))\right).
\]
Here \(\vartheta_T^{-1}[u]=[u/\ell_T]\); thus every circle in this
identity has its stated angle or arclength coordinate.

Finally let \(E=C_T^4\), let \(W_T\) be its fat wedge, and put
\(b=(\ell_T/2,\ldots,\ell_T/2)\).  For a point \(x\) with lift \(u\),
\[
 a(x):=d_E(x,W_T)=\min_j\operatorname{dist}(u_j,\ell_T\mathbb Z).
\]
The quotient length metric is
\[
 d_{E/W_T}([x],[y])
   =\min\{d_E(x,y),a(x)+a(y)\}.
\]
A path chain without a jump through \(W_T\) costs at least the
first term; one with such a jump costs at least the second term.
Projected paths in \(E\), including paths from both endpoints to
\(W_T\), give the reverse inequalities.
For \(u,v\in\overline B_R(0)\) and \(\ell_T>4R\), every nonzero
period vector \(\lambda\) satisfies
\[
 \|u-v+\lambda\|\geq\ell_T-2R>2R\geq\|u-v\|,
\]
and
\[
 a([b+u])+a([b+v])\geq\ell_T-2R>2R.
\]
Thus \(v\mapsto\rho_{24,T}[b+v]\) preserves every distance on the
Euclidean radius-\(R\) ball.
For a quotient point within distance \(R\) of \(\rho_{24,T}(b)\),
the second branch of the quotient-distance formula exceeds \(R\),
because \(a(b)=\ell_T/2>R\).  Its uncollapsed representative therefore
has product-torus distance at most \(R\) from \(b\), and has a unique
lift \(b+v\) with \(\|v\|\leq R\).  This gives the inverse and proves
surjectivity onto the entire intrinsic ball.
These maps agree on nested balls.  Since \(\ell_T\to\infty\) on the
native tail, they prove the stated exact pointed limit for the radial
restrictions of the same initial representative \(H_4(-,0)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Radial target-slice maps]
\hypertarget{tag-037N}{}\label{wb:cusp-cone-target-slice-embeddings}
{\normalfont\scriptsize tag 037N}\par
Take \(T\) in the native admissible range, with \(Y_T\) invertible and
\(\ell_T>0\), and impose
\[
 0<r_T=e^{-2\pi T}<\epsilon,
 \qquad T> -\frac{\log\epsilon}{2\pi}.
\]
The second inequality is exactly the upper radial condition.  The native
radial coordinate has interval \([0,\epsilon]\).  The basepoints of
\(\mathcal A,\mathcal B,\mathcal C\) are their radial-zero points.
The two endpoint tori of each suspension are collapsed separately.
The cone collapses its zero torus and attaches its outer torus to
\(\partial M=T_0\) by the identity.
The marked angular homeomorphisms and their inverses are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \iota_T:(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2&\longrightarrow
 Q_T=\mathbb R^2/Y_T\mathbb Z^2,&
 [a]&\longmapsto[Y_Ta],&
 [y]&\longmapsto[Y_T^{-1}y],\\
 \vartheta_T:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z&\longrightarrow
 C_T=\mathbb R/\ell_T\mathbb Z,&
 [a]&\longmapsto[\ell_Ta],&
 [u]&\longmapsto[u/\ell_T].
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(y_1,y_2\in Q_T\), put
\[
 j_T(y_1,y_2)=
 \bigl[[r_T,1,\iota_T^{-1}(y_1)],
       [r_T,1,\iota_T^{-1}(y_2)]\bigr]_{\wedge}
 \in\mathcal A^{\wedge2}.
\]
For \(c_1,\ldots,c_4\in C_T\), put
\[
 k_T^{\mathcal B}(c_1,\ldots,c_4)=
 \bigl[[r_T,1,\vartheta_T^{-1}(c_1)],\ldots,
       [r_T,1,\vartheta_T^{-1}(c_4)]\bigr]_{\wedge}
 \in\mathcal B^{\wedge4}
\]
and
\[
 k_T^{\mathcal C}(c_1,\ldots,c_4)=
 \bigwedge_{j=1}^4[r_T,(1,\vartheta_T^{-1}(c_j))]
 \in\mathcal C^{\wedge4}.
\]
In the last formula the boundary coordinates are related to the actual
torus \(T_0=\partial D_0\times S^1\) by
\[
 \rho_0(z,[a])=(\epsilon z,e^{2\pi ia}),\qquad
 \rho_0^{-1}(p,w)=(p/\epsilon,\arg(w)/(2\pi)\bmod\mathbb Z).
\]
Here the argument is a class modulo \(2\pi\), so the inverse involves no
choice of a real argument branch.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Radial embeddings and endpoint maps]
\hypertarget{tag-Q30T}{}\label{mapsIII:lem:radial-slice-embeddings}
{\normalfont\scriptsize tag Q30T}\par
The three maps of Definition~\ref{wb:cusp-cone-target-slice-embeddings}
are topological embeddings for $0<r_T<\epsilon$.
At radius zero all three are constant. At radius $\epsilon$ the
two suspension maps are constant, whereas the cone map remains an embedding.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Changing \(y\) by \(Y_Tn\) changes \(Y_T^{-1}y\) by \(n\), and changing
\(u\) by \(\ell_Tm\) changes \(u/\ell_T\) by \(m\).  Thus both pairs of
angular maps descend continuously from inverse real linear maps and have
the displayed inverse compositions.

The quotient maps defining the two suspensions restrict to homeomorphisms
on their open cylinders
\[
 (0,\epsilon)\times S^1\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2,
 \qquad (0,\epsilon)\times S^1\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z).
\]
Indeed, each open cylinder and every open subset of it are open and
saturated in the defining product, and every equivalence class there is
a singleton.  The restrictions are therefore continuous open bijections;
their inverses take the unique interior representatives.  In the
presentation of \(\mathcal C=M\cup_{T_0}\operatorname{Cone}_\epsilon(T_0)\),
the subset \((0,\epsilon)\times T_0\), with empty \(M\)-part, has the same
open and saturated property.  Its quotient restriction is a homeomorphism
as well.  Composing its inverse with \(\rho_0^{-1}\) gives the displayed
cone coordinates.

Consequently the single-factor maps
\[
 \alpha_T(y)=[r_T,1,\iota_T^{-1}(y)],\quad
 \beta_T(c)=[r_T,1,\vartheta_T^{-1}(c)],\quad
 \gamma_T(c)=[r_T,(1,\vartheta_T^{-1}(c))]
\]
are embeddings into those cylinders.  Their inverses on their images are,
respectively,
\[
 [r_T,1,a]\longmapsto\iota_T(a),\qquad
 [r_T,1,a]\longmapsto\vartheta_T(a),\qquad
 [r_T,(1,a)]\longmapsto\vartheta_T(a).
\]
All of these maps are continuous chart projections followed by the
angular homeomorphisms.  Their images avoid the radial-zero basepoints.

For each of these carriers \((X,x_0)\), the singleton \(\{x_0\}\) is
closed: its full preimage in the defining quotient is exactly the closed
radial-zero torus, with empty \(M\)-part in the cone attachment.  Hence the
fat wedge
\[
 F_n=\bigcup_{i=1}^n\operatorname{pr}_i^{-1}(\{x_0\})\subset X^n
\]
is closed.  The smash quotient restricts to the homeomorphism
\[
 q_n:(X\setminus\{x_0\})^n
 \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }X^{\wedge n}\setminus\{*\}.
\]
To verify the topology explicitly, every open subset of this complement
is open and saturated in \(X^n\); its classes are singletons.  The inverse
of this restriction sends a nonbasepoint smash class to its unique
ordered tuple of nonbasepoint factors.  Therefore
\[
 j_T=q_2\circ(\alpha_T\times\alpha_T),\qquad
 k_T^{\mathcal B}=q_4\circ\beta_T^4,\qquad
 k_T^{\mathcal C}=q_4\circ\gamma_T^4
\]
are embeddings.  On their images the inverses first take that ordered
tuple and then apply the corresponding single-factor inverse above.
This proves both inverse compositions and inverse continuity.

The strict radial scope is necessary for the common assertion.  At
\(r=0\) all three formulas take the single smash basepoint value.  At
\(r=\epsilon\), the two suspension formulas are constant at the ordered
tuple of their radial-\(\epsilon\) poles.  The distinct classes
\([0]\) and \([Y_T(1/2,0)]\) in \(Q_T\), and \([0]\) and
\([\ell_T/2]\) in \(C_T\), give explicit failures of injectivity there.
For the cone, \([\epsilon,(1,a)]\) is instead the boundary point
\((\epsilon,e^{2\pi ia})\) in \(M\).  The inclusion \(M\to\mathcal C\)
is an embedding: an open \(O\subset M\) extends to the open saturated
set with \(M\)-part \(O\) and cone part
\((\epsilon/2,\epsilon]\times(O\cap T_0)\).  The outer cone circle and its
fourfold smash map therefore remain embeddings.  Finally, passage to
unit cone radius is the homeomorphism \([r,t]\mapsto[r/\epsilon,t]\),
with inverse \([u,t]\mapsto[\epsilon u,t]\), and is the identity on \(M\)
for the attachment.  The unit-coordinate slice therefore has radius $r_T/\epsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One fixed cusp-adapted metric realizes the vertical
\(\mathbb R^4\) limits]
\hypertarget{tag-03D6}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-fixed-realization}

Use the native cusp range \(T\geq T_0>0\), with
\(r_T=e^{-2\pi T}\leq r_0=e^{-2\pi T_0}<\epsilon\), in which
\(Y_T\) is invertible and \(\ell_T>0\).  The angular coordinates
\(u,\theta\) have period one, and
\[
 T(r)=-\frac{\log r}{2\pi},\qquad
 h_T=\iota_T^*g_{Q_T},\qquad
 \iota_T[a]=[Y_Ta],\qquad \vartheta_T[a]=[\ell_Ta].
\]
There are fixed compatible length metrics
\[
 D_{12}\text{ on }Z_{12},\qquad
 D_{24}^{\mathcal B}\text{ on }Z_{24}^{\mathcal B},\qquad
 D_{24}^{\mathcal C}\text{ on }Z_{24}^{\mathcal C}
\]
with the following properties.

On the inner cone of \(\mathcal A\), the metric is induced by
\begin{equation}
 g_{\mathcal A}
 =dr^2+r^2du^2+\frac{r^2}{T(r)^2}h_{T(r)}.
 \hypertarget{tag-03CW}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-A-fixed-metric}
\end{equation}
On the cusp cone of either \(\mathcal B\) or \(\mathcal C\), it is induced
by
\begin{equation}
 g_{\mathcal D}=dr^2+r^2(du^2+d\theta^2),
 \qquad\mathcal D\in\{\mathcal B,\mathcal C\}.
 \hypertarget{tag-03CY}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-BC-fixed-metric}
\end{equation}
The metrics on the smash powers are the metric quotients of the product
length metrics after the closed fat wedge is collapsed.  Write
\(g_{Z_{12}}\) and \(g_{Z_{24}^{\mathcal D}}\) for the resulting smooth
Riemannian tensors on the open regular strata.

Let
\[
 p_T^{12}:=j_T(0,0),\qquad
 p_T^{24,\mathcal D}:=k_T^{\mathcal D}(0,0,0,0).
\]
Put
\[
 \Sigma_T^{12}:=j_T(Q_T^2),\qquad
 \Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D}:=k_T^{\mathcal D}(C_T^4).
\]
Let \(d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{slice}}\) and
\(d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{slice}}\) be the intrinsic Riemannian path
metrics of the first fundamental forms on these embedded slices.  Define
also the restricted ambient distance functions
\[
 d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{amb}}
 :=D_{12}|_{\Sigma_T^{12}\times\Sigma_T^{12}},\qquad
 d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{amb}}
 :=D_{24}^{\mathcal D}|_{\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D}
                         \times\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D}}.
\]
For all \(T\geq T_0\),
\[
 d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{amb}}\leq d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{slice}},\qquad
 d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{amb}}
 \leq d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{slice}}.
\]
For every sufficiently large \(T\), each of these inequalities is strict
on some pairs of points.

Then the induced first fundamental forms on the target slices satisfy the
exact identities
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{T}{r_T}\right)^2
  j_T^*g_{Z_{12}}
 =g_{Q_T}\oplus g_{Q_T},
 \hypertarget{tag-03CX}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-A-slice-exact}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{\ell_T}{r_T}\right)^2
  (k_T^{\mathcal D})^*g_{Z_{24}^{\mathcal D}}
 =g_{C_T}^{\oplus4}.
 \hypertarget{tag-03CZ}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-BC-slice-exact}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \left(\Sigma_T^{12},\frac{T}{r_T}d_{T,12}^{\mathrm{slice}},
       p_T^{12}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^4,0),\\
 \left(\Sigma_T^{24,\mathcal D},
       \frac{\ell_T}{r_T}d_{T,24,\mathcal D}^{\mathrm{slice}},
       p_T^{24,\mathcal D}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^4,0)
 \hypertarget{tag-03DE}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-slice-fixed-blowups}
\end{align}
in pointed local-isometric and pointed Gromov--Hausdorff topology, and
smoothly on the exhausting Euclidean slice balls.

The full ambient pointed blow-ups are
\begin{align}
 \left(Z_{12},\frac{T}{r_T}D_{12},p_T^{12}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^8,0),\\
 \left(Z_{24}^{\mathcal D},
       \frac{\ell_T}{r_T}D_{24}^{\mathcal D},
       p_T^{24,\mathcal D}\right)
 &\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{12},0).
 \hypertarget{tag-03D3}{}\label{wb:sphere-metric-ambient-fixed-blowups}
\end{align}

precisely, for every fixed radius the corresponding rescaled target ball is
eventually contained in an open regular-stratum coordinate neighborhood,
and the pulled-back Riemannian tensors converge there in every \(C^k\) norm.
The smooth convergence uses an exhaustion by these regular-stratum
neighborhoods.  Under these limits, the slice \(\mathbb R^4\) is
respectively the coordinate subspace
obtained by fixing the two radial and two base-angle coordinates, or by
fixing the four radial and four base-angle coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write the period matrix on the radial locus as
\[
 Y_T=TJ+E(r_T),\qquad
 J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 E(t)=\begin{pmatrix}6m(t)&H(t)\\B(t)-H(t)&m(t)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The entries of \(E\) are the imaginary parts on the real \(t\)-axis of
the holomorphic residual functions.  They and all their derivatives of
each fixed order are bounded on the closed cusp interval.  Put
\(C_E=\sup_{0\leq t\leq r_0}\|E(t)\|\).  Since \(J\) is orthogonal,
\[
 (T-C_E)|v|\leq |Y_Tv|\leq(T+C_E)|v|.
\]
In particular \(T^{-2}h_T\) has coefficient matrix
\((J+E(r_T)/T)^{\mathsf T}(J+E(r_T)/T)\), which tends to \(I\).
Invertibility on the remaining compact part of the parameter interval
gives constants \(0<c_-\leq1\leq c_+\) such that
\[
 c_-|v|\leq |M(r)v|\leq c_+|v|,
 \qquad M(r):=J+\frac{E(r)}{T(r)},\quad 0<r\leq r_0.
\]
The exact quotient-circle formula also gives
\[
 \ell_T=\min_{z\in\mathbb R}|Y_T(1,z)|\geq T-C_E.
\]
Thus the shortest nonzero periods of \(Q_T^2\) and \(C_T^4\) tend to
infinity.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The factor metrics and their global extensions.}
On \(\mathcal A\) use
\[
 dr^2+r^2du^2+r^2dx^{\mathsf T}M(r)^{\mathsf T}M(r)dx
\]
for \(r\leq r_0\).  Extend its positive angular coefficient matrix
smoothly over the remainder of the cylinder up to \(r=\epsilon\),
keeping the radial summand \(dr^2\).  For example, continue it over a
short interval beyond \(r_0\) and take a fixed smooth convex combination
with a constant positive angular matrix, using a cutoff equal to one
on a neighborhood of the prescribed inner interval.  The choices are
made once and are independent of the slice parameter.

Complete this cylinder at \(r=0\), retaining its outer boundary torus.
The bounds for \(M(r)\) show that a level torus has diameter \(O(r)\).
A radial segment has length \(r\), and \(r\) is a \(1\)-Lipschitz
function.  Hence all sequences whose radii tend to zero converge to
one new point, uniformly in their angular coordinates; points whose
radii stay bounded below cannot converge to it.  Away from that point
the smooth tensor gives the usual cylinder topology.  These statements
identify the completion with the compact cone with its outer torus
retained.  Radial paths to its apex and approximating cylinder paths
show directly that its completed distance is a length metric.  Collapse
the outer torus to the other suspension pole, using the metric quotient
described below.  This gives the prescribed topology of \(\mathcal A\)
and its fixed factor distance \(d_{\mathcal A}\).

For \(\mathcal B\) use
\(dr^2+r^2(du^2+d\theta^2)\) on the whole open cylinder, add the
inner apex by completion, and collapse the outer torus to its separate
pole.  For \(\mathcal C\), give its attached cone the same tensor.
The boundary-coordinate map to \(\partial M=\partial D_0\times S^1\) is
\[
 \rho_0(z,[\theta])=(\epsilon z,e^{2\pi i\theta}),\qquad
 \rho_0^{-1}(p,w)
 =\left(p/\epsilon,\arg(w)/(2\pi)\bmod\mathbb Z\right).
\]
On a collar of its compact smooth core \(M\), with coordinate
\(\tau\geq0\) directed into the core, prescribe
\[
 d\tau^2+(\epsilon+\tau)^2(du^2+d\theta^2).
\]
Under \(r=\epsilon+\tau\), this matches the cone tensor and every
derivative at the boundary.  A fixed cutoff and convex combination with
a smooth positive tensor on the rest of \(M\) extend it over the core.
Completing at the inner apex gives the compact cone-attachment topology,
by the same radial and diameter estimates.  The tensor is smooth across
the attaching torus.

The radial function descends to each suspension and remains
\(1\)-Lipschitz after the outer collapse: a route through that pole
has length at least
\((\epsilon-r(x))+(\epsilon-r(y))\geq|r(x)-r(y)|\).
For \(\mathcal C\), extend \(r\) by the constant \(\epsilon\) on
the core.  The extension is \(1\)-Lipschitz, as follows by integrating
its derivative along each piece of a path.  Consequently, for every
cone point of each factor \(X\),
\[
 d_X(x_0,[r,a])=r.
\]
The radial path proves the upper bound and the radial function proves
the lower bound.  This equality holds on the entire prescribed interval,
including \(r=r_0\).  The same function bounds the distance from an
inner point to the outer pole or to the core below by \(\epsilon-r\).

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The smash metrics.}
For a compact length space \((P,d)\) and a closed subset \(F\) that
is collapsed to a point, the quotient distance is
\[
 D([x],[y])=\min\{d(x,y),d(x,F)+d(y,F)\},\qquad
 D([x],*)=d(x,F).
\]
To verify the triangle inequality, concatenate paths giving either
candidate for each successive pair.  A path that visits the collapsed
set has length at least the sum of its endpoint distances to that set;
a path that avoids it has length at least the direct distance.  Visits
after the first can be deleted.  Approximating the displayed candidates
by paths proves that the quotient is a length metric.  It is positive
between distinct classes because \(F\) is closed.  The quotient map
is continuous and \(1\)-Lipschitz, so the continuous bijection from
the compact topological quotient to this Hausdorff metric space is a
homeomorphism.  This also justifies the outer collapses used above.

Give \(P=X^n\) the product distance
\[
 d_P(x,y)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n d_X(x_i,y_i)^2.
\]
It is the length metric of the product tensor on the regular stratum:
the lower bound follows by integrating the vector of component speeds,
and the upper bound follows by traversing constant-speed minimizing
factor paths simultaneously.  Such minimizing paths exist in these
compact length spaces, by taking a uniformly convergent subsequence of
constant-speed paths whose lengths decrease to the distance and using
lower semicontinuity of length.

For the fat wedge \(F=\bigcup_i\{x_i=x_0\}\), the product formula
gives
\[
 d_P(x,F)=\min_i d_X(x_i,x_0).
\]
Replacing only a minimizing factor by \(x_0\) gives the upper bound,
and every point of \(F\) gives the matching lower bound.  Applying
the quotient formula defines \(D_{12},D_{24}^{\mathcal B},
D_{24}^{\mathcal C}\) with their prescribed compact topologies.
If \(d_P(x,F)=\delta>0\), two points in a product ball of radius
\(\eta<\delta/2\) about \(x\) have direct distance at most
\(2\eta\), whereas a route through \(F\) costs at least
\(2(\delta-\eta)>2\eta\).  Thus the quotient is locally isometric
to the product off the fat wedge.  Restricting also away from the factor
singularities gives exactly the regular tensors in the statement.

At each synchronized basepoint, the distance to the fat wedge is
\(r_T\).  Put
\[
 K=T\quad\hbox{for }Z_{12},\qquad
 K=\ell_T\quad\hbox{for }Z_{24}^{\mathcal D},\qquad
 \lambda=K/r_T.
\]
For \(K>R\), the rescaled smash \(R\)-ball is the image of the
product \(R/\lambda\)-ball, since a route from the basepoint through
the fat wedge already costs \(K\).  Points of this product ball have
distance at least \(r_T-R/\lambda\) from the fat wedge.  A route
between two of them through it therefore has rescaled length at least
\(2(K-R)\), whereas their direct rescaled product distance is at most
\(2R\).  For \(K>2R\) the quotient is an isometry on this whole ball.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The slice forms.}
The maps of Definition~\ref{wb:cusp-cone-target-slice-embeddings} are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 j_T(y_1,y_2)
 &=\bigl[[r_T,1,[Y_T^{-1}y_1]],
          [r_T,1,[Y_T^{-1}y_2]]\bigr]_{\wedge},\\
 k_T^{\mathcal B}(c_1,\ldots,c_4)
 &=\bigwedge_{i=1}^4[r_T,1,[c_i/\ell_T]],\\
 k_T^{\mathcal C}(c_1,\ldots,c_4)
 &=\bigwedge_{i=1}^4[r_T,(1,[c_i/\ell_T])].
\end{aligned}
\]
Replacing a real representative \(y_i\) by \(y_i+Y_Tn\), or
\(c_i\) by \(c_i+\ell_Tm\), changes its displayed angular
representative by \(n\in\mathbb Z^2\) or \(m\in\mathbb Z\).
Thus these formulas have exactly the quotient domains stated above.
The inverse on each image first takes the unique nonbasepoint product
representative and then applies \(\iota_T\) or \(\vartheta_T\) to
the displayed angular class.  In particular these are smooth embeddings
in the regular stratum.  On \(j_T\), \(dr=du=0\) and
\(dx=Y_T^{-1}dy\).  Its single-factor first fundamental form is
\[
 \frac{r_T^2}{T^2}
 dy^{\mathsf T}(Y_T^{-1})^{\mathsf T}Y_T^{\mathsf T}Y_TY_T^{-1}dy
 =\frac{r_T^2}{T^2}\,dy^{\mathsf T}dy.
\]
On \(k_T^{\mathcal D}\), \(d\theta=dc/\ell_T\) and
\(dr=du=0\), so its single-factor form is
\(r_T^2dc^2/\ell_T^2\).  Summing factors proves
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-A-slice-exact} and
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-BC-slice-exact}, including the exact equalities
of intrinsic path metrics with those of \(Q_T^2\) and \(C_T^4\).

For a fixed \(R\), the period bounds eventually make every nonzero
period longer than \(4R\).  For points of a Euclidean \(R\)-ball,
a translated difference then has norm at least
\(\operatorname{sys}-2R>2R\), while the direct difference has norm
at most \(2R\).  Thus the Euclidean quotient map is an isometry on
that whole ball.  Every point in the quotient \(R\)-ball has a
shortest representative in the Euclidean ball, since a lattice is
discrete.  Composing these onto isometries with the slice embeddings
proves all the intrinsic limits in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-slice-fixed-blowups}.  Their pullback tensors
are exactly Euclidean on each such ball.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The ambient coordinate maps and their derivatives.}
In an \(\mathcal A\)-factor use
\[
 \Phi_{\mathcal A,T}(a,b,\xi)
 =\left[r_T(1+a/T),e^{2\pi ib/T},[Y_T^{-1}\xi]\right],
 \qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^2,
\]
on the open domain
\[
 |a|<T/2,\qquad |b|<T/4,\qquad
 Y_T^{-1}\xi\in(-1/4,1/4)^2.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(T\), the radial interval is contained
in \((0,r_0)\).  The inverse takes the unique angular lifts in these
windows and sends a representative to
\[
 a=T(r/r_T-1),\qquad b=Tu_{\rm lift},\qquad
 \xi=Y_Tx_{\rm lift}.
\]
Both compositions are the identity.  Take the two-factor product of
these maps and compose with the smash quotient.  Its image is an open
regular coordinate neighborhood, since the quotient has singleton
classes and is open off the fat wedge.  The domains contain every fixed
Euclidean ball eventually, by the lower singular-value bound for
\(Y_T\).

Put
\[
 \alpha=1+a/T,\qquad
 \tau_T(a)=T-\frac{\log(1+a/T)}{2\pi},\qquad
 F_T(a)=\frac{T}{\tau_T(a)},\qquad
 U_T(a)=F_T(a)Y_{\tau_T(a)}Y_T^{-1}.
\]
The exact rescaled single-factor pullback is
\[
 \left(\frac{T}{r_T}\right)^2\Phi_{\mathcal A,T}^*g_{\mathcal A}
 =da^2+\alpha^2db^2
   +\alpha^2d\xi^{\mathsf T}U_T(a)^{\mathsf T}U_T(a)d\xi.
\]
At \(a=0\), \(U_T(0)=I\).  To control all derivatives, for
\(j\geq1\) compute
\[
 \tau_T^{(j)}(a)
 =\frac{(-1)^j(j-1)!}{2\pi(T+a)^j},\qquad
 e^{-2\pi\tau_T(a)}=r_T(1+a/T),
\]
and
\[
 \frac{d^j}{da^j}E(r_T(1+a/T))
 =\left(\frac{r_T}{T}\right)^j E^{(j)}(r_T(1+a/T)).
\]
On each fixed interval \(|a|\leq L\),
\(\tau_T-T=O_L(T^{-1})\) and \(F_T-1=O_L(T^{-2})\).
Differentiating \(F_T\tau_T=T\) gives the recurrence
\[
 F_T^{(j)}
 =-\frac{1}{\tau_T}
   \sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\binom ji F_T^{(i)}\tau_T^{(j-i)},
\]
so induction yields \(F_T^{(j)}=O_{L,j}(T^{-j-1})\).  The matrix
identity
\[
 U_T(a)-I
 =\bigl[F_T(a)E(r_T(1+a/T))-E(r_T)\bigr]Y_T^{-1}
\]
and \(\|Y_T^{-1}\|\leq(T-C_E)^{-1}\) now show that
\(U_T\to I\) in every \(C^k\) norm on fixed intervals.  In fact,
for each fixed \(k\) the derivatives of order at most \(k\) of
\(U_T-I\) are \(O_{L,k}(T^{-3}+r_T/T^2)\).  This follows from
the residual chain rule, the bounded derivatives of \(E\), and the
recurrence just displayed.  It also gives
\(Y_{\tau_T(a)}Y_T^{-1}=I+O(T^{-2})\), with the same upper order
after every fixed number of derivatives.  Thus the two-factor rescaled
tensors converge in every \(C^k\) norm on bounded coordinate sets to
the Euclidean tensor of \(\mathbb R^8\).

For \(\mathcal D=\mathcal B,\mathcal C\) put \(K=\ell_T\) and use
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Phi_{\mathcal B,T}(a,b,\xi)
 &= [r_T(1+a/K),e^{2\pi ib/K},[\xi/K]],\\
 \Phi_{\mathcal C,T}(a,b,\xi)
 &= [r_T(1+a/K),(e^{2\pi ib/K},[\xi/K])]
\end{aligned}
\]
on \(|a|<K/2\), \(|b|<K/4\), \(|\xi|<K/4\).  The inverse reads
the unique lifts and sets \(a=K(r/r_T-1)\), \(b=Ku\),
\(\xi=K\theta\).  The boundary coordinate in the second line is
carried to \(\partial M\) by \(\rho_0\).  The exact pullback is
\[
 \left(\frac{\ell_T}{r_T}\right)^2
 \Phi_{\mathcal D,T}^*g_{\mathcal D}
 =da^2+(1+a/K)^2(db^2+d\xi^2).
\]
Its four-factor sum converges in every \(C^k\) norm on each bounded
coordinate set to the Euclidean tensor of \(\mathbb R^{12}\).
At \(a=b=0\), the coordinates \(\xi\) in all these charts are
exactly the physical flat coordinates of the slices.  Hence their
products identify the limiting slice with the stated coordinate
subspace in each ambient Euclidean space.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Whole ambient balls and their distances.}
In each factor consider the unscaled window
\[
 r_T/2<r<3r_T/2,\quad |u_{\rm lift}|<1/4,
\]
together with \(|x_{{\rm lift},j}|<1/4\) for \(\mathcal A\), or
\(|\theta_{\rm lift}|<1/4\) for \(\mathcal B,\mathcal C\).
A path from the center that leaves this window either reaches a
radial boundary, costing at least \(r_T/2\), or first reaches an
angular boundary while its radius is at least \(r_T/2\).  The latter
costs at least \(c_*r_T/8\), where \(c_*=\min(1,c_-)\), because
the variation of one lifted angle is at least \(1/4\).
Thus, with \(\rho=\min(1/2,c_*/8)>0\), every exit costs at least
\(\rho r_T\).  This estimate also applies to a path that subsequently
reaches a cone point, an outer pole or the core: it first leaves this
window.  Factor projections are \(1\)-Lipschitz for the product
distance, and the alternative quotient route through the fat wedge
costs \(r_T\).  Therefore the rescaled distance from \(p_T\) to
the complement of the product coordinate neighborhood is at least
\(\rho K\).

In particular every fixed rescaled \(R\)-ball is contained in the
open regular chart for all large \(T\).  The factor distances to
the inward vertex and the level \(r_0\) are respectively \(r_T\)
and \(r_0-r_T\), by the radial function and radial paths.  Their
rescaled values are
\[
 K\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 K\left(\frac{r_0}{r_T}-1\right)\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
The angular period lattices in the displayed coordinates are
\(T\mathbb Z\oplus Y_T\mathbb Z^2\) and
\(\ell_T\mathbb Z^2\); their least nonzero Euclidean lengths are
at least \(T-C_E\) and equal to \(\ell_T\), respectively.
The exit estimate above controls paths that vary their radii while
moving in these angular directions.

A minimizing path between two points of a rescaled \(R\)-ball has
length at most \(2R\), and all its points lie in the rescaled
\(3R\)-ball.  For \(\rho K>3R\) it stays in the regular chart.
On the large chart windows, \(1/2<\alpha<3/2\), and for the
\(\mathcal A\) tensor \(\tau_T=T+O(1)\).  For all large \(T\),
\[
 \sigma_{\min}(U_T)
 \geq\frac{T}{T+C_E}\left(1-\frac{C_E}{\tau_T}\right)
 \geq\frac14,\qquad
 \|U_T\|\leq\frac{T}{T-C_E}
                   \left(1+\frac{C_E}{\tau_T}\right)\leq3.
\]
The convenient common estimates for all three rescaled product tensors
are consequently
\[
 \frac18|v|\leq\sqrt{g_T(v,v)}\leq5|v|.
\]
Apply the lower bound to a minimizing origin path to a point of the
\(3R\)-ball.  Its coordinate length is at most \(24R\).
Thus the \(R\)-ball has coordinates in the Euclidean \(8R\)-ball,
and every minimizing path between its points stays in the Euclidean
\(24R\)-ball.

Choose \(0<\varepsilon_T<1/2\), tending to zero, so that the
rescaled norms on the fixed coordinate ball of radius \(24R+1\)
are between \((1-\varepsilon_T)|v|\) and
\((1+\varepsilon_T)|v|\).  A minimizing path gives the lower bound
below, and the
straight coordinate segment gives the upper bound:
\[
 (1-\varepsilon_T)|z-w|
 \leq\lambda D(\Phi_Tz,\Phi_Tw)
 \leq(1+\varepsilon_T)|z-w|
\]
for points in the target \(R\)-ball.  The origin comparison also gives
\[
 B_{R/(1+\varepsilon_T)}(0)
 \subset\Phi_T^{-1}(B_R(p_T;\lambda D))
 \subset B_{R/(1-\varepsilon_T)}(0).
\]
Radial projection of the middle set to the Euclidean \(R\)-ball
changes coordinates by \(O_R(\varepsilon_T)\), has distortion
\(O_R(\varepsilon_T)\), and has
\(O_R(\varepsilon_T)\)-dense image.  These maps prove the pointed
Gromov--Hausdorff limits of the whole target balls in
\eqref{wb:sphere-metric-ambient-fixed-blowups}.  The coordinate domains
exhaust their Euclidean spaces, their images contain every fixed
rescaled target ball eventually, and their pulled-back tensors converge
in all \(C^k\) norms.  This proves the stated smooth exhaustion.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Intrinsic and ambient paths on the slices.}
Inclusion of a slice preserves the length of every path it contains.
Taking infima over slice paths and over all ambient paths proves the
two distance inequalities in the statement.  Their strictness can be
seen directly.  In a \(\mathcal B\)- or \(\mathcal C\)-factor,
keep \(u=0\) and take character-angle endpoints \(0,\delta\), with
\(0<\delta<1/2\), at radius \(r_T\).  The map
\[
 (r,\theta)\longmapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)
\]
pulls the Euclidean tensor back to \(dr^2+r^2d\theta^2\) on this
sector.  The straight chord lifts to a cone path with radius between
\(r_T\cos(\delta/2)\) and \(r_T\), and has length
\[
 2r_T\sin(\delta/2)<r_T\delta.
\]
The right side is the intrinsic slice distance.  Holding the other
three factors fixed gives the strict inequality in each smash target.

For \(\mathcal A\) put \(G(r)=r^2M(r)^{\mathsf T}M(r)\).
Differentiation gives
\[
 rM'(r)=\frac{rE'(r)}{T(r)}+\frac{E(r)}{2\pi T(r)^2},\qquad
 r^{-1}G'(r)
 =2M^{\mathsf T}M+(rM')^{\mathsf T}M+M^{\mathsf T}(rM')
 \longrightarrow2I.
\]
Thus \(G'(r)\) is positive definite for every sufficiently small
positive \(r\).  Take such \(r_T\), with \(T-C_E>4\), and set
\(v=Y_T^{-1}(1,0)\).  The physical segment \(Y_Tsv=s(1,0)\)
is minimizing on the flat torus: every nonzero translated difference
has norm at least \(T-C_E-1>3\).  Choose a smooth nonnegative function
\(f\), supported in \((0,1)\) and positive somewhere.  The path
\[
 s\longmapsto[r_T-hf(s),1,[sv]],\qquad 0\leq s\leq1,
\]
stays in the cone for small \(h>0\) and has energy
\[
 \mathcal E(h)
 =\int_0^1\bigl(h^2f'(s)^2+v^{\mathsf T}G(r_T-hf(s))v\bigr)\,ds.
\]
Its derivative at zero is
\[
 \mathcal E'(0)
 =-\left(\int_0^1f(s)\,ds\right)v^{\mathsf T}G'(r_T)v<0.
\]
The unperturbed energy is the square of the intrinsic slice distance.
The perturbed path has length at most \(\sqrt{\mathcal E(h)}\),
which is strictly smaller for small \(h>0\).  Keeping the other
factor fixed proves strictness on \(\Sigma_T^{12}\).

On every bounded physical slice-coordinate set, the intrinsic rescaled
distance is eventually exactly Euclidean.  Restricting the ambient
distance estimates to \(a=b=0\) shows that its rescaled ambient
distance tends uniformly to the same Euclidean distance.  The whole
ambient-restricted slice \(R\)-ball lies in that coordinate subspace
by the chart-exit bound.  Intersecting the ball inclusions above with
the subspace proves its pointed Gromov--Hausdorff limit as well.
\end{proof}

The metrics on the smash powers are the metric quotients of the product

\begin{proof}
Write the period matrix on the radial locus as
\[
 Y_T=TJ+E(r_T),\qquad
 J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 E(t)=\begin{pmatrix}6m(t)&H(t)\\B(t)-H(t)&m(t)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The entries of \(E\) are the imaginary parts on the real \(t\)-axis of
the holomorphic residual functions.  They and all their derivatives of
each fixed order are bounded on the closed cusp interval.  Put
\(C_E=\sup_{0\leq t\leq r_0}\|E(t)\|\).  Since \(J\) is orthogonal,
\[
 (T-C_E)|v|\leq |Y_Tv|\leq(T+C_E)|v|.
\]
In particular $T^{-2}h_T$ has coefficient matrix
$(J+E(r_T)/T)^{\mathsf T}(J+E(r_T)/T)$, which tends to $I$.
These coefficients are constant in the fixed torus coordinates, so
the convergence holds in every $C^k$ norm.
Invertibility on the remaining compact part of the parameter interval
gives constants \(0<c_-\leq1\leq c_+\) such that
\[
 c_-|v|\leq |M(r)v|\leq c_+|v|,
 \qquad M(r):=J+\frac{E(r)}{T(r)},\quad 0<r\leq r_0.
\]
The exact quotient-circle formula also gives
\[
 \ell_T=\min_{z\in\mathbb R}|Y_T(1,z)|\geq T-C_E.
\]
Thus the shortest nonzero periods of \(Q_T^2\) and \(C_T^4\) tend to
infinity.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The factor metrics and their global extensions.}
On \(\mathcal A\) use
\[
 dr^2+r^2du^2+r^2dx^{\mathsf T}M(r)^{\mathsf T}M(r)dx
\]
for \(r\leq r_0\).  Extend its positive angular coefficient matrix
smoothly over the remainder of the cylinder up to \(r=\epsilon\),
keeping the radial summand \(dr^2\).  For example, continue it over a
short interval beyond \(r_0\) and take a fixed smooth convex combination
with a constant positive angular matrix, using a cutoff equal to one
on a neighborhood of the prescribed inner interval.  The choices are
made once and are independent of the slice parameter.

Complete this cylinder at \(r=0\), retaining its outer boundary torus.
The bounds for \(M(r)\) show that a level torus has diameter \(O(r)\).
A radial segment has length \(r\), and \(r\) is a \(1\)-Lipschitz
function.  Hence all sequences whose radii tend to zero converge to
one new point, uniformly in their angular coordinates; points whose
radii stay bounded below cannot converge to it.  Away from that point
the smooth tensor gives the usual cylinder topology.  These statements
identify the completion with the compact cone with its outer torus
retained.  Radial paths to its apex and approximating cylinder paths
show directly that its completed distance is a length metric.  Collapse
the outer torus to the other suspension pole, using the metric quotient
described below.  This gives the prescribed topology of \(\mathcal A\)
and its fixed factor distance \(d_{\mathcal A}\).

For \(\mathcal B\) use
\(dr^2+r^2(du^2+d\theta^2)\) on the whole open cylinder, add the
inner apex by completion, and collapse the outer torus to its separate
pole.  For \(\mathcal C\), give its attached cone the same tensor.
The boundary-coordinate map to \(\partial M=\partial D_0\times S^1\) is
\[
 \rho_0(z,[\theta])=(\epsilon z,e^{2\pi i\theta}),\qquad
